#3561. Why Princess Diana Dressed William and Harry Identically, Even Though They Didn’t Like It

Princess Diana had a keen sense of style. It was a talent the late princess (who arrived at court at a very young age and was therefore still unfamiliar with the ins and outs of high fashion) developed over the years with the help of experts in the field—and which has repeatedly earned her the title of style icon.

It comes as no surprise, then, that her keen eye for new trends and her passion for the most sought-after pieces were also reflected in the fashion choices she made for her two children, Prince William and Prince Harry, whom she loved to dress alike from a very young age, no matter the occasion.

Prince Charles and Princess Diana with their sons, William and Harry. July 1986.

Princess Diana, it must be said, was neither the first nor the last mother to choose identical outfits for her children, but it seems this habit was not merely a fashion game. According to a report by Marie Claire, the princess’s former butler, Paul Burrell, reportedly said that Diana’s choice to dress William and Harry identically was a way to reinforce the idea that, in her eyes, there was no difference between the two—even though everyone around her showed preferential treatment toward the eldest son, the future heir to the throne.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. August 1986.

That’s why the princess waged her own battle, even choosing to dress her two sons in matching outfits, almost as if to convey a sense of unity and equality in their appearance. If these were indeed some of the reasons behind the brothers’ identical looks, it certainly wouldn’t be surprising. We know full well how Diana insisted on equal treatment for her two sons, who, for their part, apparently didn’t much care for their mother’s tendency to choose identical outfits. “The boys hated that, by the way; they didn’t want to be dressed the same,” Burrell added.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. July 1988.

This statement has also been confirmed by Prince Harry himself. In the 2017 television documentary, Diana, Our Mother: Her Life and Legacy, which aired on the 20th anniversary of Princess Diana’s death, her two sons spoke openly about their mother. The younger son said with a smile: “I genuinely think she got satisfaction out of dressing myself and William up in the most bizarre outfits—normally matching. It was weird shorts and little shiny shoes with the old clip-on.”

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. August 1989.

Bermuda shorts and patent leather shoes with straps—all the rage in the ’80s and ’90s—were, in fact, two of the key elements of the outfits Diana put together for her boys. The lineup also included matching shirts, polos, and sweaters. “Looking back at the photos, it just makes me laugh, and I think, ‘How could you do that to us?’” Harry added with a touch of irony.

As they grew up, the two, of course, began to rebel against this tradition—particularly William, who, according to Harry’s account, at one point refused to have anything to do with being his brother’s twin. “Funnily enough, we got to the age when William would turn round and go: ‘Oh, this is ridiculous. You know, I’m the older brother. Why do I have to be dressed the same as him?’” he recalled. “Hang on a second. If you’re going to dress differently, I’m not going to be the only person dressed like this. This is just ridiculous!” Harry replied.

As with any growing boy, things gradually began to change, and the two brothers started to develop their own independent style. But one can’t help but pause to consider how every choice—even the most trivial, like picking out an outfit—was a statement of intent for the beloved princess. Always in the name of love.

Prince Charles and Princess Diana with their sons, William and Harry. December 1986.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. July 1988.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. June 1987.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. October 1990.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. May 1992.

Princess Diana with her sons, William and Harry. August 1995.

#3559. James Gunn's DC Universe Is Being 'Dismantled' As DC Studios Prepares Another Reset (Report)

These DC reboots are starting to become a bit of a tradition. In the wake of James Gunn and Peter Safran "stepping down" as DC Studios co-heads, it seems the new guard is ready to tear down almost their entire cinematic project. At least, according to a new report.

Puck's Matthew Belloni claims to have heard that "plans are already afoot" for new DC Studios head Jeremy Latcham — who steps into the role of president and chief creative officer of DC Studios as of December 1, 2026 — to scrap almost everything Gunn and Safran had planned post-"Man of Tomorrow," "The Batman: Part II," and an unnamed HBO series. As Belloni put it, "So DC goes back into reboot mode ... again."

This is the second major reset for DC's cinematic enterprise (third if you count the pre and post-Walter Hamada era), and it frankly seems like a dire state of affairs. When Gunn and Safran were brought in to head up the newly-christened DC Studios back in 2022, they had grand plans to revive the franchise following a disappointing end to the DC Extended Universe or "Snyderverse." This was supposed to be the moment DC turned things around and finally matched Marvel's cinematic success with an ambitious shared universe. Now, it's all come to a premature end as Skydance CEO David Ellison (who now oversees the newly merged Paramount and Warner Bros.) seemingly prepares to take a wrecking ball to Gunn and Safran's still fledgling DC Universe.

In his article, Matthew Belloni noted how James Gunn and Peter Safran reported to the Warner Bros. Discovery CEO, a post previously held by David Zaslav. The erstwhile head of Warners seemed perfectly happy to let his newly appointed DC Studios co-heads take full creative control. But, as Belloni noted, "Maybe it was too much freedom... hence 'Supergirl.'"

This is, of course, a reference to the box office flop that was this year's "Supergirl," a solo outing for Milly Alcock's Kara Zor-El that brought in just $126.5 million at the box office against a $170 million budget. And while /Film's own "Supergirl" review argued the movie has an aspirational and uplifting message and is nowhere near as bad as its box office returns may suggest, Belloni opined that David Ellison no doubt viewed the failure of "Supergirl" as a result of Gunn and Safran being given too much creative power. Hence, that simply won't be the case with Ellison now in charge.

This also means that while Jeremy Latcham is replacing the former DC Studios co-bosses, he will have nowhere near as much freedom and instead report only to Skydance studio heads Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein. Depending on how you felt about Gunn's creative decisions, then, this is either a good or disappointing development. But even if you like the idea of Ellison and his studio heads calling the shots and keeping DC on a tight leash, none of this bodes well for the brand's cinematic fortunes moving forward — especially if Ellison and co. really do intend to discard Gunn's entire DC roadmap and start from scratch.

When James Gunn and Peter Safran were appointed co-heads of DC Studios, the franchise desperately needed a hard reset. A string of flops in 2023, which included the box office bomb of superheroic proportions that was "The Flash" (a movie which, as it happens, Gunn once called "probably one of the greatest superhero movies ever made"), marked an ignoble end for the DC Extended Universe, and it was Gunn's job to reset, regroup, and revitalize the entire thing. Instead, he opted for a soft reboot that retained several elements of the DCEU. Even at the time, it seemed misguided, and it feels like all the more of a misstep in hindsight.

Now, David Ellison and his executives are, according to Puck, rebooting the entire thing. But it seems like it's all too late. Audiences were never going to be won over by animated "Creature Commandos" series or a potential Mister Miracle animated show. By all means, take a few risks, but maybe save them for after DC has regained some respect among mainstream viewers. Instead, we're at a point where the whole thing is being scrapped yet again, and most people simply do not care about these behind the scenes developments. They just want good movies (which, at this point, have been in short supply).

As Matthew Belloni observed in his report, the last decade has really "only solidified Kevin Feige's run at Marvel [Studios] as all the more remarkable" when compared to DC's struggles. Of course, with Jeremy Latcham having spent many years as a Marvel Studios producer, there's a chance he might turn things around. But by now, audiences are surely tired of having to keep up with these reboots, soft or otherwise.

It's an exciting time in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. What we know about Avengers: Doomsday is limited, so there are countless fans and theories about what The Russo Brothers might have up their sleeve. In a clip from ET's Twitter, Mackie spoke about the experience of shooting the mysterious blockbuster offering:

These movies, they're like summer camp. You know, everybody comes together. And it's 'Oh how have you been? Oh, you have a kid now. Oh you're married now.' It's one of those things where you catch up with everybody. I got to hang out with Paul Bettany, who I love.

If Mackie's comments are to be believed, we should expect to see Paul Bettany appear. But considering how many characters he's portrayed in the shared universe, there's no guarantee he'll actually be Vision. My head is truly spinning from all the possibilities.

#3557. No Reservations: Jessica Craig-Martin Serves Up a Rowdy, Inside Account of ’80s Indochine

No one is famous when they are at home. In New York in 1984, all it took to be famous was to leave the house with intent to commit fame. Beautiful youths were shot through the fame cannon at a rate that made Warhol’s fifteen minutes seem like a century. A cloud of new money hovered over the city, ominously gathering dollars, dropping sudden fortunes on those who knew how to make it rain. No veneer of philanthropy was needed to whitewash the excesses of the wealthy. Conspicuous consumption was the new normal. The new designer clothes all had giant shoulder pads. So did the buildings. The thick-walleted and soft-bellied moved around the city at night in chauffeur-driven carapaces. Eurotrash was the latest import. Fast-talking cocaine replaced nodding-out heroin. The words supermodel and art star fell from heavily glossed lips. Everyone wanted to see and be seen. But where? Studio 54 was closed, disco was dead. Brian McNally’s new restaurant, Indochine, was poised to become the epicenter of ’80s decadence.

Jessica and another waitress with Rupert E at Indochine, 1986.

Waitressing seemed like the best way to make money. I’d met Brian while traveling with the Mardens in France, and he’d mentioned he was opening a restaurant. I had left New York as a hip urban waif with short dark hair and pale skin. I returned curvy and brown-skinned, with long hair that had turned blond in the sun. I wore no makeup and had no interest in fashion, feeling I’d done all that as a teen. I wore vintage ’40s dresses from flea markets, and plastic jelly sandals. When I dropped by 420 Lafayette to ask for a job, Brian looked me up and down and gave me a sly wink. “Yeah, you’ll do.” The question of waitressing experience did not come up.

On opening day, I arrived to find the staff running around frantically with hammers and paintbrushes; stenciling palm leaves on the walls; putting up wallpaper; accepting deliveries of banana trees, ducks, orchids, MSG, and Champagne. There was no way in hell we were going to be ready. I grabbed a brush.

Indochine opened that night, walls still wet, with a private party for Julian Schnabel’s opening at the Mary Boone Gallery. Art dealer Pat Hearn sang Patsy Cline songs wearing a tight 1950s gold brocade dress. Warhol superstar, writer, and genius-about-town Taylor Mead got up on a table to give a hilarious impromptu speech. The crowd danced all night. With one private event after another, opening night lasted a month.

Brian was truly brilliant with people. He made everyone feel like they were in the right place at the right time, and that they were clever, sexy, witty, charming, or all of the above. He was just as comfortable with Henry Geldzahler as he was with Madonna. He could converse on any topic and did so with an easy British charm and lack of pretension that disarmed even the worst snobs.

Moira Hodgson gave us two stars, but other critics found the food “rather ordinary” or “unspectacular,” and everyone agreed that the service was appalling. Ironically, as Brian pointed out later, this became part of the charm of the place. Brian had a strict policy of never refusing a reservation, no matter how overbooked we were. He knew the frenzy at the bar and long waits for booked tables only increased our status as the most sought-after restaurant in town.

When Brian told me my shirt was wrinkled, I said, “Brian, chill out. This is linen. It’s supposed to be wrinkled.” In fact, the shirt could have done with a quick press, but I had only one white shirt and no intention of buying an iron or paying for dry cleaning. Fortunately the waitstaff started to add increased personal touches to the black-and-white dress code until it disappeared. Brian stopped objecting when he saw that the stylish staff was becoming one of the draws of the place. Soon most of us were unrecognizable as waitstaff, leading to many a black-suited banker being called upon for drinks or the check while navigating his way to the bathroom.

Taylor Mead became a nightly fixture at the bar, offering brilliant quips while dining on Dewar’s. Larissa slept on her barstool, her lit cigarette in an elegantly raised hand until someone said, “Larissa!” causing her to reanimate and flick her ash while shouting: “Dahhhh-ling!” She was a movie star who didn’t need movies. If Larissa came to Indochine to sleep, John F. Kennedy Jr. and Daryl Hannah came to break up and reunite, using the vestibule to break up and the bathroom for make-up sex. Carol Channing brought her own silver. Dolly Parton brought her own food. She was on a raw-vegetable and booze diet: “Just gimme the most expensive bottle in the house, honey.” Bianca Jagger ordered her meals in one low, unsmiling breath: “Steamed vegetables no soy sauce no hot sauce no sugar no salt no MSG.” What she didn’t know was that in the kitchen there were three tubs of white powder that went into every single dish: salt, sugar, and MSG.

Dead-eyed debutantes danced in their Manolo’s on tables strewn with platters of spicy beef salad, celebrating an addition to the Guinness dynasty. I wouldn't start using a camera for another eight years, but my mother says Indochine is where I became a photographer.

One night Lena Horne spat her gum directly into my hand. “Gum,” she’d said, after beckoning me over, after which I’d instinctively put my hand out. I gave it to my boyfriend Nick for his birthday. A strand of Cindy Crawford’s hair was the following year’s gift. (We never did get around to cloning her.) Saturday nights were Bridge and Tunnel. I opened the bathroom door to find a woman in high-heeled white boots giving a blowjob to some guy, his soft leather pants around his ankles. Laurie Anderson and I waited to pee while they finished. After that we referred to Saturdays as “White Boot Nights.” Warren Beatty leaned casually against a column, asking a waitress, “You’re a dancer, right? I can see the dance in your body.” A few months later, there he was, leaning against the column again. He asked the same waitress, Robin, “You’re a dancer, right?” Robert De Niro would sit at the end of the bar checking out the scene. Then he’d leave and call the restaurant from his idling limo. He’d ask the maître d’ to tell a woman he found attractive that he was on the phone. Sometimes women simply left their dates mid-meal to join him. One night the Beastie Boys brought a homeless man to dinner who’d asked them if they could spare some change. Even the odd exiled dictator made an appearance. The shah of Iran booked one table for himself and his wife, and three for his bodyguards. I noted their ankle holsters.

The waitstaff was made up of ambitious, creative young New Yorkers. Among them were Fidel Márquez, a painter; Masha Calloway, a fashion designer; and Darrell Maupin, who would open his own successful restaurant, Flamingo East. They and Robin Renzi, the dancer, became my close friends. Robin would later launch the jewelry line Me&Ro with Michelle Quan, who left Indochine for a modeling career. All I had going on outside of work were drawing classes at the New York Academy of Art a few days a week. I had not yet located any particular ambition. I went for dinner with friends, danced all night, and had sex all day. I remember being furious with Brian for a remark he made when I arrived at work: “You look like you just got fucked all day.” I was outraged, but it occurred to me later that he was absolutely right.

There was an ecstasy dealer who took to dropping by the restaurant around midnight. We’d take the pills toward the end of our shifts, hoping no customers would linger too long. After work we’d head to the clubs, needing catharsis and easily spending the money we had just spent hours earning. The Sisyphean irony of this went unnoticed. I was amused to discover that working at Indochine had a certain cachet. Waiters and waitresses were swept past the velvet ropes into all the clubs. I was initially surprised by the mini celebrity status conferred by waiting tables, but it says a lot about the era, which was all about tipping status on its head. Julian Schnabel was flipping burgers ten minutes before he became famous overnight with his broken-plate paintings. With his sensational-looking wife, Jacqueline, on his arm and New York at his feet, he seemed to be starring in his own biopic as he swept into Indochine night after night. “Jessica, get yourself a glass—have some of this Cristal,” he would say with a beneficent wave of his arm. It was the only restaurant in town where you could see Madonna, Sean Penn, Chris Walken, and Andy Warhol in one booth, John Waters and Divine in the next, and Henry Kissinger and his wife having a quiet dinner in another.

A certain high-powered lawyer was easily the restaurant’s most repugnant client, a considerable achievement. On one occasion he was approached by his waitress, Demetrious, a Black, bald, and beautiful torch singer who always wore huge brass earrings in the shape of Africa.

“Can I offer you something from the bar?” she asked him.

“Yes. I would like a different waitress,” he told her without looking up. She ignored him, went away, and returned calmly.

“I already told you, I want another fucking waitress,” he spat.

She shrugged. “I’m your waitress. I guess you’ll just have to deal with it.”

“GET THE FUCK AWAY FROM ME YOU UGLY BLACK BALD BITCH!”

She leaned in. “Sitthefuckdownandshutthefuckupyoudumbwhite-muthafucka,” she said in one breath. Beaten, he sat. I begged Brian to ban him, but Demetrious just shrugged it off. She was used to fighting her own battles and had already moved on.

At first, I was shocked by the overtly sexist behavior and banter at the restaurant. In the art world men did not compare the sex appeal of women in the presence of other women—or to their faces. There was rampant sexism and misogyny in the art world, of course, but it was generally more institutional and less visible to the naked eye. Men in the art world were less likely to openly grab one’s ass, or to make saliva-drenched comments about the run in your stockings inspiring in them an urge to bend you over a table. The art world had its share of knuckle-draggers—but the likelihood of being kneed in the balls by the objects of their desire kept them somewhat held in check. The women who raised me considered that feminism had “worked.” Their very existence was proof. No one thought the work was over—the ERA had failed to pass, after all—but the essential equality of women was beyond question, and the idea of acting coyly around men was considered absurd. However, the liberation train I’d been raised on had not reached restaurant culture. I was shocked to see so many women pushing out their tits, wiggling and giggling for their power-suited dates. Ironically, I’d been sheltered by my avant-garde upbringing.

I met Huy Chi Le on my first shift at Indochine. He was my age and had just arrived in New York from Vietnam. He spoke almost no English. Huy worked six nights a week at Indochine and seven days at another restaurant, working twice the number of hours to make the same amount of money as a waiter. When Huy was promoted at both venues to waiter, he kept both jobs, still taking just a half day off a week. He sent funds to his family and saved the rest. He established credit, obtaining an Amex gold card while we waiters were living out of tip envelopes and dancing all night. He bought a house in Brooklyn and sponsored his family to come over one by one. By the time Brian was ready to sell, Huy was poised to buy. He is now the owner of several businesses, a multimillionaire, and—with former manager Michael Callahan and former waiter Jean-Marc Houmard—co-owner of the still incredibly popular, and now legendary Indochine.

From I REGRET I AM ABLE TO ATTEND: A Life Among Artists by Jessica Craig-Martin, to be published on November 10th, 2026, by Random House, a division of Penguin Random House, LLC. Copyright (c) 2026 by Jessica Craig-Martin.

#3556. If You Loved 'Below,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Foggy, cold, and hardscrabble, the community of Snook’s Arm, Newfoundland, is the perfect spot for ocean-borne horror in Netflix's Below. This sense of place sets the series apart, though the characters who inhabit it are equally fascinating. Led by Josh Hartnett’s grounded performance as Calvin, the show has atmosphere for days, and a creepy and compelling story that effortlessly balances chills and deep emotional beats.

If you ate this show up like a voracious sea creature and you’re craving more slow-burn, deeply human horror (and you’ve already explored all the similar streaming series out there), it’s time to move on to feature-length terror, and there's one classic movie that fits the bill.

When it comes to kindred sea monster stories, Jaws is the obvious choice. Seaside setting? Check—a pre-glam Martha’s Vineyard stands in for Amity Island, with beautiful beaches and crashing waves to spare. A tight community under threat? Check—Amity Island feels like a very real place, and its citizens have concerns and grudges as legitimate as Calvin’s in Below. Shocks and frights? This is Jaws, a film that transformed the entire business of blockbuster movies, renowned to this day for its masterful depiction of a relentless natural force threatening an entire town.

The basic story also echoes Below's: When a young woman is killed by a shark during a night swim, Amity Island Police Chief Martin Brody (Roy Scheider) tries to close the beaches to protect the public, but Mayor Vaughn (Murray Hamilton) refuses, as Amity Island depends on the tourist trade for its survival. After a young boy is killed, Brody teams up with shark hunter Quint (Robert Shaw) and oceanographer Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss) to hunt the beast, and the three soon find themselves in over their heads as they discover how big and relentless the shark really is. Both stories share themes of economic necessity trumping safety in a changing world and concepts of a small group of people fighting a terrifying natural threat.

Like almost every horror film or series since 1975, Below owes a debt to Jaws in terms of storytelling and technique. From the isolated, ocean-centric setting (and monster) to the way Below shows you only flashes of its central terror, if you enjoyed the series, you will absolutely love the classic that influenced it. Stream Jaws on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

Already seen Jaws, or rewatched it, and still in need of more terrifying movies in the same vein as Below? Here are a few more movies that you’ll love.

The Bay takes a different approach to its scares than Below—it’s a found-footage horror film. But it shares the remote, water-centric setting, the focus on a small community, and a story that pulls from the terror of a fundamental element—water—being polluted and corrupted. In the coastal community of Claridge, Maryland, citizens fall severely ill and begin dying in large numbers, sparking chaos. As investigators race to discover the source of the affliction, the carnage gets seriously gnarly. Just like in Below, the ultimate threat stems from the way people recklessly abuse the world we depend on for survival, and the local residents are center stage in the fight. Stream The Bay on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

One aspect of Below that resonates strongly with viewers is the human element; the Penney family’s internal tensions feel earned and real, and the way the larger community struggles with several existential crises is messy in a gloriously human way. The Host is also about a family struggling against a horrific, waterborne monster—when a mutant creature attacks a crowd near the Han River, Park Gang-du loses his grip on his young daughter, and she’s snatched up by the monster. But when Gang-du receives a phone call from his daughter telling him she’s still alive but trapped with the creature in the sewers, his family escapes quarantine, gears up, and goes after her, no matter the odds (or the corrupt government agencies standing in the way). Stream The Host on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Based on H.P. Lovecraft’s The Shadow Over Innsmouth, Dagon begins with four friends on a boat off the coast of Spain. When a storm wrecks the boat and injures one of them, a couple—Paul and Barbara—travel on foot to a nearby village to seek help. What they find instead is a terrifying place paying the price for worshiping a demon named Dagon in exchange for wealth and safety—but at a price that slowly rose, eventually transforming the villagers into something inhuman. Just like Below, the movie explores the choices communities make to survive, and the personal costs that aren’t always clearly understood. Stream Dagon on The Roku Channel or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you loved Below’s foggy, liminal feel and the constant dread of what might be lurking in the mist or under the waves, unseen until it’s too late, John Carpenter’s classic is a must-watch. As the small coastal town of Antonio Bay approaches the centennial of its founding, a strange fog rolls in from the sea and envelopes the town. As the body count rises, the true story of the town’s founding and subsequent prosperity is revealed—and the long-deferred price for the crimes of the town’s ancestors is in the fog, determined to find some element of justice. Stream The Fog on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

If remote communities like Snook’s Arm are inherently creepy to you, check out Offseason. When Marie (Jocelin Donahue) learns that her mother has passed away and has been buried in Lone Palm, the isolated beach town where she grew up, she’s outraged—her mother was very clear that she didn’t want to be buried there. Marie travels to Lone Palm as tourist season ends, just a day before the bridge to the mainland closes for the year, which gives the town a liminal, nightmarish aspect familiar to anyone who’s lived in a tourist town during the offseason. As a storm moves in, Marie and her boyfriend find the townsfolk behaving quite strangely—and soon, it all whips up into a maelstrom of terror that fans of Below will appreciate. Stream Offseason on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

#3555. DC Studios' Biggest Superhero Movie Priorities After James Gunn's Exit, Explained

The DC Universe on film is once again under new management, as Warner Bros.' new parent company Skydance has replaced DC Studios co-presidents James Gunn and Peter Safran with Marvel Studios' alum Jeremy Latcham. The reasons for Gunn and Safran's exit are still under scrutiny, but it seems inevitable that whatever plans they had for DC are now going to shift.

According to reporting by The Wrap, Skydance CEO David Ellison is pushing Latcham to focus on DC's A-list characters and get a "Justice League" movie out "as soon as possible." The Wrap adds that even "modestly-known" DC heroes like Supergirl won't be getting the greenlight for now. (The poor box office of "Supergirl" didn't help her specific case.)

One hypothesis for Gunn and Safran's departure, which looks more plausible in light of this reporting, is that they weren't focusing enough on those A-list DC characters. Sure, they started with Superman, but DCU Batman and Wonder Woman movies never moved past development prior to their departure. Making "Clayface," a movie about a B-list Batman villain, before introducing Batman himself is one of those decisions that would be ridiculous to imagine, except it actually happened. It's also a meme among DC fans that Gunn's DCU was frontloading Rick Flag Sr. (Frank Grillo) yet hadn't even introduced the full DC Trinity yet.

But leopards can't change their spots. Gunn's passion for superheroes has always been reinventing C-list characters. Directing for Marvel Studios, he made the Guardians of the Galaxy into household names, and across those movies, it's clear the character he loved most was the biggest oddball among oddballs, Rocket Racoon (Bradley Cooper). He first came to DC directing "The Suicide Squad," and he even packed "Superman" with more obscure DC heroes like Metamorpho (Anthony Carrigan) and Mister Terrific (Edi Gathegi).

In an irony worthy of Alanis Morissette, it appears James Gunn's DCU was finally getting to those A-list characters that David Ellison wants spotlighted. "Lanterns" introduced John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) as Green Lantern, who will be returning in "Superman" sequel "Man of Tomorrow." It's also practically an open secret that Adria Arjona is playing Wonder Woman in "Man of Tomorrow." New reporting suggests that Gunn had also begun writing his third "Superman" movie and was considering tweaking it to a Justice League movie.

Now, I've speculated in the past that if/when Gunn got to the Justice League, he would be basing it on the 1980s comic run "Justice League International" by J.M. DeMatteis, Kevin Maguire and Keith Giffen. That run is basically the blueprint for every James Gunn superhero movie, as it took C-List characters (Booster Gold, Blue Beetle, Guy Gardner Green Lantern, Fire and Ice, etc.) and made their adventures more of a workplace comedy. The JLI was headed up by businessman Maxwell Lord, who appears in "Superman" (played by Sean Gunn) sponsoring the proto Justice League.

But I wouldn't expect that now. DC Studios' "Justice League" movie will surely feature the A-listers: Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman, Green Lantern, The Flash, and Aquaman. By largely holding off on those characters, Gunn and Safran may have given Jeremy Latcham more leeway to mold the DCU's headliners.

Now, it's still unclear if DC Studios will do a full continuity reboot or merely a creative pivot. If the latter, it's plausible Corenswet's Superman stays. If Adria Arjona is indeed playing Wonder Woman, a swift recast would probably be awkward, too.

"Lanterns" was also a huge hit for HBO, and TheWrap explicitly names Green Lantern as one of the A-List characters DC Studios is prioritizing. Does that mean Pierre's John Stewart will get a movie?

As for Batman, DC Studios has been in a tight bind with their cash cow the last half-decade. Matt Reeves' "The Batman," commissioned by the previous regime, hit theaters in March 2022, months before James Gunn and Peter Safran's hiring. Gunn was extremely accommodating to Reeves, even as "The Batman Part II" faced numerous scheduling delays. (Reeves has reportedly been dealing with a family crisis, hence him stepping away from shooting "The Batman Part II" as Steven Soderbergh takes over as a stand-in.)

I'm personally grateful we're seeing "The Batman Part II" finished and on Reeves' terms. But the sharper business move would've been to reboot or make Robert Pattinson's Batman part of the DCU. Gunn did neither, only announcing a "Batman" movie, "The Brave and the Bold" in 2023 that never really got rolling. I'd say, now, though, there's a better than likely chance that Reeves and Pattinson's "Batman" series ends with "Part II" to clear the way for a DCU Batman.

So what about the other in-development projects at DC that spotlighted smaller characters, i.e. "Swamp Thing" and the Bane & Deathstroke team-up movie? I think it's a fair bet those are dead. The announced "Teen Titans" movie is a toss-up — the 2003 "Teen Titans" cartoon remains a cultural touchstone for younger millennials and older Gen Zers, but the team might still fit into the "modestly known" box like Supergirl apparently does.

For better or worse, DC fans should expect to see the Justice League back onscreen sooner rather than later.

60 Minutes has entered a new era amid the 2026 TV schedule, and a person who’s been overseeing much of the work behind the scenes is CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss. In conjunction with the news magazine show’s EP, Nick Bilton, Weiss has been looking to update the program, and those efforts have been accompanied by major staff changes and backlash. Some of the criticisms have come from former staff members, including ex-EP Bill Owens, who recently shared his biggest concerns over the series he once shepherded.

Owens worked at CBS News for 37 years and, in 2019, he was named the EP of 60 Minutes after having spent 12 years overseeing its content in other roles. He ultimately resigned from his post in April 2025 amid a flurry of behind-the-scenes changes at 60. Since his departure, Owens has discussed his time with the show, and he notably shared thoughts ahead of the Season 59 premiere, which aired in September. At Semafor’s New Media & Marketing Playbook event, Owens was asked for his thoughts on his former workplace and said:

Not a lot. [Skydance owns] the company, they can do whatever they want. But the ratings are telling. There’s no doubt that linear television is in decline. But the numbers the other day were less than 6 million people. It’s like the evening news. 60 Minutes? That would have freaked me out.

Ratings for the latest season of 60 have reportedly been down compared to those of Season 58. The season premiere notched lower viewership and, despite some forward progress in subsequent weeks, more recent numbers haven’t been so strong. For instance, per data on the show’s October 25 broadcast, the episode only drew 5.6 million live viewers, which fell well below Season 58’s 9.1 million average. Despite that, when Bari Weiss addressed concerns, she stated that the show was doing “tremendously well.”

As for Owens, he’s been candid about leaving 60 Minutes, and he has attributed that move to no longer having the editorial independence he and his colleagues had long been granted. During the Semafor event, Owens also criticized the show’s interview with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and argued that better questions should’ve been asked. On a separate note, the veteran journalist also admitted that he wished his departure would’ve had a different effect on 60:

When I left, I really hoped that I was going to cause enough of a commotion that they would kind of back off. And the people, my senior team, the correspondents, they’ve tried their best. But it’s just a really difficult circumstance.

May 2026 marked the beginning of major personnel changes at 60 Minutes, as several high-profile staffers were let go, including correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega as well as former EP Tanya Simon. Days later, fellow host Scott Pelley was fired as well after he reportedly accused Weiss of “murdering” the show. Around that time, Owens defended Pelley’s comments, saying that he “stood up the way that I did a year ago and I couldn’t be prouder of him, and I know all the people at 60 Minutes couldn’t be prouder of him.”

Bill Owens has since moved on to other ventures and, beginning in March 2027, he’ll executive-produce a YouTube-based outlet known as NewPress. It’s also been rumored that Owens will spill tea about his time at 60 Minutes through a tell-all memoir, but that’s yet to materialize. At the very least, though, Owens still seems somewhat interested about what the future holds for 60.

#3553. Who Is Jeremy Latcham? Everything We Know About The New Head Of DC Studios

As Hollywood reels from the shock of James Gunn and Peter Safran getting shown the door at DC Studios, the industry is trying to get a bead on how their replacement, Jeremy Latcham, will approach the job. It's highly unlikely he'll continue with Gunn and Safran's development slate, though if Gunn's "Superman" sequel, "Man of Tomorrow," does significantly better than the first film at the box office, there could be a possibility he'll let Gunn close out a potential trilogy. Latcham is also inheriting HBO shows like "Lanterns" and "The People v. Gorilla Grodd," and as of this writing, neither has been greenlit for a second season.

Like most executives do when they take over a studio, Latcham is reportedly poised to wipe the slate clean and put his personal stamp on whatever comes next. Latcham is no stranger to making superhero movies. He was one of Kevin Feige's right-hand men at Marvel Studios, where he helped his boss set the "Avengers Initiative" in motion with "Iron Man." His track record is strong, and he's well regarded as a no-bulls*** guy. If Skydance executive David Ellison and his production executives Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg were going to take a chance on someone who'd never run a Hollywood studio before, Latcham at least had a promising pedigree.

As for that personal stamp, it's fair to wonder if Latcham's strong Christian faith will impact the types of filmmakers he pursues to, presumably, make his all-new iterations of Superman, Batman, and Wonder Woman. Talking with the Bible Bros about his work for the faith-based Wonder Project, where he helped develop "Flyer" (an uplifting biopic about the Wright Brothers) and the Biblical TV series "House of David," Latcham expressed a desire to make movies that meant something to him. How will this gibe with mainstream moviegoers, many of whom aren't Christian?

During that BibleBros appearance, Latcham said, "Let's be the HBO for the faith and family audience. Let's try to make movies and television shows that restore faith in things worth believing in." As we've seen over the last couple of decades, there's definitely an audience for this. But a successful faith-based company like Angel Studios has never made a movie that's sniffed $1 billion worldwide. Not even close.

At Marvel, Latcham was famous for asking if his grandmother would approve of certain moments or the overall themes of MCU movies. As he told the Bible Bros, "That became the stand-in for, like, 'Is this going to work for regular people that are outside the bubble of Hollywood? Is this safe for a regular family?" He went on to say that his grandmother's pastor gave a sermon on how "Iron Man" was an effective tale of redemption.

Right now, the clearest indication we have of how Latcham will run DC Studios comes from his Bible Bros visit, where he extolled virtues of "faith in God, obviously, faith in country, faith in family, faith in fathers, faith in all these institutions that we believe in in America. The idea of America, the idea of a democratic, free capitalist society." He then added that he'd like to make these virtues "front and center" in his movies.

Latcham has strong ties with many notable filmmakers and actors who seem to genuinely like him. He certainly comes off as very likable in his interviews. But he's got one heck of a challenge ahead of him. DC Studios is rebooting for the third time in 13 years, and moviegoers certainly have a case of superhero fatigue. They'll show up for Batman and Spider-Man and events like an "Avengers" installment, but if you keep pulling the rug out from under your audience, they will eventually abandon you.

Matt Reeves' "The Batman: Part II" is guaranteed to be a massive hit when it arrives in 2028, but the first film probably didn't go down well with Latcham's grandmother. I have no idea what a Latcham Batman will look like, but that hardcore fan base expects the Caped Crusader to go hard. Take your foot off the gas, and you might see grosses on par with "Batman & Robin."

Latcham has the added burden of reporting to Greenstein and Goldberg, who report to CEO David Ellison, who seemingly wants broad-appeal blockbusters with as little artistry as possible. Latcham knows how this works from his Marvel Studios days, but he was just one voice in their by-committee process. He'll assemble his own team, and we'll just have to wait and see what that looks like. In the meantime, it'll be interesting to see what kind of directors and stars he pursues, as well as which properties he prioritizes. He'd do well to look at Gunn's "Superman" and go for a tone that's tough but fun and hopeful. And while he has every right to imbue these movies with elements of his faith, he needs to be careful not to alienate people who don't worship at his church. Because that's a small bubble, too.

#3552. I Tested Strava's New Integration With Gemini, and I Have Thoughts

Once connected, you can ask questions like:

"Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?"

"Can you give me a detailed analysis of how I performed in my last race?"

"How is my strength training impacting my running?"

Some important context here: Strava's AI "insights" have sort of sucked, and annoyed me, in the past. Athlete Intelligence (conveniently abbreviated as AI) is the Strava feature that writes text responses to your workouts. Strava calls these "insights," but as far as I can tell they mostly regurgitate the information from the workout description, sometimes with added errors. I've found AI fitness summaries largely useless, and Strava's version checks every box: It doesn't use enough context to understand what's going on, it presents generic advice as if it were personal, and it's overconfident in incomplete data. So, skeptical as I am, I gave Strava's latest Google Gemini integration a whirl. Here's what it does, how to set it up, and whether it's worth it.

The first question I asked was one of Strava’s examples, "Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?" Gemini said yes, I was seeing solid efficiency gains. Like many AI tools, it told me what I wanted to hear. I had to point out that heat and temperature are huge variables. When I steered the chat in that direction, Gemini, of course, agreed immediately ("you hit the nail on the head") and explained that my mid-September long runs happened in 75–84°F weather with higher humidity, which inflates heart rate, while October's cooler temperatures made the same effort look better. That's an important caveat the first answer left out entirely.

I then asked it to compare my past marathons, and in many ways, I had fun here. For instance, the suggested follow-ups prompted me to think of questions I hadn't put on my list, like comparing my weekly running volume and long-run frequency leading into different races in different years.

Unfortunately, the results weren't reliable at first. When I asked for a detailed analysis of every marathon-distance effort since 2019, Gemini said I had exactly one, the Marine Corps Marathon on October 25, 2026. In reality, I've logged at least eight. When I asked why it couldn't see them, it explained that its access is limited to my recent history, roughly summer 2026 onward, because of how pagination limits the number of past activities returned at once. It also offered a workaround: Give it specific dates and locations.

That workaround works, but it means you have to already know what you're looking for. And still, it wasn't consistent. In other answers, Gemini referenced my 2025 NYC Marathon and 2024 Philadelphia race, so the data's reach seems uneven. You need to be able to query older date ranges as directly and specifically as possible, and even still, double-check any numbers that matter to you.

I then asked "What am I doing right and what am I doing wrong as a runner?" After knowing the queries need to be so specific, I intentionally wanted to test a vague, simplistic question. The answer was, true to form, overly flattering—though I didn't disagree with the guidance itself. I need more speed workouts! I know this! I didn't need a chatbot to tell me, though maybe some other Strava user does. Gemini's suggestions (polarize training, add one dedicated threshold day) are sound, yes, but they’re also generic. Most recreational runners could glance at my Strava and spot the same strengths and weaknesses. Similarly, Gemini then set itself up for a slam dunk by prompting me to ask whether my easy runs were too fast. The answer: My easy days were happening at nearly my marathon pace (about 9:43/mi), and I should slow down by 45–90 seconds per mile, to roughly 10:30–11:15/mi. I completely agree. That being said, my big takeaway here remains the same: Don't confuse AI-generated advice as some newfound, personalized insight. It’s often the same conventional wisdom you already know, or could figure out with a tiny bit of research from a real, human source.

If you ask me—a human!—this is a classic case of using AI for rote tasks, but then saving critical thinking for your own human brain. Gemini didn't surface anything wildly insightful, and it skipped important considerations like the effect of heat on heart rate, until I raised them myself. But it pulled data faster than I could have by hand, and its follow-up prompts nudged me toward comparisons I might not have thought of.

For many users, the smartest approach may be to skip AI summaries and focus on raw data. After all, your training load, sleep duration, and heart rate trends are already perfectly actionable.

As with all things AI, it’s important to mind the gap between data and wisdom. So much wisdom gets lost—forfeited, even—when you blindly trust an AI coach. Make sure you aren’t offloading all the other skills you need as a runner and as a human, like your ability to listen to your body and maybe run a little slower in the heat, even when it makes your data look “worse.”

If you do use Google Gemini to analyze your Strava data:

Be specific about dates and locations when asking about older activities.

Push back. Ask about weather, terrain, and fatigue before accepting a flattering conclusion.

Treat the output as a fast data pull, not a personal coach.

#3551. Stephen Miller Into the Breach: How Susie Wiles’s Failures Portend Miller’s Future

There’s a time-honored tradition for new White House chiefs of staff: The outgoing chief invites former holders of the office, Republicans and Democrats, to a get-together (usually in the West Wing), where the newcomer is offered advice. But Donald Trump’s new chief, Stephen Miller—appointed in a jaw-dropping Truth Social post on Friday—won’t be getting a party. First, because the tradition applies only to a president’s first chief. Second, because no Democratic chief would likely want to be caught dead with Miller, a longtime basher of the opposition party. Shortly after hearing that Trump had picked the hard-right firebrand as his new chief, James Carville sent me a text that summed up the prevailing attitude: “This is like Caligula’s appointment of his horse as consul.”

It was different when Susie Wiles came to town. On the evening of November 19, 2024, she was the guest of honor at a dinner party thrown by Jeffrey Zients, Joe Biden’s outgoing White House chief of staff. They were joined by eight of Zients’s predecessors. It was an occasion for bipartisan bonhomie, a tradition started in 2008 by George W. Bush’s chief Joshua Bolten. In a spirit of goodwill and generosity, Bolten had thrown a gathering in his West Wing office for Barack Obama’s incoming chief, Rahm Emanuel. The informal meetup was intended as a way to convey the chiefs’ collective wisdom and experience—and to offer, in miniature, a nuts-and-bolts version of the transition of executive power that is a hallmark of American democracy.

Now evicted from her West Wing corner office, with the president’s agenda in tatters, Wiles has learned that fealty to Trump almost always ends badly.

On the night of the dinner for Wiles, however, a cloud hung over the occasion. Virtually no one at the table thought she could succeed as Donald Trump’s chief of staff.

For almost two years, Wiles was the second most powerful person in the West Wing. Had Trump been interested in governing, she might have helped him solidify a GOP majority in Congress for years to come. But she was unwilling, or unable, to save Trump from himself. On Wiles’s watch, he squandered his second term with a reign of revenge, retribution, and recklessness. Now evicted from her West Wing corner office, with the president’s agenda in tatters, Wiles has learned that fealty to Trump almost always ends badly.

And if past experience is any guide, Wiles’s replacement, Stephen Miller, may well crash and burn in even more spectacular fashion.

There was no one the president relied on or trusted more than Wiles. From their first meeting in 2015 at Trump Tower to her impressive stint as his winning 2024 presidential campaign co-manager, the “ice maiden” had Trump’s back. And he had hers—until last Tuesday’s epic Democratic blowout. Wiles would resign two days later. Indeed, the Republicans’ midterm apocalypse was an extinction event that not even Wiles could have survived.

Ironically, Trump’s savvy political strategist was the architect of what turned out to be a big blue bloodbath. “We’re going to win the midterms,” Wiles told me boldly when I interviewed her for Vanity Fair just a year ago. Even then, three months before Trump initiated a war on Iran, that was a ridiculously rosy prediction. The president’s approval rating was in the gutter. He’d failed to address, much less solve, voters’ primary concerns: affordability, inflation, health care, and housing—and had still not released the remaining Epstein files. How could a battle-hardened political pro like Wiles be so starry-eyed? The answer, I believe, is that in the fog of MAGA-land, she’d lost touch with the real world.

In almost every presidency, the West Wing is a bubble where like-minded acolytes engage in groupthink. But in Trump’s West Wing this phenomenon is exponentially magnified. It’s a parallel universe, one in which the 2020 election was stolen, violent insurrectionists are “patriots,” and the prosecution of political enemies—with scant evidence—is a presidential perk. (“Who would blame him?” Wiles said to me of Trump’s campaign to settle scores.) That, to my mind, is why Wiles seemed so stunned by the firestorm that erupted when her words appeared in my 10,000-word Vanity Fair series last December. She had no idea they would land like bombs on planet Earth.

Wiles invested Trump with almost otherworldly powers. He would lead the GOP to victory in the 2026 midterms, she believed, because of his preternatural ability to rally his base. That’s why, on the eve of the midterms, Wiles was all-in on sending Trump almost everywhere all at once, admonishing people to “vote like I’m on the ballot.” The trouble was voters saw all too clearly what she apparently couldn’t see: Trump was deeply unpopular; on his watch, the country was coming apart.

A year ago, when Wiles made her electoral prediction, I challenged her. “I admire your confidence about the midterms,” I said, “but the stakes are huge, right? And history is not encouraging. Incumbents do stuff and there’s a reaction. And usually, as Obama said, you get shellacked.”

Wiles seemed to shrug off that possibility. “Can you ever imagine Donald Trump saying that?” she said. “No, no.”

Wiles was right. Trump could never say such a thing—because he could never accept the fact that his electoral magic had waned. Neither, it seemed, could Wiles. But as his chief of staff and top political strategist, she was paid to know better.

Even before the election debacle, Trump had reportedly started privately inquiring about her on phone calls, although he lashed out at accounts of such purported conversations. Then, once the carnage sunk in, the die was cast. Wiles offered her resignation. And Trump accepted it.

At the start of her West Wing tenure, I believed Wiles stood a chance of succeeding. If Trump would listen to anyone, I thought, it was the loyal, organized, no-nonsense Wiles. Yet during 10 conversations with her over 10 months, I watched as she abdicated the most important duty of the White House chief: telling the president hard truths. Wiles told me she’d read my book, The Gatekeepers: How the White House Chiefs of Staff Define Every Presidency, and she understood the importance of heeding Reagan chief James Baker’s advice. “You do not serve your president well if you are just a yes man,” he said. In a phone call, she told me, Baker “reminded me that my job wasn’t to be a fangirl.” I asked Wiles, “Have you had any gut check moments where you had to tell the president something he didn’t want to hear?” She paused. “I probably have one a day,” she said. “But they’re over little things, not big.”

Wiles should have known that the midterms would spell disaster. She carried around a list of her priorities, on an index card. Number five: “Don’t forget about organized labor. Don’t forget about young Black men and women and Hispanics…because that’s the future of the country and the backbone of his support. And if we don’t convert those people to being enthusiastic Republicans, then if the Democrats were even just a little bit better, they might win an election.”

Miller is a zealot, a hard-boiled ideologue—an advocate of Trump’s notorious first-term Muslim ban, the brutal paramilitary tactics of ICE, the deployment of the National Guard to Democrat-run cities, and the lethal air strikes on boats in the Caribbean.

They might—and they did. And now Wiles is out, taking up shop, so Trump himself has said, within his political operation. Last November she hinted that she knew this day might come: “You go to bed at night, you say your prayers, you take stock of what the day was and what your day is tomorrow, and you get up and do it again…. So as long as that’s the case and the president’s pleased…” Wiles paused. “He could fire you tomorrow.”

She’s sensitive about her legacy as the first female White House chief. “I’m not an enabler,” she insisted. “I’m also, like, not a bitch. I try to be thoughtful about what I engage in, and what I disagree [with the president] about. I guess time will tell whether I’ve been effective.”

What about Wiles’s successor, Stephen Miller?

Miller is the antithesis of Ronald Reagan’s chief James Baker, a cool pragmatist who could push back on the president’s half-baked ideas. Miller, by contrast, is a zealot, a hard-boiled ideologue—an advocate of Trump’s notorious first-term Muslim ban, the brutal paramilitary tactics of ICE, the deployment of the National Guard to Democrat-run cities, and the lethal air strikes on boats in the Caribbean. He believes in a Hobbesian world, he has stated, “that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power.” Now he’ll be the last person in the room when Trump makes life-and-death decisions about law and order and war and peace.

The man who decreed that the president’s powers “are very substantial and will not be questioned” is now the official charged with questioning the president’s decisions. It’s hard to imagine Miller doing that without a personality transplant. He’s already alienated the House minority leader, and soon to be Speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, who has called Miller “a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands,” insisting, “I’ve got zero interest in working with that kind of individual.”

At the White House last November, after a Vanity Fair photo session, I spoke with Miller at length about the midterms, still a year away; about his portfolio in the Trump administration; and about the role of the White House chief of staff. Perched on a chair in the Roosevelt Room, he eyed me warily. He seemed impatient to get back to work. “I understand that your need for me is quite limited, right?” he said.

I asked Miller about his interactions with the president—specifically an Oval Office meeting in which he and Trump reportedly talked about blowing up boats in the Caribbean. “I would never talk about…whether a meeting occurred or didn’t occur,” he said, “or whether it was in a meeting that did occur, or was not in that meeting if it occurred, which I would never say either way.”

Miller was more forthcoming about Wiles’s prediction—that Trump and the GOP would triumph at the polls in 2026. “What about you?” I asked him. “I am confident that we’ll win the midterms,” he replied. History might be against them, he said, “but we have every expectation that we’re going to defy that history.” “Why?” I asked. Miller replied, “Because of the president’s unprecedentedly successful first nine months in office.”

What followed was a black-is-white, up-is-down litany of Trump’s accomplishments, a revisionist history that might have made Karoline Leavitt, another world-class propagandist, blush. “In no particular order,” Miller said, “the taming and defeating of inflation. As you know, we inherited record double-digit inflation and the president made his first priority to bring down the cost of living…cutting the price of energy by high double digits. For many Americans, gas prices have been cut in half since we took over.” None of this, of course, has proved true—but Miller was just warming up.

“And the passage of the largest package of tax cuts and reforms in American history in the form of the One Big Beautiful Bill. Fully securing the Southern border, the most secure border in history, zero illegal crossings, four months in a row. And also the largest number of deportations in American history…. The president has…achieved more in foreign policy than any president in our lifetimes, ending eight wars in eight months—which includes, but is not limited to, securing the historic peace deal between Israel and Gaza, Thailand and Cambodia, Congo and Rwanda, Azerbaijan and Armenia, Israel and Iran, and so on…”

Miller still wasn’t done. The president, he said, “has executed on every promise he’s made to the American people and that includes also taking back our culture and fighting against whether you call it radical leftism or woke or Marxism—a lot of people just call it plain crazy—but taking back our culture and restoring sanity to American life.

“It is my extraordinary privilege and blessing,” Miller added, “to be able to work for the president of the United States, to implement an agenda that I believe in wholly and completely and with every fiber of my being.”

I was there, of course, because I was writing a story on Susie Wiles and her West Wing team. I asked him, point-blank: “Would you agree, though, that it’s also the chief of staff’s job to tell the president what he doesn’t want to hear?”

“No, I wouldn’t say that,” Miller replied, finding fault with my framing of the question and insisting that this president wants to hear everything. “The chief of staff would never have to encounter the scenario you’re describing.” Miller said. “President Trump craves, he loves the every-minute detail of management, having every piece of information, having every side of everything, having inputs into the Oval Office from every square, every quarter, every person.”

As for the president’s staff, Miller said, their job is “implementing the president’s vision, the president’s directions, the president’s agenda, the president’s plans for the future…. We’re just here on his behalf to see that that is done.”

As the great political columnist Molly Ivins once wrote, “It probably sounded better in the original German.”

Chris Whipple is a contributing writer at Vanity Fair and a Fall 2026 Resident Fellow at Harvard’s Kennedy School Institute of Politics. You can follow him on Substack.

#3550. Why Those Flashy Halloween Contacts Are a Bad Idea

Contacts with cat pupils or neon colors can be fun, but are you sure you want to put a piece of plastic from a costume store into your eye? Experts, like those at the American Academy of Ophthalmology, warn against it. These non-prescription contacts are technically illegal in the U.S. (even though plenty of companies sell them anyway). The CDC warns that the risks include "eye sores and vision loss."

Cheap Halloween contacts tend to be one-size-fits-all, but the AAO points out that contacts should never be one-size-fits-all. A contact that is too large or too small for your eye can cause corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, and can result in infections like keratitis. Infections can, in severe cases, lead to blindness. A 2017 report from the FDA found bacterial contamination in 27% of costume contacts.

If you do wear contacts (Halloween or otherwise), the AAO recommends keeping an eye out for symptoms like redness, swelling, pain, or excessive discharge. Seek care as soon as you suspect an infection. Your eyes are more sensitive to infections than other parts of the body, so be cautious.

Legally, contacts require a prescription, so if those colored contacts you're eyeing can be bought without showing a doctor’s prescription, they’re not legit. The real thing can be expensive, though: I found prices of $40 and up from lens.com, Discount Contacts, and Wicked Eyez.

These websites all let you order online, but you’ll have to provide your prescription information before you can check out. Fortunately, the Federal Trade Commission has ruled that providers must give you your contact prescription after a fitting so that you can take the prescription elsewhere. And they cannot charge you extra for this.

Once you’ve got the lenses, you have to know how to take care of them. If you wear contacts every day, you already know the drill. But if you’re just picking up a pair to use with a costume, here are the basics:

Wash your hands before handling the lenses.

Store them in contact lens solution, and keep the lenses and their case clean.

And for Pete’s sake, don’t share them with your friends!

Just remember, the bloodshot look stops being cool after you take your zombie costume off.

#3549. The Big Bang Theory's Downfall Can Be Traced Back To One Moment

Ever since it ended in 2019, "The Big Bang Theory," the CBS sitcom created by Chuck Lorre and Bill Prady, has remained exceedingly popular. Not only is it still a hit on its exclusive streaming home (HBO Max), it's spawned two prequel spin-offs ("Young Sheldon" and "Georgie & Mandy's First Marriage"), creating a small-screen cinematic universe. So did it ever jump the shark? Yeah, and I'll tell you how, when, and why.

At the beginning of "The Big Bang Theory," Sheldon Cooper and Leonard Hofstadter (Jim Parsons and Johnny Galecki) meet their new neighbor Penny (Kaley Cuoco), with whom Leonard is immediately smitten. Despite a rocky start, Penny and Sheldon ultimately overcome their differences and become good friends. More than that, Penny is a sort of audience surrogate, helping translate Sheldon and Leonard's nerdiness — as well as that of their friends Howard Wolowitz (Simon Helberg) and Raj Koothrappali (Kunal Nayyar) — for the masses. The guys work together at the California Institute of Technology as physicists, engineers, and astrophysicists, and spend their time reading comic books.

Eventually, Melissa Rauch and Mayim Bialik join the series as microbiologist Bernadette Rostenkowski and neuroscientist Amy Farrah Fowler, and they add some much-needed feminine energy to the proceedings — and give Penny some much-needed storylines that don't center around the guys. (Helberg agrees that they generally improved the series too.) Unfortunately, though, Amy and Bernadette's introduction on "The Big Bang Theory" was the beginning of the end for the show's better years. The downfall of "The Big Bang Theory" doesn't quite kick off at the end of Season 5 when Howard and Bernadette tie the knot, but when others start following suit, the quality decline is obvious. The real downfall, though, is the Season 9 premiere.

At the beginning of "The Big Bang Theory" Season 9, Leonard and Penny hastily decide to get married at a Las Vegas wedding chapel — without any of their friends or family present. The whole thing is weird, and honestly, the Season 9 premiere "The Matrimonial Momentum" is one of the show's all-time worst episodes). On the drive there, Leonard admits that he kissed another woman during a lengthy research trip in the North Sea two years beforehand, and Penny is understandably upset to discover that her then-boyfriend cheated on her and hid it from her for years. Still, they determinedly go through with the chapel wedding anyway, culminating in a less-than-satisfying wedding night at a Vegas hotel and the two returning to their respective apartments to sleep separately when they get back to Pasadena.

So, this episode stinks, but it also points to a much bigger structural problem in later seasons of "The Big Bang Theory." Once everyone starts pairing off, the show focuses less on the genuinely delightful interplay between the entire cast, and we get way more storylines about relationship problems, which start to feel flat-out repetitive and boring. By the time Penny and Leonard have their second wedding (with their loved ones in attendance) in the Season 10 premiere and Amy and Sheldon get married in the Season 11 finale, "The Big Bang Theory" is stuck in a cycle, especially because Howard and Bernadette have children in that same timeframe. As "The Big Bang Theory" pairs off all of its main characters (except poor Raj), it experiences a fall from greatness and becomes a run-of-the-mill sitcom ... and also makes one issue glaringly obvious.

There is not, and I'm not exaggerating, one healthy couple to be found within the later seasons of "The Big Bang Theory." Even after Leonard and Penny finally get together and stay that way, they have to get married twice after that botched first attempt. They constantly disagree on major issues like having children and career choices, and Leonard still sees himself as intellectually superior to Penny. Howard does put his time as a wannabe womanizer behind him and settle down with Bernadette, but throughout their marriage he proves to be a total manchild who was coddled by his mother for so long that he expects the same treatment from Bernadette. Then there's Sheldon and Amy, who experience the slowest-moving relationship possible due to Sheldon's issues with physical intimacy. This is a very real thing that could have been explored with sensitivity, but instead, Sheldon treats Amy like a sick, depraved pervert for wanting to sleep with her romantic partner — and the show does the same by extension, making her desire for more physicality with Sheldon into a running joke.

"The Big Bang Theory" features a ton of terrible relationship behavior. It almost exclusively comes from the male partners, and it almost all occurs from Season 9 onwards. That's why the downfall of "The Big Bang Theory" can be pinned to that terrible Season 9 premiere, which isn't just an uncomfortable, awkward, and largely unfunny half hour of the series — it's a stark indicator of the doldrums that follow as the show reaches its endpoint.

"The Big Bang Theory" is streaming on HBO Max now.

The Blade Runner saga is set to continue amid the 2026 TV schedule, thanks to an upcoming limited series. Blade Runner 2099 presents the next chapter in this science-fiction-infused tale of humans and replicants and puts new protagonists at the forefront. Given what’s come before, it’s only natural to wonder whether the show has direct connections to Ridley Scott’s original 1982 film and Denis Villeneuve’s 2017 sequel, 2049. Well, the showrunner is now shedding some light on that front.

If it weren’t already clear due to the title, 2099 picks up fifty years after the events of the critically acclaimed Blade Runner 2049. That film left quite a few plot threads on the table, including the revelation that the late Eldon Tyrell gave replicants the ability to reproduce. Heading up the new show is Silka Luisa, who is a longtime fan of the franchise. Luisa recently spoke with SFX Magazine on CinemaBlend and was asked if events from 2049 would come into play. With that, she gave a very clear answer:

No, [Blade Runner 2049] is not directly connected to the show. What was an important early mandate was that audiences could come to the show not having seen the films, and this could stand alone. This could be an introduction to the world of Blade Runner, and it wouldn’t be dependent on you having watched 2049, you having watched the first Blade Runner. In that sense, we had to divorce ourselves from the narrative.

Why Edward James Olmos Says He Owes His Battlestar Galactica Legacy To Blade Runner

Some fans may be a tad disappointed to learn that replicant reproduction won’t be expanded upon during the events of the show. Yet Luisa’s “mandate” does indeed make a lot of sense. What she and her collaborators ultimately want is a show that fits snugly into the continuity but also doesn’t require watching the movies. (Of course, both of those films are excellent and deserve to be watched regardless.) In short, the Shining Girls creator is promising a series that works on its own, and that could do away with any trepidation newcomers may have about jumping in.

Blade Runner 2099 takes viewers to a Los Angeles that’s now fully controlled by replicants, and humans must essentially live within the lower levels of society. At the center of the story is Olwen, a Replicant Blade Runner (played by Michelle Yeoh) who is only days away from dying. She is eventually partnered with Marion Jessop to take on a case. However, unbeknownst to Olwen, “Marion” is actually a human named Cora (Hunter Schafer), who is only masquerading as a Replicant to achieve her own goals.

Per what’s been shared thus far, Yeoh and Schafer forged a strong bond on set not unlike Harrison Ford and Ryan Gosling did while making 2049. However, as far as we know, Yeoh didn’t accidentally punch Schafer in the face like Ford did to Gosling. In fact, Yeoh was protective of her co-star amid production and, in a truly mom-coded move, she even bought Schafer a baby helmet.

The trailers for 2099 would suggest that such headgear was necessary, because a lot of intense moments have been teased thus far. Although fans won’t see any direct links to the Blade Runner films, Silka Luisa is aiming to dish out the action-infused thrills, heightened visuals and deep themes that have long permeated this franchise.

Check out Blade Runner 2099 when all eight episodes are released for Prime Video subscription holders on November 25. In the meantime, anyone who’s curious can stream the original movie for free on Pluto TV and check out 2049 on Prime as well.

#3546. The Rings Of Power Season 3 Review: Prime Video's Lord Of The Rings Series Still Falls Short

If there's one theme the latest installment of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" highlights above the rest, it's this: Time comes for us all. Whether it's the glacial pace experienced by immortal Elves or the nonstop blur the rest of Middle-earth's mere mortals have been doomed (or gifted?) to receive, this army's inevitable march is one that nobody — not even a Dark Lord — can hope to defeat.

Four years after the Prime Video series first made waves among a passionate, if divisive fanbase, it's clear co-showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay have felt this pressure as keenly as anyone. An up-and-down debut season with glimpses of potential eventually found itself surpassed by a sophomore effort that went darker, bolder, and better than before. But, to date, fans have been left waiting for the moment when this J.R.R. Tolkien adaptation truly comes into its own.

Time, unfortunately, is a commodity that "The Rings of Power" doesn't have on its side this year. There's Amazon's head-scratching release strategy that (mostly) becomes clear in retrospect, with eight episodes of streaming television squeezed into three total weeks. More troublingly, the actual story does itself very few favors. There are simply too many far-flung locations to check in on, too many main characters and uninteresting supporting players to service, too much nerdy lore for casuals to digest (if any are even left) ... and, despite some of the most sluggish pacing in streaming, there's hardly enough space to let them breathe. It's an issue that rears its ugly, Balrog-shaped head again and again.

In short, Season 3 is an encapsulation of "The Rings of Power" as a whole: some incredibly high highs, several frustrating lows, and the creeping feeling that time is finally starting to run out.

Season 3's big claim to fame has been heavily teased as the creation of the legendary One Ring, which is the one doomsday event overshadowing over every single storyline this year. Five years after the conclusion of Season 2, as Galadriel's exposition-dump narration explains in the premiere, Sauron's armies wage war on the rest of Middle-earth. Only the Elves and their magical, untarnished rings remain capable of holding out. But when a suspicious Orc arrives (Adam Young as Marnûkh, easily one of the season's best new additions) bearing game-changing news of Sauron's plans, this kicks off a series of events that will either lead to good's greatest triumph over evil ... or as stunning a failure as anything in Tolkien's legendarium.

As a prequel, of course, "The Rings of Power" uses our knowledge of what's to come in "The Lord of the Rings" to its advantage. As a result, every moment Sauron is on screen trying (and failing) to forge his superweapon to rule them all absolutely soars. Whether he's cruelly bossing powerless underlings around, casually committing murder, arguing with the ghosts in his head, or generally sulking over his inability to seduce Galadriel to his cause, Charlie Vickers's Sauron will have you rooting for the villain every step of the way. He brings a delightful sense of theatricality and purpose to every evil act, while the long-awaited introduction of Galadriel's MIA husband Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower, another major highlight of Season 3) finally provides the third point of the unlikeliest love triangle in the canon.

But if Sauron is the main driving force behind the best narrative arc of them all, "The Rings of Power" fares far worse everywhere else.

This "Lord of the Rings" series has always had trouble finding the right balance among its varying subplots, separated by narrative relevance and theme just as much as by distance. Nowhere does that feel more glaring than in Season 3. The courtly intrigue and succession struggles taking place in the Dwarven realm of Khazad-dûm aim for "House of the Dragon"-like dramatics, but neither of the plucky performances by Owain Arthur's King Durin or Sophia Nomvete's Queen Disa can make this feel like anything less than a misguided detour.

Similarly, the brewing civil war in Númenór takes ages to click into place (and, even then, not because of any established locals, but because Robert Aramayo's ever-conflicted Elf Elrond finally gets involved). And don't forget there's another B-plot entirely in the desert of Rhûn, with Daniel Weyman's Gandalf and Ciarán Hinds' Dark Wizard circling one another.

The further we get from Sauron's antics in Mordor, the less effective "The Rings of Power" undeniably becomes.

The five-year time jump should've allowed for J.D Payne, Patrick McKay, and co-writer Justin Doble to regroup strategically and reset the creative board a bit. And, to an extent, they do manage to cut things down to a more manageable size. A major character death or two helps trim an unwieldy ensemble that has only grown more so over the years, while others undergo some overdo changes in both personality and role. Even the lovable, pint-sized Harfoots have been written out completely this time around. But these are half-measures, at best. As this saga hits its midway point, viewers will be left with the impression that merely reshuffling the deck wasn't nearly enough.

These structural issues extend to the main conflict of Season 3, as well. In the early episodes, the creative team struggles with establishing the stakes of such an abstract threat as the One Ring. Season 1 had the (seemingly) unseen menace of Sauron working in its favor, while Season 2 organically built up to the epic siege of Eregion and the manipulation of Celebrimbor as its big emotional payoff. Season 3 pays lip service to the idea of Mordor's forces on the brink of total victory; but, other than a few minor skirmishes here and the aftermath of some battles there, we barely actually see this for ourselves.

It's a shame because, creatively and technically, the most expensive series on streaming has never looked better nor felt more cinematic. Directors Charlotte Brändström, Sanaa Hamri, and Stefan Schwartz depict a breathtaking level of scope and scale that modern viewers have almost become inured to these days. Together, J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay dream up some of the most spectacular fantasy concepts Tolkien nerds could only ever dare to imagine. As of the seven episodes out of eight made available for critics to review, it all builds up to the moment we've all been waiting for — one that, for a moment, absolutely lives up to the hype.

Is that enough? "Always is a long time," Galadriel suggests with a twinkle in her eye early on. With its five-season plan hopefully still in place, "The Rings of Power" doesn't have anywhere near that long to make up for lost time.

"The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3 premieres with four episodes November 11, 2026 on Prime Video.
