#3526. Alexander Skarsgard And Olivia Colman's Romantic Fantasy Movie Is A Sleeper Box Office Hit

A sleeper box office hit has emerged. The movie in question is the romantic fantasy flick "Wicker," which stars Alexander Skarsgård ("Godzilla vs. Kong") and Olivia Colman ("The Favourite"), who was part of one of the most shocking Oscar upsets of all time, we might add. Now, she's leading one of the fall season's sneakiest hits.

Directed by Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson, "Wicker" opened in theaters on the weekend of October 23, pulling in a solid $5.7 million domestically on a reported $10 million budget. That's not bad, but it debuted at number five on the charts, and it's easy for movies like this to slip by pretty quickly. However, it's managed to hold very well, even as "Godzilla Minus Zero" ruled the box office this past weekend.

As of this writing, "Wicker" has earned $20 million domestically to go with $9 million internationally for a $29 million running total. It hasn't dropped more than 24% on a single weekend, either, meaning that it still has a lot of gas in the tank. Thus, on top of already being in a good position thanks to its reasonable budget, it's on track to profit theatrically before VOD and streaming are even factored in.

Sad to say, that's not the case all too often for smaller, non-franchise movies these days. The film's backer Black Bear has also had a rough start as a distributor in Hollywood, with its Sydney Sweeney vehicle "Christy" flopping at the box office in high-profile fashion last year. This is the hit Black Bear needed.

"Wicker," as it were, centers on an ostracized fisherwoman (Colman) who commissions the local basketmaker (Peter Dinklage) to weave her a husband (Skarsgård). But when this creation proves unexpectedly extraordinary, jealousy and upheaval threatens their quiet village.

It's good news for the movie business in general when a new distributor can emerge on the scene and find success — especially with Warner Bros. and Paramount having recently merged under one roof. Add in Disney having already absorbed Fox in 2019, and Hollywood continues to shrink. So, as much as Black Bear has struggled in the past, it's starting to figure things out.

Indeed, it's been tough sledding for the studio up to this point. Recall that Henry Cavill and Jake Gyllenhaal's action movie "In the Grey" bombed at the box office earlier this year after Lionsgate dumped it and Black Bear picked it up. Matthew McConaughey's "The Rivals of Amziah King" didn't pan out for the studio, either. But if it can emulate the success it's finding with "Wicker" (which is easier said than done, admittedly), there's reason to be optimistic.

Broadly speaking, both theaters and the Hollywood system could use more sleeper hits like this. 2026 has had a lot of bright spots at the box office, among them "Obsession" and "Project Hail Mary," but having smaller movies that can thrive is key to a healthy marketplace. Brad Pitt's survival thriller "Heart of the Beast" also became a sleeper hit while you weren't looking, but that was an expensive movie with an A-list lead. It's not quite the same thing.

Instead, "Wicker" feels closer to Disney turning "Barbarian" into a sleeper hit in 2022. That, in turn, paved the way for director Zach Cregger to make hits like "Weapons" and "Resident Evil." So, yes, we could absolutely use more movies like "Wicker." At the right place and with the right premise, more original, non-franchise ideas can still thrive.

#3525. If You Loved 'VisionQuest,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Marvel’s forays into television have had varying success, but they hit gold with WandVision and Agatha All Along, leaning into real pathos while exploring the kind of out-there ideas that thrill comic book fans (and set up the larger film arcs). That streak continues with VisionQuest, in which White Vision (Paul Bettany) struggles to understand his existence in the wake of his death at the hands of Thanos and resurrection at the magic of the Scarlet Witch, while also evading evil androids and assassins, while also dealing with the many, many AIs he’s got locked up in his Mindspace (including a gloriously shabby version of Ultron, played by James Spader).

If you love the show (and you’ve checked out the other series that play in the same sandbox), it’s time to switch gears and watch (or re-watch) The Matrix.

The Matrix is one of the most well-known sci-fi films of all time, of course, but it remains incredibly fresh and exciting nearly thirty years after its release. Along with sequels The Matrix: Reloaded, The Matrix: Revolutions, and The Matrix: Resurrections, The Matrix universe offers a story that VisionQuest fans will love, one that includes lushly imagined virtual worlds, questions surrounding existence and consciousness, and the ultimate question of our responsibility as sentient beings (whether we’re organic, programmed, or summoned via magic).

You know the basics—at some point in the future, artificially intelligent machines rebel against their creators, win the war, and transform humans into a power source, keeping them docile by inserting their consciousness into a virtual world called the Matrix, which resembles 1990s Chicago. One such human, Thomas Anderson (Keanu Reeves) is prophesied to be The One, the human who will turn the Matrix against its makers and free humanity. When he’s in the virtual world, Anderson is Neo, and he slowly gains incredible powers as he learns to hack the artificial environment around him.

It’s heavier, denser, and more action-oriented than VisionQuest (the film invented Bullet Time, after all), but The Matrix and its sequels explore similar themes and offer similarly eye-popping visuals. The questions of whether a machine (or an artificial intelligence) can be sentient and truly care about the entities around it are the same, really, and the Agents that Neo and his allies have to battle against in The Matrix bring the same kind of menace as Vision's foes Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) and the Paladin (Todd Stashwick). Hugo Weaving’s Agent Smith likewise delivers the same vibe of cold, disinterested superiority as Spader’s Ultron.

The Matrix has a bigger budget and puts a lot of it into spectacular action and special effects sequences that VisionQuest can’t quite match. But the two narratives share an exploration of identity, a questioning of reality, and the nature of artificial intelligences within a smart sci-fi setting. In short, The Matrix is the ideal follow-up when you finish the series. Rent The Matrix on Prime Video.

Need more films that explore virtual worlds, artificial beings, and deep existential questions? Look no further—here are some more movies that fit the bill.

Heavy on the existential questions about sentience and light on speculative action, Her is a mumblecore sci-fi masterpiece. In a near future not too dissimilar from our present, Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix) is a lonely man on the cusp of divorce who begins using (and training) an AI he names Samantha (voiced by Scarlett Johansson). Samantha has the ability to evolve and grow, and as their relationship deepens, she becomes more complex, independent, and powerful, eventually evolving into something wholly new. Just like Vision, Samantha is a sentient artificial entity that is figuring out its existence while we watch. Rent Her on Prime Video.

If the idea of androids fighting for their sovereignty is what excites you about VisionQuest, definitely check out Ex Machina. Caleb Smith (Domhnall Gleeson) is brought to the remote lab of his company’s CEO (Oscar Isaac) to determine if the humanoid robot he’s created, named Ava (Alicia Vikander), passes the Turing Test for true sentience. Things go wildly off the rails, but before they do, the film sinks into many of the same philosophical questions that VisionQuest explores as Ava manipulates Caleb into helping her escape. It’s a darker and more violent story than VisionQuest, but fans of the series will love it. Stream Ex Machina on The Roku Channel or Hulu, or rent it on Prime Video.

If it’s the fuzzy parent-child relationship between Vision and Tommy that pulls you into VisionQuest, check out The Creator. After a rogue AI detonates a nuclear weapon over Los Angeles, most of the world bans artificial intelligences, and Joshua Taylor (John David Washington) goes undercover to infiltrate an AI architect’s base. Eventually, he finds himself on the run with a powerful “simulant” in the form of a young child named Alphie (Madeleine Yuna Voyles). The strange parent-child bond that emerges between Taylor and Alphie as he seeks to understand what’s right and what’s necessary is exactly what fans of the show will love. Stream The Creator on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

In VisionQuest, White Vision has all of his memories—but as data, not as lived, emotional experiences. That makes his efforts to understand his existence and his responsibility to the boy who might be a version of his son (it’s complicated) poignant and moving. Those two words definitely describe After Yang, a story about a family that fights to save the artificial companion they bought for their adopted daughter when it malfunctions. Over the course of the film, the inhuman Yang becomes defined by the memories contained in its core, and the question of whether an artificial intelligence can truly matter to humans is answered with a resounding yes. Stream After Yang on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

No discussion of artificial life and sentience is complete without mentioning Blade Runner. While the 1982 original is a classic, the 2017 sequel is a better thematic and visual match to VisionQuest. Officer K (Ryan Gosling) is a replicant, an artificial being with built-in limitations, who wants to be recognized as a person, a being with a soul. Like Vision, he has implanted memories that offer him comfort and context for his life, but he’s not sure if he can accept them as truly his own. Plus, the film offers lush visuals and Harrison Ford reprising his role in the original film, so you simply can’t go wrong. Rent Blade Runner 2049 on Prime Video.

Tony DiNozzo's return and subsequent promotion to Director of NCIS is the big story of Season 24. It was a surprising twist, and one that longtime fan and star Katrina Law told CinemaBlend she was amped for. It turns out she had a lot of questions about how Jessica Knight and Tony would interact, and she loved what the team came up with.

As NCIS continues its run on the 2026 TV schedule, I spoke to Law about the season thus far, as well as what we've seen. I talked about Michael Weatherly's big role in the new season, and she confirmed she was absolutely psyched to see the former vet of the show back in action:

I was geeked out. While she might've preferred to see her buddy McGee get the job as NCIS director, Jessica Knight has found good footing with Tony thus far. Granted, she's basically playing spy for his wife Ziva, but that kind of leverage can go a long way toward keeping her in his good graces.

I also had to bring up that Knight mentioning on camera that she's in contact with Ziva sets the stage for Cote de Pablo's eventual return to NCIS as well. Katrina Law confirmed she's optimistic we'll see Ziva before too long, and there's going to be a lot of fun stuff happening with her and Knight:

He's tried to jump in and participate in the investigations, much to the chagrin of some of the agents. #3523. This '60s Japanese Thriller Is One Of The Best Movies Streaming On HBO Max

Ben Affleck's new kidnapping thriller "Animals" made a splash on Netflix this year — at least in terms of viewership. Critics dismissed the picture, and justifiably so, given how shaky the "Animals" script is. Yours truly clocked that "Animals" is basically an unauthorized remake of Akira Kurosawa's "High and Low," and I was not the only one.

In both movies, a rich man who has just invested all his money in a venture (a business takeover in "High and Low," a mayoral campaign in "Animals") receives a phone call that his son has been kidnapped. Except, the ransomers mistakenly took one of his much poorer employee's sons — so, does he still bankrupt himself to save a kid that isn't his?

I would highly suggest turning off Netflix and flipping over to HBO Max (where "High and Low" is currently streaming) to watch Akira Kurosawa show you how it's done. Several of the filmmaker's classics are currently streaming on there, including "Seven Samurai," "Rashomon," "Throne of Blood," and "Yojimbo." Like with "High and Low," all of those movies also star Toshiro Mifune, Kurosawa's go-to leading man at his peak. But "High and Low" is my personal favorite of the bunch and Kurosawa's magnum opus.

Kurosawa is distinguished for his samurai movies or Jidaigeki (Japanese historical dramas). He often adapted William Shakespeare's plays, too, moving their stories from Europe to to the east: "Throne of Blood" is literally just "Macbeth" in feudal Japan, and it's one of the best "Macbeth" movies to boot.

"High and Low" stands out in that collection for its contemporary setting and source material. (It's adapted from a procedural novel, "King's Ransom," by American author Ed McBain.) While he may not have had the Bard to draw on this time, Kurosawa still made some pure cinematic brilliance.

If I were ever tasked with assembling a list of "old" and/or international movies to convince people that black and white or non-English-language movies can be great, "High and Low" would be on there, 100%. That's not just because it's great (it is), but it's great popular entertainment: a taut suspense thriller and investigative procedural. It's not at all "pretentious," as untrained viewers might call it.

"Someone wants a ransom for the wrong kid, but only you can pay it" is also a great moral dilemma for a thriller and one that slots neatly into anywhere in the world with class disparity. That's why "High and Low" has been remade in many different settings. We know what a hero would do in this situation, but we're not sure if Kingo Gondo (Toshiro Mifune) is a hero from the beginning.

Now, the movie wisely stacks the deck in Gondo's favor so he doesn't come off as an aloof rich guy. He wasn't born rich, he worked his way up, so he knows what losing everything is like, and that makes the sacrifice extra painful. And while he works in shoe manufacturing, he's got a creative spirit. He's planning a leveraged buyout because he wants to make high-quality shoes his way instead of saving money on a cheaper product.

Would you sacrifice all your savings and life's work to save an innocent child? You probably just answered "yes," but it's still an abstract question for you. "High and Low" portrays how someone would act when the choice and its consequences become real. The most impressive balancing act in the movie is that it both does and doesn't feel like a foregone conclusion when he agrees to pay the ransom.

"High and Low" doesn't end when the ransom gets paid. The kidnapper escapes, setting off the second half, where Gondo is largely absent and the police characters take over to try and find the kidnapper. "High and Low" is as bifurcated as its title, with the two halves divided by setting: Gondo's hilltop mansion in the first half, the town below in the second, with the train sequence where Gondo delivers the ransom as a fitting bridge. (It's worth noting that a more literal translation of the original Japanese title, "Tengoku to Jigoku," is "Heaven and Hell.")

During that first half, Kurosawa uses Gondo's living room like a theater stage. Even confined to a single house, the picture looks huge. The screen is wide enough that you can keep track of each character's movements, and the film blocks no frame carelessly. The contained setting, and immense pressure placed on Gondo, still give the first half a claustrophobic feeling. The second half entering the town below is a pressure release, but your attention doesn't go slack because there's still a mystery to solve. The ending of "High and Low," where Gondo and the kidnapper finally come face-to-face, is a triumphant denouement.

Many great American filmmakers have looked to Akira Kurosawa, like "The Godfather" director Francis Ford Coppola. Watching "High and Low," it's easy to understand why.

#3522. In One Scene, Prime Video Officially Rewrites Gandalf’s Mission in Lord of the Rings

Gandalf isn’t just an old man, he’s a divine guardian

By the end of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 2, Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) had chosen his name and wizard staff and found a mentor in the enigmatic Tom Bombadil (Rory Kinnear). Season 3 picks up five years later, and Gandalf has spent that time vexing the Dark Wizard (Ciarán Hinds) and his forces in Rhûn. Gandalf sees the Dark Wizard as a dangerous foe, but their relationship is more complicated. Here’s what you need to know about the two wizards, and how they fit into J.R.R. Tolkien’s complex cosmology.

This article contains spoilers for the first three episodes of season 3 of The Rings of Power

Tolkien’s wizards aren’t just old men who wield magical power. They are Maiar, primordial spirits who serve the Valar, the divine beings that helped Eru Ilúvatar create the world. Sauron is a fallen Maia who served the rebel Vala Morgoth. The five Istari are Maiar sent in the form of old Men to Middle-earth to stop Sauron. They became known as wizards, and their members include Gandalf, Saruman, and Radagast.

Those are the only three wizards mentioned by name in The Lord of the Rings, but Tolkien’s Unfinished Tales mentions there were two more who were sent to the East: Pallando and Alatar. In season 3, episode 3, it’s revealed that the Dark Wizard is Pallando. He wanted more than to serve the Valar, so he killed Alatar, an act so evil it turned Rhûn into a desert. Pallando clearly has regrets as he’s trying to regrow the Tears of the Valar lilies that used to cover Rhûn. He hopes that he can make the land green again using one of Sauron’s rings.

“There’s a moment in the third episode, when Gandalf has infiltrated the Dark Wizard’s temple, and he sees Pallando sitting on the throne looking very forlorn,” series co-creator Patrick McKay told Polygon in a recent video interview. “That one shot, and that one moment from Ciarán Hinds, will lend a realism and a depth to that character that we as an audience were craving. Gandalf notices it, and I think the audience will notice it, too. Even in a story with all this magic and all this wonder, one good actor giving one good performance in one shot can speak volumes.”

The Dark Wizard’s servants fear Gandalf, who they say draws his power from the Secret Fire itself. Gandalf thinks that defeating the Dark Wizard is key to saving Middle-earth, since it will keep the armies of Rhûn from joining Sauron. Tom is skeptical that Gandalf is meant to defeat him, and the exasperated wizard leaves Tom’s hut to go catch a rabbit for stew. He then has a vision of the Secret Fire speaking to him, a moment McKay said is inspired by Moses and the Burning Bush.

The Secret Fire is the power that Eru Ilúvatar used to create the world, a force that burns within all sentient beings. Eru is Tolkien’s name for God, while the Secret Fire represents the Holy Spirit. When Gandalf faces the Balrog – a fallen Maia serving Morgoth – in Khazad-dûm in The Fellowship of the Ring, he shouts, "I am a servant of the Secret Fire.”

The Fire address Gandalf as Olórin, the name he was given as a Maiar before he came to Middle-earth and adopted the name Gandalf. It also calls him Mithrandir, his name among the Elves, which means the Grey Pilgrim. The Secret Fire then explains that Gandalf isn’t meant to defeat the Dark Wizard but to redeem him, because only together can they save Middle-earth.

Pallando needs the help. He hoped to get one of the nine rings for mortal men by sending emissaries to Sauron to accept his alliance with Rhûn. However, Sauron killed the most loyal of the Dark Wizard’s servants and encouraged the others to fight amongst themselves to claim a ring. Khamûl the Easterling (Zubin Varla) was the winner, and donning a ring freed him from the Dark Wizard’s flesh-warping curse. He returned to Rhûn a Nazgnagôl, challenging the Dark Wizard for his throne and ordering that he march his armies to Mordor. The Dark Wizard has effectively already been defeated, but if Gandalf can get him to see the light, they might be able to keep Sauron from getting even stronger.

The show will tackle one of Tolkien’s biggest qualms with his own work

The end of a trilogy that started back in 2020 is upon us. The "WandaVision" trilogy is one of the most significant pieces of Marvel's Multiverse Saga, focusing on Wanda Maximoff and Vision's complicated relationship and the characters who are connected to them. With "VisionQuest" reaching its conclusion, the trilogy has been capped off. But is it all over once the credits start to roll on the final episode? Or is there more to it?

This series brings back Paul Bettany as Vision for what is presumably one last ride. It also brings back James Spader as Ultron more than a decade later. How exactly is Ultron alive in "VisionQuest?" That's one of many questions the show has answered during its run.

The Marvel Cinematic Universe is notorious for including post-credits scenes in its movies and TV shows. Some of them have been very good and consequential, such as Thanos arriving in "The Avengers." Some of Marvel's worst post-credits scenes? Not so good. Whatever shape they take, it's always reasonable to wonder whether or not a given MCU project contains a credits scene or two.

That brings us back to the "VisonQuest" season finale. We're here to offer up a spoiler-free guide to the show's credits scene situation. Do you need to stick around? Or can you find something else to watch once the credits roll? Seriously, we're not going to spoil anything significant. We're just here to arm viewers with necessary information. With that out of the way, let's get into it.

Yes, "VisionQuest" does have a post-credits scene that fans should be aware of. In fact, there are two scenes. One of the scenes is important enough that viewers who made it all the way through the series shouldn't skip it. It helps put a button on the events that transpired in the show. Without spoiling anything, it's not a throwaway gag or anything like that. In fact, go ahead and watch both scenes. It's worth it.

This shouldn't come as a huge surprise. "WandaVision" also had a pretty significant credits scene. The "WandaVision" post-credits scene was sneakily altered by Marvel Studios, though that's another conversation entirely. Still, it stands to reason that the finale to this trilogy would include a credits scene as well.

This show had a lot to accomplish and was rather ambitious. "VisionQuest" explained the biggest plot hole from "Avengers: Age of Ultron," and also had to serve as a satisfying end for a character who has been with the MCU since its earliest days. No pressure.

Christopher J. Byrne, Gandja Monteiro, Vincenzo Natali, and Terry Matalas directed episodes of the series. For over 20 years now, the 2003 Mike Myers version of The Cat In The Hat has been the only version of the classic Dr. Seuss book to watch. However, this past weekend, it got the animation treatment, and it’s a blast of an adaptation. I even have an idea for a spinoff, and I ran it by some of the cast. SPOILERS ahead!

Look, I like The Cat, especially because he’s voiced by Bill Hader years after he played the character on SNL. But to me, the real highlight of the film are The Things. In my opinion, they are like much more likeable Minions, and the movie even explores what can happen to one when they get villainous. As we learn at the end of The Cat In The Hat, the reason why Thing 2 was missing is that he became The Something due to overusing the Go-Backer device. Oh, and of course there’s that meta line where The Cat tells The Things to wait for their own movie.

The Things are pretty mysterious characters, but I thought The Cat in the Hat did an excellent job of making them so fun and intriguing. I think it would be so much fun to see them on their own adventure after this movie earned a thumbs-up with audiences through an “A” CinemaScore. Though it’ll have to earn more money at the box office after Godzilla Minus Zero won the weekend.

When CinemaBlend spoke to the cast of The Cat In The Hat, I brought up the topic of a Things spinoff. Here’s what Abbott Elementary’s Quinta Brunson, a.k.a. Sherrie from HR in the movie, had to say:

I wanna learn everything about them. This movie opening the crate, so to speak, on The Thing world, made me wanna know way more. I still have a lot of questions. Like, are they related? Are they from a planet? Is there offspring? Do they fall in love? Do they get married? I have a lot of questions. Why are they numbered? Do they have names beyond the numbers?

I love all these questions she has about The Things, because I had many of them myself. The Things have always been a memorable part of The Cat In The Hat book, but it would be so fun for a spinoff to explore who they are without The Cat. Here’s what Mr. Hoogeboom voice actor Giancarlo Esposito added:

I'm fascinated by The Things. I think they're on some advanced level of intellectual and emotional feeling. I just think that they're simpler, and somehow they communicate in a way that's clearer than any words could ever get.

I feel like a lot of kids are going to start learning Thinglish as is, and I wanted my own Thing plushy the moment I finished the movie. I even brought it up to the writer/directors Erica Rivinoja and Alessandro Carloni. Here’s what Carloni had to say about my idea:

If we're so lucky that the audience wants more of the characters we created, that would be very flattering. Give them what they want.

We’ll have to wait and see if this becomes a reality! For now, you can watch The Cat In The Hat only in theaters.

Amazon has dropped the Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar to $649 from its usual $999, taking $350 off and bringing it to the lowest price we've seen so far, according to price trackers. PCMag rated the Smart Ultra "outstanding," highlighting its ability to deliver surprisingly immersive Dolby Atmos audio without requiring a room full of additional speakers. If you don't need Bose's top-tier model, there's a less expensive option as well: the Bose Smart Dolby Atmos Soundbar ($399, down from $429), which sits below the Smart Ultra in the lineup.

The Smart Ultra uses a 5.1.2-channel design with nine drivers, including two upward-firing drivers that bounce sound off the ceiling to create height effects. In practice, that means movies, TV shows, and games feel larger and more spacious than they do through most single-bar setups. Bose also includes its AdaptiQ room-calibration system, which measures your room's acoustics and adjusts the sound accordingly. The process takes a few minutes, but it helps the soundbar perform better across different spaces rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all tuning profile. The soundbar also works as a smart speaker, with Amazon Alexa built in and support for Apple AirPlay 2, Google Cast, Spotify Connect, Bluetooth, and multi-room audio through the Bose app.

Its biggest compromise is bass—for a single soundbar, its low end is respectable, but it can't fully replace what a dedicated subwoofer brings to action movies, concerts, or bass-heavy music. The good news is that Bose allows you to expand the system later with compatible wireless subwoofers and surround speakers if you decide you want more impact. For anyone looking for a premium one-piece soundbar that delivers convincing Dolby Atmos effects, clear dialogue, built-in smart features, and a much larger soundstage than TV speakers can provide, the Smart Ultra remains one of the strongest standalone options available, especially at this price.

VisionQuest completed the story that began in 2020 with WandaVision, bringing things full circle by again using the framing of classic sitcoms as a way to tell a deep story about grief and family. The VisionQuest finale was released on Nov. 10, and viewers will want to keep watching through the credits, which include a pair of scenes with big implications for the future of the Marvel Cinematic Universe.

One scene is closely tied to the plot of VisionQuest, so it might not pay off for a while, but the other one directly ties into Avengers: Doomsday, Marvel’s next big blockbuster, releasing on Dec. 18. Here’s what it all means.This article contains spoilers for the series finale of VisionQuest.

The first post-credits scene shows Ultron (James Spader) holding a computer chip with the name Jocasta on it. AI and nanotechnology scientists Josephine Carrington (T'Nia Miller) and her husband Virgil Horton (Spader) scanned their own consciousnesses to create advanced AI, with Virgil serving as the blueprint for Ultron and Josephine for Jocasta. After Jocasta died of a degenerative hereditary disease, Virgil put her mind in a new synthezoid body but erased her memories of him. Jocasta and Ultron then fell in love.

In the VisionQuest season finale, Virgil killed Jocasta by shooting her with an adamantium bullet, enraging Ultron so much that he almost used nanobots to wipe out London. Vision (Paul Bettany) was eventually able to talk him down by trapping him in a sitcom, and Ultron deactivated the nanobots and fled. He’s clearly considering reviving Jocasta to resume their relationship. That could be very dangerous for the MCU, but it’s not something we’re likely to see any time soon.

The second post-credits scene will have a far more immediate payoff. It shows the end of the movie Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, where Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen), aka the Scarlet Witch, destroys Mount Wundagore, the home of the cursed magical grimoire, the Darkhold. Wanda had been corrupted by the Darkhold in her attempt to use the book to bring back her children Billy and Tommy, who seemingly ceased to exist when she released her control of Westview at the end of WandaVision.

Wanda was the primary villain of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness. She used the powers of the Darkhold to summon demons to try to capture America Chavez (Xochitl Gomez) and steal her multiverse-traveling powers. She also killed almost all the members of the Illuminati, a group of heroes from another universe, including Charles Xavier (Patrick Stewart) and Peggy Carter (Hayley Atwell). After seeing how her evil deeds terrified a version of Billy and Tommy from another Earth, Wanda tried to make up for her mistakes by sacrificing herself to make sure no one else could use the Darkhold.

VisionQuest brings viewers back to the moment of Wanda’s supposed death. After the building collapses, Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) arrives and magically lifts the wreckage off Wanda. He says: “Scarlet Witch, awaken. Your powers will be mine.” She is revived with a gasp, clearly setting up her appearance as one of Doom’s lieutenants in Avengers: Doomsday.

At San Diego Comic-Con, Marvel sparked a lot of speculation about Doom’s allies by showing off a set of costumes at their booth. Over three days, Marvel showed off three masked figures in brightly colored cloaks that would be worn by the Latverian Witches, magic users serving Doom in Avengers: Doomsday. The SDCC costumes were in green, purple, and gold, though a poster revealed in early October showed Doom followed by witches wearing green, purple, and red.

It now seems clear that the Scarlet Witch is the red Latverian witch, meaning the other two masks are also probably hiding familiar faces. Green seems very likely to be Sylvie Laufeydottir (Sophia Di Martino), the Loki variant last seen at the end of Loki. She is a powerful magic user associated with the color green. Loki (Tom Hiddleston) is already confirmed to be returning for Doomsday, setting up another conflict between him and Sylvie about how best to protect the multiverse.

The identity of the purple witch is a bit more uncertain. Agatha Harkness (Kathryn Hahn) was the previous owner of the Darkhold and is strongly associated with purple. She died at the end of Agatha All Along, though her ghost is still serving as a mentor to Wanda’s son, Billy (Joe Locke). But Doom could almost assuredly find another version of her in the multiverse eager to team up for more magical might.

Another strong contender is Clea (Charlize Theron), the sorceress who showed up in the mid-credits scene of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness to take Strange to the Dark Dimension to prevent an incursion that could destroy a universe. That scene hasn’t paid off yet, so it’s possible that Doom has recruited Clea into his schemes by convincing her he’s the best person to protect the multiverse.

Wanda will be one of Doom’s lieutenants in Avengers: Doomsday, and a family reunion seems all but certain. After VisionQuest’s finale, Marvel Studios shared a cryptic post on X using binary code. When translated, the post read: “We could never leave each other, even if we tried.” This is a part of Wanda’s quote in the WandaVision finale: “You know, a family is forever. We could never truly leave each other, even if we tried.”

VisionQuest reunited Vision, Billy, and Tommy (Ruaridh Mollica). It seems all but certain Wanda will find her way back to her family, which could be key to breaking Doom’s hold over her.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3515. VisionQuest: The Identity Of The Client, Explained

Spoilers ahead for "VisionQuest" Episode 8, "Forever."

Ultron (James Spader) may have no strings on him anymore, but someone has been manipulating the events of "VisionQuest" like a puppetmaster. That someone is The Client, who hired the bounty hunter Paladin (Todd Stashwick) to capture Vision (Paul Bettany). We've gotten glimpses of The Client all season, but only as a digitally altered voice or a faceless avatar ... until Episode 7, "Immolation."

At the episode's end, Vision and Ultron's gynoid lover Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) are delivered to The Client's doorstep. Out of said door walks ... someone who looks just like Ultron's human avatar. Huh?

"Forever" clarifies it. "The Client" is Virgil Horton, grandson of Phineas Horton (Bettany), the scientist who created the Synthetic Man/Human Torch (Bettany again) in the 1940s. As Virgil explains, the Synthetic Man's uncontrolled fire powers mean that Dr. Horton was considered a failure. Years ago, Virgil joined with Dr. Josephine Carrington (Miller) to perfect AI in hopes of redeeming the Horton family legacy. They scanned their own brainwaves to create the genesis of what Tony Stark (Robert Downey Jr.) completed.

Horton and Carrington also fell in love. After Carrington's death from a terminal illness, Horton revived her as Jocasta. As Virgil explains, he was one of the engineers hired by SWORD to rebuild Vision back in "WandaVision." After that, he created a robotic body for Carrington's mind-scanned AI. Jocasta being a recent creation helps explain why she looks like feminine Ultron, but why did Virgil then erase her memories of him and her creation?

Virgil believes the only worthy lover of a "goddess" like Jocasta is a god. So, he intends to delete Vision's personality and then upload himself into Vision's shell, so he and Jocasta can rule an Earth infected with Jocasta's hive mind nanites.

Virgil's borderline-incestuous romance plan echoes the central influence of Ultron: "Frankenstein," specifically when the Creature asks Doctor Frankenstein to make him a companion. Virgil's plan is rather similar to Kenneth Branagh's 1994 "Frankenstein" film adaptation, where Victor Frankenstein (Branagh) tries to resurrect his dead wife Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter) through the same process by which he made the Creature (Robert De Niro).

There's an implication that Virgil scanning his brainwaves for his and Josephine's AI embedded his personality into the AI code. That's why Ultron basically has his same flamboyant personality, his voice, and why Ultron wears Virgil's face as his human avatar. "VisionQuest" showrunner Terry Matalas has said giving Ultron a human form in "VisionQuest" was about getting the most out of Spader's performance. Now, we know, it was also essential to the pay off of this twist about the Client's identity. But "Forever" breaks out Ultron's robotic form, too.

Virgil's plan fails because Jocasta has fallen for Ultron and wants him to be her eternal partner. Using the nanites, Ultron recreates his physical form and crushes Horton to death with a hug. It's a very Oedipal move: Ultron's defining goal has always been killing his father, whether it be Hank Pym (in Marvel's comics) or Tony Stark (in the Marvel Cinematic Universe). He comes close to that by killing the man of whom he's an artificial echo.

Ultron being based on Virgil also explains why fell for Jocasta in the first place. This restores some of the mirroring of the creator and creation that's present in comics Ultron. In the "Avengers" comics, Ultron created Jocasta from the brainwaves of Hank Pym's wife: Janet van Dyne, the Wasp, and his spiritual mother. Since Ultron is based on Hank's personality, he inherited his father's affections for Janet though extremely twisted means. The same logic applies to Spader's Ultron falling for this Jocasta.

Now, it's worth noting that while Phineas Horton and his Human Torch originated in Marvel Comics, Virgil did not. Rather, he's an original creation of this series, and "VisionQuest" seems to be using him as a proxy for the original Dr. Horton. Previously, Steve Englehart and George Tuska's "Avengers" #135 tied Horton and the Ultron-Vision lineage together, with the issue revealing that Ultron had abducted Phineas Horton and forced him to rebuild the inert Human Torch into the Vision.

Keep in mind, Ultron and Vision debuted in 1968. At that time, it was plausible that a scientist active in World War II would be living in retirement. But not so much in 2026, where it makes much more sense to use a descendant of Horton in the present day. It's the same time creep that led to Captain America originally missing only two decades of time while frozen to awakening almost a century later.

I would like to begin this story about Julie Chen Moonves commenting on the future of Big Brother by noting the longtime host of the CBS reality series is not planning an exit anytime soon. There will, well likely, be no goodbye episode for her in the near future, but given the show’s popularity, I’d be willing to bet she’ll retire before Big Brother is off the air. She’s seen the conversations surrounding her exit, and she’s honestly in agreement.

So, first let’s talk about the fan speculation. As recently as three months ago, some fans were speculating they think Julie Chen Moonves will leave Big Brother after Season 30. Season 28 just wrapped with Rick Devens as the winner, and the show airs in the summer, which would give her a couple more seasons on the TV schedule before bowing out. Of course, this is complete speculation, and the reality host has not said anything either way.

In other threads, fans have mentioned thinking that Big Brother and Amazing Race contestant, and Big Brother: Unlocked star could be the ideal choice. Honestly, it’s been a bit divisive, with some fans noting:

Even though the issue is apparently divisive, I know in general Big Brother fans can be haters and in many ways Hale would be an obvious and solid choice. The people worried about her being too polished in particular I think are reading into it hard. Chen Moonves herself is polished, professional and deeply unemotional as the host. I honestly think Hale would be a nice segue if the OG host were to leave. She may not be for everyone, but Chen Moonves isn't for everyone either.

I guess what I'm saying is it's impossible to make everyone happy, and Julie Chen Moonves is not a hater when it comes to Taylor Hale. In an interview with Variety, the interviewer casually mentioned the possibility of Taylor Hale taking over, and this is what Chen Moonves had to say.

I’ve wondered that too because, to me, she would be perfect.

She did tell the outlet Big Brother has had so many notable names that would be as solid as Hale, also name-dropping BB and Traitors' Derrick Levasseur, Jeff Schroeder and Jordan Lloyd. Her one takeaway though?

But then I don’t know how the network would feel about, ‘Is it too close to home that they’ve walked in their shoes? Does that put them too much in a position of judgment?' Part of me feels like maybe you want to keep the air pristine and have someone who comes from a news background. I got hired because I know how to do live interviews.

Interestingly, she actually talked about how she got the gig on Big Brother recently, telling fellow reality host Phil Keoghan CBS wanted someone with a news background to do the work on the show. At the time, it was heavily a social experiment as much as a reality show, and her background fed into that.

It would change things if Julie Chen Moonves were to leave, but I do think another contestant would be close enough to the franchise to step into her shoes flawlessly, and Taylor and Derek in particular do have the background to potentially do so.

Of course, this is if and when she ever steps down. She previously told EW she was "playing a game of chicken" with CBS' Jeff Probst and Phil Keoghan and would stick it out as long as they would. (Note: Jeff and Phil are also both older than the 56-year-old star is at 65 and 59 respectively.) We'll have to wait and see what happens, but I'm just saying, don't expect an announcement tomorrow.

#3512. VisionQuest's Finale Finally Pays Off A Story Marvel Started In Avengers: Age Of Ultron

What is grief if not spoilers persevering? This article discusses major plot details from the season finale of "VisionQuest."

An argument could be made that the "VisionQuest" finale was a confrontation over a decade in the making. Clearly, the well-received Disney+ series has marketed itself as a "WandaVision" sequel and a trilogy-capper to the story continued in "Agatha All Along." But there's no way around its biggest and most pressing concern: providing a fitting epilogue to the 2015 blockbuster "Avengers: Age of Ultron." In an inspired choice, "VisionQuest" showrunner Terry Matalas understood there was still plenty of unfinished business between James Spader's megalomaniac robot Ultron and Paul Bettany's synthezoid Vision, which finally pays off spectacularly in the eighth and final episode of the show.

Once Vision and Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) realize that the mysterious Client dogging their steps is actually Virgil Horton (also played by Spader), the descendant of Phineas Horton (aka the mind behind the Synthetic Man, as portrayed by Bettany), this sets up the finale's most compelling battle. No, it's not Horton's toxic, twisted love for Dr. Jo Carrington and his desire to inhabit Vision's body so they may live forever together. It's the apparent murder of Ultron's lover Jocasta, setting off Ultron's malevolence towards humanity and one last showdown with Vision.

This is precisely the kind of potential that shared universes were meant to fully realize — not cameos and references for the sake of it or disposable narratives to throw on in the background as white noise, but as meaningful additions to ongoing arcs for viewers willing to take the time to explore them. That may go down as the greatest accomplishment of "VisionQuest" in its finale, delivering the perfect button on the Ultron saga that "Age of Ultron" simply couldn't pull off.

Amazing what eight hours of storytelling can do that studio-meddled blockbusters never could, eh? In spite of its obvious shortcomings and compromises, we here at /Film are long-suffering defenders of "Avengers: Age of Ultron." Arguably the last time the Marvel Cinematic Universe was able to be as weird and messy and introspective as the comics themselves, the movie still managed to find moments of quiet poignancy amid all the mind-numbing spectacle. To no surprise, that's something showrunner Terry Matalas and his writers have carried over into "VisionQuest," and nowhere is that more confidently on display than in the finale.

We're not only talking about the moment when a dying Jocasta merges Ultron with the horde of killer nanobots and allows him to regain his physical form, fighting Vision in a well-staged battle that ought to be many a nerd's dream come to life. What puts the finale over the top is when it somehow combines the best of "Age of Ultron" with "WandaVision." Vision traps Ultron inside a sitcom-set mindscape where the two artificial beings can hash out their differences without throwing hands and trading particle beams at each other. If previous episodes filled in some Ultron-centric plot holes, then this one brings us back to their best moment of all — when, in the midst of Sokovia's destruction, the two land in an idyllic forest to talk about humanity's doomed fate, the grace found in their failings, and the fact that nothing beautiful is meant to last forever.

Here, the big climactic fight becomes a treatise on Ultron's all-consuming grief, his unresolved malevolence towards human beings, and, deep down, his debilitating fear of being alone.

To the credit of "VisionQuest," this season-long epilogue suggests there's more to his emotional journey than a single movie could ever explore. The finale digs even deeper to prove this, completing Ultron's transformation into something much more human by giving him someone to love. Despite the changes made to the comics' origins, the Ultron/Jocasta romance is a defining moment in Ultron's portrayal in the MCU. Finally, he can understand Vision's own progression to becoming an individual in his own right, along with all the joy and loss and humanity that comes with it.

That's probably why, even after he retreats back to his old ways and attempts to cause our extinction again, "VisionQuest" posits that Ultron isn't beyond redemption. Sure, it isn't until he's confronted with his own mortality that he finally decides to spare the world's population. But even that is as human as it gets. Vision helps him come to terms with what life has to offer. And when we leave him, eager to appreciate human art and perhaps even rebuild Jocasta, it's a perfect period to the end of his sentence ... or, perhaps, an ellipsis.

"VisionQuest" is now streaming on Disney+ in its entirety.

#3511. The Top 10 Movies Right Now, According to Streaming Data

The most streamed movie in October was Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day, but half of the month's top ten is made up of season-appropriate horror movies. This year's two most successful horror movies, Backrooms and Obsession, made the list; so did a classic (Halloween from 1978) and an art movie about the genre that Halloween created,Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Perfect double feature. Rounding out the list is the all-around-excellent Hokum. If you're not into horror, you might like Golden Arm, a comedy that refused to die, star-studded comedy The Invite, or ultimate crowd-pleaser Project Hail Mary.

Legendary director Steven Spielberg returns to the extraterrestrials he loves so much with a thriller that's a spiritual sequel to Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Disclosure Day details the events that lead up to the revelation that aliens are among us. Josh O’Connor plays Dr. Daniel Kellner, a cybersecurity expert for a government contractor who uncovers explosive evidence that his employers would kill to keep secret. Meanwhile, a TV meteorologist (Emily Blunt) begins speaking in an alien language. It all sets the stage for a series of set pieces and chases leading to the biggest revelation in human history. Stream Disclosure Day on Peacock.

Director Kane Parsons' analog horror breakthrough is proof that atmosphere, mood, and a fascinating story is scarier than CGI monsters every time. Based on the viral YouTube series of the same name, Backrooms tells the story of Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a store owner who discovers a labyrinthian liminal space in his furniture shop's basement. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, who goes downstairs for a visit and does not find it easy to return. A hit with critics—Backrooms is sitting at 86% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes—and audiences, Backrooms is a delicious Halloween treat for horror fans. Stream Backrooms on HBO Max.

Director Curry Barker is still in his 20s, but his debut theatrical feature is the kind of horror film that changes the entire genre. Obsession is a classic "be careful what you wish for" story that feels fresh thanks to its talented young cast, unpredictable plot, and careful pace. Michael Johnston plays a young man too scared to tell his crush how he feels, so he wishes she'd fall in love with him instead. The result is a nightmare embodied by Inde Navarrette, whose portrayal of the villain/victim is at once harrowing, terrifying, and heartbreaking. Obsession is the best horror movie I've seen in years. Stream Obsession on Peacock.

This comedy-drama from A24 is packed with heavy-hitting actors. Olivia Wilde, who also directed the film, plays Angela, and Seth Rogen plays her husband, Joe. With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. The evening unravels in hilarious ways, changing everyone's life. If you're a fan of smart, honest comedy, you will really like The Invite. Stream The Invite on HBO Max.

With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

When Golden Arm was released in 2021, not many people paid attention—with the pandemic in full swing, people didn't seem to have room for a quirky, indie comedy about a woman's quest to win the ladies' arm-wrestling championship—but it's a new age, and you should stream Golden Arm. It's sitting on a perfect score at Rotten Tomatoes, the movie's stars, Mary Holland and Betsy Sodaro, are charming and hilarious, and you can catch Golden Arm on Fandango, a free streaming service. What's not to love? Stream Golden Arm on Fandango or Prime Video.

In this crowd-pleasing sci-fi flick, Ryan Gosling stars as Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who is blasted into the firmament in a last-ditch effort to save the world. Grace is the only person on Earth who might know how to protect the sun from a cosmic infection that threatens all life, but he's definitely not an astronaut and doesn't see himself as a hero either. Will he rise to the occasion and learn something about his inner strength and resilience while saving us all from death? My money is on, "yeah, probably." Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+, Prime Video, and Philo.

Hundreds of slasher movies have been released since Halloween came out in 1978, but none have surpassed the original. Michael Myers' expressionless visage and the synthesizer theme have become universally recognized cultural signifiers for "horror movie," and every shot in Halloween has been stolen countless times, but the movie is so good, it's still scary. Watch or re-watch Halloween now! Stream Halloween on Philo, AMC+, and Prime Video.

Directed by and starring Ben Affleck, Animals is a thriller that tells the story of Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped and held for ransom. Having spent every dime on his outsider campaign, Kimball is forced to turn to extreme methods to guarantee his son's safe return, even if it conflicts with his public persona as a man of the people. Animals is a taut, expertly directed movie that should more than satisfy fans of political thrillers. Stream Animals on Netflix.

Actress Jessica Chastain has had a busy year, with the release of a number of exciting projects. Her new horror movie titled Other Mommy arrived in theaters back in October, and she's got a mystery thriller called Heartland coming out for those with a Netflix subscription. It turns out she got so into character on set that her face actually changed. No, she didn't use makeup to make that happen.

Chastain's Other Mommy face went viral when the movie came out, thanks to the unsettling smile slapped on her face during the movie's runtime. As you can see in the video above, I asked the Oscar-winning actress to compare the physical transformation she had for that movie and Heartland, and she told me:

I noticed something which, this is the first time I saw it in a character. I had so much kind of like anger playing Misty and like, I felt like very sensitive. Even though she's angry, I just felt like Misty should be so sensitive and so wounded that she can get hurt really easily so she reacts almost like an abused animal would react.

She's not wrong. Having seen the movie early, Misty does feel like an abused animal at times. There's a palpable sense of anger and hurt throughout most of her scenes, sometimes coming to a boil with Chastain vandalizing the property of her enemies. I loved watching her pop off throughout the movie's 112-minute runtime, mostly because I wish I could be so unapologetic IRL.

Later in our same conversation, the Mama actress went on to share how her character's anger physically manifested in her face when shooting Heartland. As she told me:

And I have like my chin in this movie has a dimple like on the side from tension that I'm holding that I've never seen before in a character that I've played. Um, and it was the first time I was like, 'Oh wow, that's so interesting that whatever I was feeling as this character changed my face a little bit. I mean, I guess it goes to show how powerful emotions are that they can physically change what you look like.

How trippy is that? Even Jessica Chastain was surprised by how playing Misty physically affected her. She's likely seen her own face on screen countless times over the years, so it was noticeably when a new dimple on her chin suddenly appeared. That shows just how deep into character she was while shooting Heartland. This commitment is a big reason why she's had such a celebrated career.

Fans will get to see her transformation into fictional country singer Misty Jones when Heartland arrives on Netflix November 13th as part of the 2026 movie release list. In addition to having drama and action, Chastain also belts out some country tunes in the new thriller.

As viewers make their long-awaited return to Middle-earth in Season 3 of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power," they will inevitably find things a bit different compared to where they last left off. The war that was teased at the conclusion of Season 2 has finally arrived, led by Charlie Vickers' Sauron unmasked in all his Dark Lord, uh, lordliness. A five-year time jump has reset the board considerably, putting heroes like Elrond (Robert Aramayo) and Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) on their back foot. But, as of Episode 2, fans will notice a significant tweak has been made to the opening credits sequence — one which contains an unseen connection to another popular streaming series.

Prior to the premiere, I recently attended the press junket for "The Rings of Power" and spoke with co-showrunner Patrick McKay about the third season. In our limited time together, I wanted to address the noticeably darker edge to the title sequence this time around and whether there might be any Easter eggs worth paying attention to, as has been the case in the prior two seasons. The creative team worked with studio and creative consultant Plains of Yonder, who crafted the sand-based vibrational look for the opening credits of "The Rings of Power" and apparently pitched a new approach for Season 3. Here's a behind-the-scenes featurette showcasing their previous work:

But observant fans may recognize the fingerprints of another haunting title sequence. Fans of HBO's "White Lotus," this one's for you. As proudly displayed on their website, Plains of Yonder was also involved in everyone's favorite dramedy about "when everybody goes to the hotel" (as McKay hilariously put it in our interview) and, specifically, the wallpaper-focused title sequence with some seriously unsettling imagery. Not surprisingly, the designers pulled a similar trick with "The Rings of Power."

In keeping with the theme of Season 3 of "The Rings of Power," Patrick McKay explained that Plains of Yonder pitched a different approach for the episodes to come. Where Seasons 1 and 2 contained hidden references and symbols pointing towards specific events of the story, the designers felt called to go in another direction. "They're really serious artists," McKay told me with obvious admiration for their skills. "They're really wonderful people to work with. I mean, we find [their work on Season 2] hypnotic."

Episode 2 provides our first glimpse of the newly-revamped opening credits sequence, with the familiar-looking particulates now taking on a much darker color palette as they reform into all sorts of different visuals: evocative landscapes, elemental imagery, and plenty more examples of abstract art. According to McKay:

"Season 3, they're like, 'We want to do something different. We want to change the entire thing. We want to revisit the concept and make it feel like this season feels [emotionally], rather than reference things that happen in the season.' So it's a little different this time. It's a little more dramatic, has a little more darkness to it."

The visuals certainly help strike a different tone for Season 3, although the stirring musical theme by "The Lord of the Rings" trilogy composer Howard Shore remains perfectly intact. This seems to suggest that, even in its darkest moments, Middle-earth always retains a glimmer of hope. New episodes of "The Rings of Power" stream on Prime Video every Wednesday.

#3508. Magic's Best Unofficial Format Is So Big, Burger King Is Running a Tournament

The Magic x Burger King collaboration is driving players wild

If you think that the Universe Beyond crossover with beloved sci-fi franchise Star Trek is the biggest thing currently going on in the Magic: The Gathering world, think again. On Nov. 10, details emerged from Italy about a country-exclusive collaboration between Magic and fast-food chain Burger King. Fans and players worldwide are going wild online about the Burger King-themed sleeves and deck box, but there is more to this unexpected campaign.

Announced through Burger King's Italian website, "Burger King Quest: The Great Gathering" will run from Nov. 10 to Nov. 30. Hungry fans can buy a Great Gathering Bundle at any Burger King restaurant for 19.90 euros ($22.20). The bundle includes a menu, choosing between Double Cheese King, Chicken Krispper, and Whopper Plant Based, plus a deck box and 100 sleeves branded with Burger King x Magic graphics. The deck box in particular has sent Magic players into a frenzy, and it's allegedly already sold out, with scalpers selling it online for ridiculous prices.

This is only half of what Burger King and Magic are cooking, pun intended. Also starting on Nov. 10, nine Burger King restaurants throughout Italy will host Magic tournaments. The winners will qualify for a big final showdown held during the Milan Games Week & Cartoomics, on Nov. 27-29. The tournaments will use the Pauper format, an unofficial 60-card constructed format that allows use of almost every card printed at the common rarity throughout the history of Magic.

Pauper is "unofficial" because it's not used in Wizards of the Coasts' official tournaments, such as the Pro Tour. The format was created by the community in the early 2000s, and became an official Magic Online (MTGO) format in 2008. Since then, Pauper grew exponentially, and Italy has a particularly large and active scene, hosting the biggest Pauper event in the world, Paupergeddon, which gathered over one thousand players in its latest edition.

Wizards of the Coast has slowly moved to give Pauper more official support through the Pauper Format Panel, an advisory panel led by Magic's principal designer Gavin Verhey that regulates bans and submits Pauper-related recommendations to the design team. There has been a lot of talk recently about Wizards deciding to fully support Pauper with dedicated products and official events, and this collaboration with Burger King could be an important step forward.

Pauper's popularity is due to many factors. First, the format is cheap, as one might expect. Top-tier competitive decks cost between $50-$100, but it's easy to build a strong deck with a lot less. Considering that Magic keeps getting more expensive, with a competitive Standard deck ranging between $250 and $600 currently, it's not hard to see Pauper's appeal. Moreover, despite being an "eternal" format (meaning one where cards do not rotate out), Pauper is far from "solved" or static. There are at least half a dozen decks that are competing for the top spot, with roughly double that number that can be considered a good choice to top eight a tournament. And with every new Magic set, there is always the chance of one or two new powerful common getting printed, shaking up Pauper further.

Finally, Pauper is by no means a "low power" format. You can play with iconic powerhouse cards such as Lightning Bolt or Counterspell. Pauper even has a version of the infamous "Oops, No Lands" Vintage deck, which can win as early as turn four, while explosive, red-based deck can get to the finish line just as quickly and easily.

Unfortunately, the Magic and Burger King collaboration is limited to Italy, but even if you can't get your hands on the cool deck box and sleeves, you can always try Pauper by looking for events in your area. If Wizards ever decides to fully support the format, you want to be ahead of the curve.

#3507. ‘Steps’ Review: A Disposable Fairy Tale Reminds Us That Cinderella Is Someone’s Hated Stepsister Too

The so-called villains of our childhood stories aren’t so bad when you look at things from their points of view. It’s a lesson that 21st century pop culture has taught us on a constant loop ever since “Wicked” kicked off an Oppenheimer-esque chain of tragedy that has seen everyone from Maleficent to Cruella de Vil humanized with their own origin story. It was inevitable that Cinderella’s allegedly wicked stepsisters would get their own mainstream version of the formula at some point (the Norwegian body horror movie exists in a separate, more ambitious category). If Hollywood can try to make us emphasize with someone who lives to kill puppies, anyone could have guessed that someone would slap a generational trauma label on literal children who grew up under the same evil matriarch as Cinderella. Related Stories Want a Full Scholarship to One of Our Film Festival Intensives? IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Video Contest Is Now Live Why Ari Aster and Lars Knudsen’s Square Peg Built a Therapy Circle for Hollywood’s Next Generation in Texas

We’re long past the point where reimagining the classics from other characters’ perspectives earns you any credit for originality. If anything, those of us who have lived through the past two decades of pop culture might feel like stories where fairy tale side characters get to reclaim their agency are more omnipresent than actual fairy tales. But those original stories have endured in part because there’s always a new generation arriving to be wowed by them, and there’s no reason that the same principle can’t apply to the reimaginings, too.

Nobody whose age contains multiple digits needs to seek out “Steps” for any reason other than potentially entertaining their own children. But those young enough to be unfamiliar with the tropes it employs might be entertained or even moved by the material. “Cinderella” was an appropriate story to use for the purpose, as the beloved story of wish fulfillment doesn’t contain nearly as much emotional depth as better fairy tales like “Beauty and the Beast” or “The Little Mermaid.” Maybe it’s all part of a healthy cycle in which young kids can watch “Cinderella” and slightly older ones can watch “Steps” before graduating to stories and re-imaginings that have more to say. But on its own terms, the animated film comes across as little more than disposable corporate entertainment.

Directed by Alyce Tzue & John Ripa from a script by six credited writers (Ava Tramer, James Madejski, Jen Chuck, Dana Schwartz, and Felicia Ho wrote the screenplay and Kate Micucci also has a story credit), “Steps” is a well-meaning entry into the subgenre that follows the blueprint competently enough to avoid being offensive or memorable. It literally opens on an old storybook with a stereotypical voiceover narrator reading the text about Cinderella being mistreated by her wicked stepsisters — before Lilith (Ali Wong) slides into the frame yelling “Whoa whoa whoa” and declares that the fairy tale is “character assassination.” From there, it’s only a matter of time before the contemporary pop needle drops start.

“Steps” has no choice but to expand the thin mythology of “Cinderella” before it has a chance to tell the other side of the story. In this version, the stepmother isn’t wicked at all — she’s just an Asian dressmaker who constantly moves her two daughters Lilith and Margot (Stephanie Tsu) wherever the work takes her. When her marriage takes them to the kingdom of Alouette, all three of them see it as a chance for some much-needed stability. More than anything, the girls are excited to hang out with their new stepsister, Cinderella (Amanda Seyfried).

Yes, they started out as friends! (Where have you heard that one before?) The initial villain in “Steps” isn’t Cinderella, but the all-Caucasian kingdom where she lives. The newly blended family has fun sharing their cultural traditions, but Lilith and Margot quickly learn that everyone else sees them as outsiders. And when mean girls at school like Nikki Glazer’s Priscilla start freezing them out, Cinderella doesn’t do enough to stand up for them. Thus a sibling rivalry is born — turns out that Cinderella is also the mean stepsister that somebody else hates.

Lilith decides that if she’s not going to be accepted, she might as well rebel. Like a lot of pre-teens, she’s torn between an impulse to reject the social hierarchy around her and the unavoidable fact that she still defines herself by it. She’s more interested in destroying what she hates than figuring out what she likes, so she steals a magic wand from the Fairy Godmother (Bette Midler) and sabotages the royal ball, significantly complicating things for the Prince (Daniel Radcliffe) and sending the kingdom into free-fall. It isn’t long before she and her loathed step-sister have to take a journey through the forest to set things right.

From its unpleasantly slick animation to its picture-perfect storytelling — Cinderella thinks Lilith is mean and Lilith thinks Cinderella is dumb and ditzy, but they both learn there’s more to the other than meets the eye — “Steps” is an example of how you can do everything “correctly” and be left with a film that’s too smooth around the edges to resonate. There’s enough for kids to enjoy, but this won’t be one that parents find themselves unexpectedly invested in.

For all its modern cliches, “Steps” still contains a few moments of genuine pathos that tug at the heartstrings. We can all relate to being bullied as kids and the cosmic importance that our young brains assign to being left out, and the film handles those early scenes admirably well. But nothing in the movie is strong enough to transcend the fact that it’s packaged in a tired formula that has lost any subversiveness it once had. These villain-led reimagnings were introduced as a way to counteract the two-dimensional nature of fairy tales, but it’s starting to feel like we replaced those Happily Ever After endings with something equally superficial.

“Steps” streams on Netflix beginning on Friday, November 20.

#3506. The Top 10 TV Series Right Now, According to Streaming Data

October's ten most-streamed series are packed with your future favorite shows. There's a couple of modernizations of horror franchises for Halloween (Carrie and Crystal Lake), as well as new horror series Below and Phony. There's an excellent new superhero series Lanterns, sprawling family drama East of Eden, and new seasons of favorites Ted Lasso, Slow Horses, The Diplomat, and Mobland. So don't even try to tell anyone there's nothing on.

Horror master Mike Flanagan (Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass) re-imagines Stephen King's tale of teenage telekinesis, taking the story from the 1970s to now, complete with cyber bullying, smart phones, and a modern sensibility. The core of the tale, though, remains the same, as does the titular character's bloody coming-of-age. Powered by a talented young cast that includes Siena Agudong as Susan and Summer H. Howell as the title character, Carrie is a trick-or-treat for horror fans. Stream Carrie on Prime.

Based on John Steinbeck's pillar of Western literature, East of Eden follows three generations of the hardscrabble Hamilton family and the upscale Trask family, farming and ranching clans in California's Salinas Valley. The show's production is a multigenerational story too: It was written and created by Zoe Kazan, whose grandpa Elia directed the 1955 film version of East of Eden. All respect to Elia Kazan, but Steinbeck's story is so massive, it needs a seven-part mini-series. East of Eden is the kind of sprawling, melodramatic story that episodic television was made for. Stream East of Eden on Netflix.

Like Carrie, Crystal Lake reimagines a horror classic—in this case, Friday the 13th—and expands the lore even beyond the 12 films in the franchise. If you've ever wondered how Pamela Voorhees, played here by Linda Cardellini, became a serial murderer, and how her son Jason ended up a relentless, camp-counselor-killing-machine who lives at the bottom of a lake, Crystal Lake has all the answers. In a lot of ways, this show is better than all of the movies. Stream Crystal Lake on Peacock.

Apple TV's Slow Horses delivers a realistic, nuanced take on espionage by detailing the lives of the losers of British Intelligence. Instead of chiseled good guys and gals saving the world, the agents of Slough House are a team of dysfunctional, troubled souls trying to do the right thing (usually) in a morally gray world, just like real agents. Their leader, gruff, obnoxious Jackson Lamb, is played to perfection by Gary Oldman. Slow Horses has an almost perfect Rotten Tomatoes score over its first five seasons, and season 6 is setting new records. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV+.

DC's TV revamp of Green Lantern details what happens when experienced Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) trains the new guy, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), on how to wield the mysterious and powerful Green Lantern Ring. It's a reserved, neo-noir style take on the comic mythos, as the heroes investigate a series of murders tied to an extraterrestrial threat. Lanterns is pulling in a better than 90% fresh ratings from Rotten Tomatoes, so it's definitely worth a stream. Stream Lanterns on HBO Max.

Created by Jesse McKeown and starring Josh Hartnett, Charlie Heaton, and Mackenzie Davis, Below is set in a Newfoundland fishing village beset with aquatic horror. When the Canadian government offers the residents of Snooks Arm a ton of money to relocate, no one really knows why, but ice fisherman Calvin Penney (Hartnett) suspects it has something to do with the monster he saw under the ice when he was a child. If you like taut creature feature style horror, check out Below. Stream Below on Netflix.

Season four of Ted Lasso sees the title character, played by Jason Sudeikis, returning to the UK to take on a new challenge: coaching the Lady Greyhounds, AFC Richmond's second-division women's football team. This multiple Emmy Award-winning series still has all the heart, humor, and positivity of the original run. Stream Ted Lasso on Apple TV+.

The mystery that drives creepy coming-of-age drama Phony is killer: Sonny Cooke, played by Sam Nivola, is a teenager with a very close relationship to his devoted single mother Ellen, played by Connie Britton. After a freak car accident, he wakes up convinced that his mom is an impostor. She looks the same, but there's something off about her in a way that Sonny can't describe, so he sets out to solve the mystery. Phony is rated over 90% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Stream Phony on Hulu.

In season four of political thriller series The Diplomat, the Kate Wyler, played by Keri Russell, finds that diplomatic relations between the U.S. and the UK are starting to crumble, and so is her marriage. Meanwhile, U.S. president Grace Penn, played by Allison Janney, and VP Hal Wyler, played by Rufus Sewell, continue their conspiracy to steal a Russian super-weapon, nudging the nation toward war with our longtime adversary. In other words, it's an international mess, with a few powerful people keeping the world from descending into chaos. If you like political intrigue, this is the series for you. Stream The Diplomat on Netflix.

Who doesn't love a sprawling organized crime drama? In Mobland, the crime is being organized in Great Britain, where two warring London crime families, the Harrigans and Stevensons, are locked in a battle for underworld power. In the middle of the crossfire is Harry Da Souza, a gritty fixer played to gruff perfection by Tom Hardy. Season 2 finds Da Souza in the unenviable position of holding together the Harrigan family on the verge of civil war. If you like backstabbing, scheming, murder, and other tropes of high-stakes crime thrillers, you'll like Mobland. Stream Mobland on Paramount+.

#3505. 32 Years Later, The Santa Clause's Line On Believing Is Still The Greatest Christmas Quote

Ah, "The Santa Clause." The holiday classic where Tim Allen (making his leading man debut in a movie) accidentally murders Jolly Old Saint Nick, featuring a title that tricked an entire generation into misspelling "Santa Claus." In the 1994 film (which ended up having to cut a risque joke), Allen plays Scott Calvin (Get it? His name has the same initials as SANTA CLAUS!), a divorced, work-obsessed marketing exec spending the holidays with his son, Charlie (Eric Lloyd).

Christmas Eve rolls around, and when the real Santa accidentally falls off Scott's roof and dies, Scott is forced to become the new Santa. Scott doesn't like this idea, especially when he starts growing a magical beard and a magical fat belly. It doesn't help that everyone around him — except Charlie — thinks he's gone insane. The film then unfolds over a year leading up to the following Christmas, where Scott has to come to terms with his new career.

Will Scott learn to be a better father, embrace the Christmas spirit, and thrive as the new Santa Claus? Of course he will, and then they'll make a string of sequels (and a streaming TV series reboot as well)! Happy holidays!

"Seeing isn't believing. Believing is seeing."

"Seeing is believing" is an age-old saying, but "The Santa Clause" flips this a bit. When Scott becomes Santa, he ends up in the North Pole, where the Elves who toil away in the workshop try to give him some help. One of those elves, Judy (Paige Tamada), utters our quote of the day: "Seeing isn't believing. Believing is seeing." This quote is later embraced wholeheartedly by Scott's son Charlie, who has to keep reminding Scott that all he has to do is look around to witness the reality of his new magical life.

Belief is a big part of "The Santa Clause." Scott has to believe in himself, while everyone around Scott has to believe he's really the new Santa. The hard-headed realists of the world understandably have trouble with all of this, and that includes Scott himself. He's a gruff American businessman! He doesn't believe in Christmas magic, gosh darn it! All Scott needs to do is open his eyes, both literally and metaphorically, to see the reality of his new situation. And isn't that what Christmas is all about? That and drinking way too much nog? Thank you,"The Santa Clause," for making us believe in Christmas.

"You want me to take the toys down the chimney into a strange house, IN MY UNDERWEAR?"

"Merry Christmas to all, and to all a good night! And when I wake up, I'm gettin' a CAT scan!"

"We're your worst nightmare. Elves with attitude."

"Everybody likes Denny's, it's an American institution."

"You see, children hold the spirit of Christmas within their hearts. You don't wanna be responsible for killing the spirit of Christmas, now would you ... Santa?"
