#3504. Rings of Power Episode 4 Ending Explained: What Happens to Galadriel, Celeborn, and Arondir?

A devastating betrayal, a long-awaited reunion, and a shocking death hit Middle-earth

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 3 sees Middle-earth in the midst of full-on war as Sauron (Charlie Vickers) continues his conquest. Yet he still hasn’t figured out how to forge the one weapon he knows will solidify his title as the Dark Lord: the One Ring.

The first batch of four episodes was released Nov. 11, bringing audiences back up to speed with many of the various characters and factions in Prime Video's sprawling Lord of the Rings prequel. As Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) grapples with the nature of his true purpose in Rhûn, both Numenor and Khazad-dûm are mired in political turmoil. Meanwhile the elves are struggling in the war as Sauron continues recruiting men to become his Nazgnagôl. (What about the Harfoots? We'll get to them later. Maybe.)

It all leads up to one of the show's most devastating moments yet at the end of The Rings of Power season 3, episode 4. What begins as a daring rescue mission inside the orc stronghold of Gundabad ends with an emotional reunion, a shocking death, and another demonstration of just how thoroughly Sauron corrupts those around him. Here's what happens at the end of The Rings of Power season 3, episode 4, and what it all means for the show going forward.

The episode's most important storyline unfolds as Galadriel (Morfydd Clark), Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova), and the orc general Marnûkh (Adam Young) reach the fortress of Gundabad, where they hope to find an Elven smith they believe Sauron needs to forge the One Ring. Unfortunately, it’s all essentially a waste of time because Marnûkh and Arondir discover that the smith is already dead. But just across the way, in another cell, they find Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower), Galadriel's long-lost husband, who has been held captive for centuries.

Celeborn proves instrumental in their escape, since Marnûkh’s knowledge of the fortress is a bit outdated. While Celeborn initially plans to flee by himself, once he hears them mention Galadriel, who has become separated from the group, he quickly helps them find her. After a touching reunion, they have to fight their way through the fortress to reach the roof. Galadriel’s plan involves lighting off a sort of flare with an arrow to call Landroval, the prince of the Great Eagles, who will carry them to safety. But with orcs closing in on them and firing arrows, Landroval has to hide until it’s safe for him to swoop in.

Then everything falls apart when one of the Nazgnagôl shows up and cuts Marnûkh down. Galadriel pleads with Arondir to run away, but he stands his ground. The Nazgnagôl encourages Arondir to flee and then takes off his helmet, revealing that it’s Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin), the son of Arondir’s former human lover, Bronwyn (Nazanin Boniadi), who had died in season 2. For a moment, it actually appears like Arondir might be able to convince Theo to take off the ring, but then Sauron arrives. He commands Theo to kill Arondir, and the swift way the attack happens make it seem like Sauron was controlling him directly.

Celeborn drags Galadriel over the ledge where they’re caught by Landroval, but the episode ends on a shot of Arondir's lifeless face.

It's a particularly cruel end for a character who has spent his entire story protecting others. Arondir even risks his life to save Marnûkh, an orc he really doesn’t like to begin with, only to die because he refuses to give up on Theo. The scene also makes Sauron’s control over the Nazgnagôl abundantly clear, even before he forges the One Ring. Theo’s hesitation, however, indicates that this control isn’t absolute without the One Ring.

Season 3 also introduces Durin’s (Owain Arthur) older brother Thráin (Eddie Marsan), and though their reunion seems mostly cheerful at first, it quickly descends into outright betrayal. By episode 4, Thráin openly challenges Durin's authority after the other Dwarf-lords demand access to the Seven Rings. They believe the rings could help protect their kingdoms, but Durin rightfully doesn’t trust their influence after seeing first-hand how it drove their father mad.

Thráin cleverly turns that argument against him. If their father was no longer of sound mind while wearing the ring, Thráin reasons, then his decision to name Durin as heir may not have been legitimate. This leads Thráin to formally challenge Durin to a trial by combat. But Thráin wants the rings more than he wants the throne. Before the fight, he tries to manipulate Disa into getting him the rings.

Before Disa and Durin were married, they had a fight and briefly split up. During that time, she and Thráin had a brief romantic encounter. Thráin threatens to tell Durin unless Disa convinces Durin to give him the Seven Rings, and he promises to abandon his claim to the throne in exchange.

Rather than submit to the blackmail, Disa confesses everything to Durin, and he forgives her. For a moment, it seems like Durin just needs to beat his brother and all will be well. But right before the duel, Durin’s son Gamli tells his father that he saw Disa with Thráin. This sends Durin flying into a rage, attacking his brother, ultimately leading to Thráin winning. We don’t see the aftermath, but the implication is clear: Thráin now has the throne and likely control of the rings (if he’s able to find them).

A contingent of Númenorians — called the Faithful — including Elendil (Lloyd Owen) and Isildur (Maxim Baldry) have been working behind the scenes to defy Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle) with the help of Eärien (Emma Horvath), who remains in Numenorian court. After she’s found out and dies at the end of episode 2, however, Pharazôn makes a play at kidnapping Elendil that ultimately fails when Elendil’s son Anárion (Andrew Richardson) saves him. All of this infighting is probably why, after the elves request aid from Numenor, Pharazôn sends them a rejection letter.

In episode 4, we see the elf leaders Círdan (Ben Daniels) and Gil-galad (Benjamin Walker) lamenting the state of the war in the aftermath of a battle against orcs. In a meeting with Elrond, he argues that the elves need to seek military assistance from Númenor. Elrond believes a personal appeal from the elven king might change the situation, and Círdan suggests that Elrond accompany him. Not only does Elrond have a great deal of experience in dealing with the other races, but his identical twin brother Elros was the founder and first king of Númenor.

That sets up a pretty clear trajectory for the show moving forward as some of these disconnected plotlines start to converge: Gil-galad and Elrond are heading to Númenor, while war continues to rage. Middle-earth history paints a pretty clear picture of where things go from here.

For now, however, the most immediate consequences of episode 4 are felt in Gundabad. Galadriel has finally recovered her husband, but Arondir is dead, Theo remains under the Dark Lord’s influence, and Sauron is inching ever closer to finally creating the One Ring.

Adapted for the screen by novelist Virginia Feito from her own work, the book comes recommended alongside its predecessor, “Mrs. March,” for anyone drawn to entertainment with “psycho” in the title.Beloved scream queen Maika Monroe (“It Follows,” “The Guest,” “Longlegs”) may be switching sides here, offering a twist on who horror fans root for once the blood starts flowing. (Hint: it’s the psycho.)

When we first meet Winifred, the Victorian-era governess is bound for her next assignment to teach the children of Mr. and Mrs. Pounds (Jason Isaacs and a sneaky-great Ruth Wilson, respectively) at their sprawling Yorkshire estate. “This won’t be like the other times,” she tells herself, winking mightily at how all those other times turned out. Our Winifred sports dead eyes and a rictus grin she works so very hard to fix in place. It’s even better when she attempts to imitate those around her, all the better to approximate “being human.”

No question, there’s something very wrong with Winifred. But what? You’ll find out soon enough. Possessed of “a darkness” she cannot shake, Monroe’s Winifred practically vibrates with the need to hold things together. It does not always work for her, but it is nearly always funny, deliciously and dementedly so.

Wigon and Freito don’t balk at the “psycho” promise of their story, as Winifred happily whacks away (often literally) at everyone icky, from gardeners to nurses (Thomasin McKenzie) and, yes, at least one baby. Killing scenes are elegantly, amusingly cut by editors Dustin Chow and Lance Edmands and designed for maximum gasps. Blood flows, then spurts, then pools. Sometimes it gets on Winifred’s face or her collar. She moves on, grimly and happily.

Cinematographer Nico Aguilar brings a similar energy to his work, shooting in and through keyholes, swinging his camera like a clock pendulum, even briefly adapting the perspective of a swallowed (redacted, for spoilers) as it travels into Winifred’s belly. It’s playful and gross, wholly fitting the material. Mostly, it’s so dark and fucked up you can’t help but laugh. OH! Did they do that? Yes, yes they did.

Possessed by the notion that she’s meant to be a part of the Pounds family (who would want to be? these aristocrats are monstrous), Winifred continues to fray. Bloodlusty audiences will be charmed by her go-for-broke attitude (more like go-for-the-throat), plus a steady stream of visual cues as to her current state. Dreams and nightmares merge, she’s haunted by the Pounds’ family mascot of a wild boar (particularly in an ever-morphing tapestry), and she simply can’t stop sneaking into places to stare at people while they sleep.

Clocking in at a tight 90 minutes, some changes to the also-slim book are smart, while others dilute its darkest impulses. Gone is the countdown to a Christmas massacre, which frames the novel; hell, gone is the whole Christmas massacre. Freito’s script leads up to a different sort of celebration, doing away with many of the most colorful supporting characters in the process (Mrs. Fancey, we hardly knew ye!).

That choice isn’t disastrous, although the execution of the big! final! event! is oddly watered down. Here it’s imagined as a battle of Winifred’s wills… but, erm, what wills? The book and the film each offer enough reasons for why our heroine is the way she is, Wigon’s film oddly bisects her spirit by implying she’s not fully on board with all the evil she commits.

For fans of the novel and its wonderfully unrepentant star, this choice might rankle; it’s also odd that Freito would go this route with her own adaptation. “Well, that’s not my ‘Victorian Psycho’ — and she’s not. That’s such a shame because for much of the film, she’s even better. By tempering her impulses and inner monologue, the film ends with less of the giddy gore that makes the rest of it such a dark treat. Dare we say it? We would have loved for this one to go full, ahem, boar.

“Victorian Psycho” premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Bleecker Street will release it in theaters on Friday, September 25.

#3502. VisionQuest's Avengers: Doomsday Post-Credits Scene Explained: [SPOILER] Returns

This article contains spoilers for "VisionQuest" Season 1, Episode 8, "Forever."

The season (series?) finale of "VisionQuest" teases that the Vision-Maximoff family still has a future in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. There are two post-credits scenes in "VisionQuest." One is vaguer: Ultron (James Spader), now free and convinced not to kill all of humanity for now, has a backup drive of Jocasta (T'Nia Miller). So, yeah, it looks like this isn't the last we've seen of the Living Automaton in the MCU.

Towards the end of the episode, Tommy Shepherd (Ruaridh Mollica) asks Vision (Paul Bettany) if they'll ever see his mom, Wanda Maximoff/The Scarlet Witch (Elizabeth Olsen) again. The second post-credit scene all but confirms, yes, they will.

The scene replays the climax of 2022's "Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness," where Wanda buries herself under the rubble of Mount Wundagore to destroy the grimoire, the Darkhold. But then the scene shows green energy telekinetically lifting the rubble away, as a shadowed, hooded figure stands over Wanda. "Scarlet Witch, awaken. Your power will be mine," he says in a European accent as green light bathes Wanda, and her eyes shoot open. Three guesses who Wanda's savior is and the first two don't count. (But you will get a hint — his name rhymes with "zoom.")

This basically confirms Olsen will be appearing as Wanda in "Avengers: Doomsday," and as a servant of Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) This scene also aligns rather well with a post-credits scene included in the "Avengers Endgame: Encore" rerelease earlier this year, which depicted Doom freeing Bruce Banner (Mark Ruffalo) from imprisonment after the events of "Spider-Man: Brand New Day."

Many now vindicated Marvel fans refused to believe that Wanda was really dead after Wundagore's destruction. Elizabeth Olsen had previously said she was open to returning as Scarlet Witch, and it seems Marvel must've given her a call.

In "Avengers: Doomsday," Doom will have at least three "Latverian witches" under his command, and they will wear steel masks much like their boss does. That'll be a fitting homage to the three Brides of Dracula — Doom, as a caped, castle-dwelling Eastern European king, is very much a villain modeled in Dracula's image. But there's also rampant speculation the witches' masks hide familiar faces, including Wanda's. This "VisionQuest" post-credits scene all but confirms it.

(In the "Time Runs Out" storyline that "Doomsday" is loosely adapting, Doom had all female acolytes called Black Swans serving him. The Latverian witches might be a simplified version of that concept.)

While I'm hoping Marvel doesn't make Doom, their greatest villain, a literal variant of Tony Stark, the fact is Robert Downey Jr.'s casting means a lot of the audience will read Doom as "evil Iron Man." There'd be some fitting narrative symmetry then if Doom has corrupted Avengers, like Hulk and Scarlet Witch, on his side.

Doom has manipulated Wanda before in the comics, too. "Young Avengers: The Children's Crusade" by Allan Heinberg and Jim Cheung revealed that, after Wanda's infamous "No more mutants" crash-out in "House of M," Doom sheltered her in Latveria to try and gain her powers. This is the storyline that reunited Wanda with Tommy and Billy as well. With how "VisionQuest" leaves the Maximoff boys, and with Marvel Studios having planted the seeds for Young Avengers, I think a "Children's Crusade" adaptation is in the near future.

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Chrome is making it easier to autofill online forms with more than just contact information and credit card numbers. For users with Personal Intelligence enabled, Gemini will now suggest items like order numbers, tracking information, membership IDs, and booking confirmations from Gmail messages when completing forms in Chrome.

Chrome's expanded autofill capabilities use Gemini to read your emails and surface suggestions, meaning you don't have to click back and forth between tabs or manually search for codes or confirmations in your inbox. When you click a form field that has a corresponding piece of data, a pop-up menu appears and indicates that an item is "Suggested by Gemini." You can click this to autofill the suggestion as well as open an additional menu to see the specific source (the original email) or remove the suggestion. The latter doesn't delete anything from Gmail; it simply dismisses the suggestion in Chrome.

As Android Police reports, Google started testing enhanced autofill in Chrome this summer using data from other connected apps like Google Photos. The feature currently rolling out is specific to Gmail and is coming first to U.S. users who have Personal Intelligence enabled on desktop as well as in the Android and iOS apps when using Gemini in Chrome.

In the blog post announcing the enhanced autofill feature, Google states that "sensitive data is encrypted" and that users can manage autofill, including enabling or disabling enhanced suggestions, via Chrome's settings.

#3499. Ryan Gosling's R-Rated 2016 Comedy Is Officially Apple TV's Biggest Streaming Hit

I have never seen an actor resist Hollywood stardom more stubbornly than Ryan Gosling. Three years after his 2001 breakout performance as a Jewish skinhead in Henry Bean's incendiary "The Believer," (for which he should've been nominated for an Academy Award), he was transformed into a big-screen heartthrob via his portrayal of Noah Calhoun in Nick Cassavetes' "The Notebook." Gosling could've dined out on hunky leading men roles for the next decade, but, over the next few years, he chose instead to play a freebasing high school teacher in "Half Nelson," a self-destructive husband in the soul-hollowing "Blue Valentine" and an emotionally remote getaway driver in "Drive." "Crazy, Stupid, Love" was a bright box-office spot, but it wasn't the showcase he needed. If he wanted to be a star. Which, in 2011, seemed to be in question.

In 2016, Gosling made a play to become a star on his own off-kilter terms as alcoholic private detective Holland March in Shane Black's "The Nice Guys." The legendary screenwriter behind "Lethal Weapon," "The Last Boy Scout" and "Kiss Kiss, Bang Bang" cooked up an elegantly seared filet mignon for Gosling, and he savored every moment. "The Nice Guys," which pairs Gosling with an over-it Russell Crowe (as a Yoo-hoo swilling enforcer) is an audience movie, but the audience, for whatever reason, didn't show up in 2016.

28 days after "The Nice Guys" went live on Apple TV, it's now the service's most watched movie. I'm thrilled that more people are discovering this shaggy detective classic 10 years after its release, but under Ellison's Skydance rule, Warner Bros. isn't trying to resuscitate commercial misfires. This is it. That said, it's got more going on in its 116 minutes than the entire Marvel Cinematic Universe oeuvre.

I read "The Nice Guys" when it was pitched as a network television pilot by Black and Anthony Bagarozzi (one of these men had the pleasure of watching a stray kitten urinate on my lap). It was sharp, hilarious and fertile ground for a series – if the writers could get around CBS' standards and practices. Not since "The Monster Squad" had Black written with such ease and eloquence at a PG-ish level.

When "The Nice Guys" got greenlit as a film, producer Joel Silver starred it up with Gosling and Crowe. The idea seemed to be that Crowe, a major movie star and Academy Award-winner, would play straight man to Gosling's goofball PI, and the film would sell itself. This just didn't happen. Set in the late 1970s, Black's stumblebum neo-noir is a skillfully plotted romp that finds Gosling and Crowe trying to piece together the disappearance of anti-pollution activist Amelia Kuttner (Margaret Qualley).

Gosling is dopey perfection as Holland March, a single father who's battling against a boozy haze to solve a case that could save his profession and his life. He's funny and heartbreaking in this role. As is Black's wont, you're left with a wacky, whimsically moralistic Donald Westlake riff with blockbuster trimmings. Gosling and Crowe are scrambling to take down men who abuse women. Spoiler: they get their dastardly dudes, and you'll shed tears along the way.

I'm thrilled that Gosling is now an A-lister making films for Lucasfilm, and he was wonderful in "Project Hail Mary," but we've yet to see his best. I just want to watch him blossom.

#3498. 10 Biggest Changes Rings Of Power Season 3, Episodes 1-4 Make To Tolkien's Story

Warning! Spoilers for Rings of Power season 3, episodes 1-4 ahead!

Prime Video is back at it with Rings of Power season 3! The platform was kind enough to premiere with four episodes, which will ultimately be exactly half of the complete eight-episode season. We've therefore covered quite a bit of ground in a short amount of time, and Rings of Power has absolutely delivered on all the thrilling intensity that was promised. Of course, as was expected, not all of this is strictly in line with what J.R.R. Tolkien wrote in his various works.

Rings of Power has taken a lot of flak for its various changes to canon, but that's not always exactly fair. The Second Age of Middle-earth was never written about within a novel or traditional narrative. Instead, Tolkien described these events as an impartial historian would. This ultimately meant that large gaps in the details had to be filled in. For this reason, there's no point in listing all the ways brand-new characters like Arondir or Theo don't have a place in canon. Still, there are a good handful of elements in Rings of Power season 3 that do specifically contradict that canon version of the story.

Tolkien didn't describe in much detail the actual process of Sauron creating the One Ring, nor did he ever mention whether the Dark Lord faced any significant failures or challenges. In Rings of Power season 3, however, we pick up with the understanding that Sauron has been at this for quite some time. The show establishes that Celebrimbor kept a key secret from Sauron and that he needs to discover what it is to create a ring that can control not just all the others but the Three Elven Rings as well. It's an entertaining struggle, but certainly not canon.

In canon, Sauron had possession of the Three Elven Rings and gave them to the Elves, even though he didn't craft them himself. It therefore doesn't make sense that he would need one back to study it and create the One Ring.

Rings of Power's orcs have been rather controversial across the board. Last season, we saw orc parents with their baby, which, though frequently challenged, is not out of line with the Tolkien canon. Season 3 takes things a bit further, however, and we see what the showrunners are calling an "orc with an arc." Marnûkh seemingly betrays Sauron to help the Elves prevent the creation of the One Ring. There's absolutely no mention of such an event in Tolkien's works; neither is there any orc that ever went good.

We now know that the Stranger is actually Gandalf the Grey, and Rings of Power season 3 has officially revealed that the Dark Wizard is one of the Blue Wizards. More specifically, he is Pallando. This makes some sense in canon, since one of Tolkien's explanations for what happened to these wizards is that they formed magical cults in Rhûn. What the author never wrote about, however, is this idea that Pallando murdered his companion, Alatar, and that this is what caused Rhûn to become a desert wasteland.

In Tolkien's legendarium, there was a King Durin III who ruled Khazad-dûm around the time that Sauron's Rings were created. However, he did not have a son named Durin IV who lived at the same time. The name "Durin" was given to dwarves that were believed to be incarnations of Durin the Deathless, so there couldn't be two at once. Durin IV ruled generations later, during the Last Alliance of Elves and Men. All of this means that the family drama seen in Rings of Power season 3 between Durin and Thráin absolutely did not happen.

While it's conceivable that Tolkien would have written about brotherly rivalry among the dwarven heirs, the dramatic misunderstanding about Disa and Thráin's relationship feels less like something that would ever appear in his works.

Rings of Power season 3 hinges on the idea that none of the Elven Smiths survived the fall of Eregion. In the show, Sauron specifically ordered that all of them be executed and Celebrimbor's records be burned. This bites him in the butt, since he now needs answers that only an Eregion smith would have. This wouldn't necessarily have been an issue in canon, since it's specifically noted that several smiths (Gwaith-i-Mírdain) were among the elves that escaped to Rivendell. Whether Sauron could have gained access to them is another matter, but they certainly existed.

Sauron's entire process of handing out his Rings of Power is quite different in Prime Video's TV show compared to Tolkien works. According to canon, Sauron intended for all of his rings to go to elves, but they proved too difficult to corrupt. He had to gather them all back up again before ultimately deciding to redistribute them to Dwarves and Men. As for the Nine specifically, Sauron chose men of influence and power—the Great Kings of Men. There's no real reason to think that he had ordinary men fight one another to the death to claim rings for themselves.

The idea of Elendil leading a group known as the Faithful is absolutely canon. It didn't really happen until much later, when Pharazon embraced Sauron's cult, and Númenor began worshiping and giving human sacrifices to Morgoth. Even then, however, the Faithful were a peaceful resistance to the new practices. They simply refused to participate. Rings of Power portrays the Faithful as being an army in training that plans and carries out assassinations and other forms of violence. This is, once again, far more dramatic, but not a part of Tolkien's story.

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

It's no big secret that Rings of Power invented the implied romance between Galadriel and Sauron. While it's certainly possible that the Dark Lord would have wanted Galadriel on his side, perhaps even as his queen (pretty much everyone fell immediately in love with Galadriel), there's no concrete proof. Moreover, the idea of Galadriel having nightmares about Sauron being in her bed doesn't fit with anything we know about these canon characters. Galadriel was among those who were never fooled by Annatar, and while she knew Sauron was dangerous, she never had this traumatized fear response toward him.

When Gandalf faces the Balrog in The Fellowship of the Ring, he announces that he is a servant to the Secret Fire. Rings of Power has incorporated this idea, but with some odd twists. The Secret Fire is the source of all life in Tolkien's works, and the only being with access to it is the supreme god, Eru Ilúvatar. When Gandalf says he is a servant to the Secret Fire, he means that he serves Ilúvatar's will for life. There's no reason to think the wizard could ever speak to the flame directly, or that the flame could ever talk back. If this is just meant to be a vision that Ilúvatar used to communicate with Gandalf, then perhaps it works.

Rings of Power had already headed in its own direction regarding the character Celeborn, since it was claimed by Galadriel in season 1 that her husband had died. We all knew that couldn't possibly be true, and Rings of Power delivered in season 3 with the reveal that Celeborn had just been taken captive. Galadriel finds him at Gundabad, but it's hard to imagine he was kept there for the several thousand years since the First Age. It's all a big oddity, but we will have to see where this non-canon story goes as Rings of Power season 3 continues.

#3495. 15 Years Ago Today: Henry Cavill Starred In An Epic Fantasy Movie Before Superman

With now-former DC Studios heads James Gunn and Peter Safran's version of the DC Universe coming to a premature end, it's times like these when we would do well to look back at what has worked, and what hasn't worked, when it comes to DC's films. One thing that kinda worked was Henry Cavill, a great Superman who never got a great Superman movie during his run in the DC Extended Universe. Without doubt, the actor had both the charisma and physicality to make you believe a man can fly.

And yet, just two years before debuting as Superman in "Man of Steel," Cavill made audiences believe a man could battle gods with a sword. It was November 11, 2011, and Indian director Tarsem Singh Dhandwar had just released his film "Immortals," an epic fantasy movie inspired by Greek mythology.

In the film, Henry Cavill plays Theseus, a humble stonemason with the physique of a Kryptonian who is chosen by Zeus himself (Luke Evans) to lead humanity in their resistance against Hyperion (Mickey Rourke), a tyrant king wreaking havoc on Greece in search of a mythical bow that would allow him to free the Titans and overthrow the gods of Olympus. No, this movie isn't really based on any particular myth. Rather, it borrows from a number of legends and blends them together in a nonsensical yet very cool tale full of superhero-like action, incredible costumes, and some of the most stunning imagery in any fantasy movie out there.

Back in its day, critics generally praised "Immortals" for its stunning visuals while admitting its story left a lot to be desired. Nowadays, though, the movie represents an underrated entry in Cavill's body of work, as it showed he was ready to be a star and lead a franchise (or two).

"Immortals" is, admittedly, not a well-written movie. And yet, Tarsem Singh Dhandwar went about crafting this movie like it was going to mark the last time he ever set foot on a film set, leaving it all on the screen. Case in point, he tapped Eiko Ishioka ("Bram Stoker's Dracula") to design the movie's impossibly flamboyant costumes, which make the human characters look so extravagant that they almost overshadow the literal gods around them.

Then there's the film's visual style, which Singh once described as "Caravaggio meets 'Fight Club.'" He wanted to make a hardcore action flick in the manner of a Renaissance painting, and it shows, resulting in a movie that blends the desaturated colors and slow motion of something like "300" with a striking painterly aesthetic. When it comes to its spectacle, "Immortals" similarly combines gods with mythical weapons that tear down city walls and intimate, grounded sword clashes, making its violence feel huge in its scope and scale. Indeed, the first scenes involving gods are especially stunning, as they move at full speed while the humans they're reducing to smithereens are slowed way down. It's a great way to illustrate the awesome powers of these deities.

Speaking of awesome powers, "Immortals" is further bolstered by Henry Cavill, who very much proves his ability to carry a big-budget movie ihere. To be sure, his performance matches the wild tone of everything else around him, all while bringing some needed humanity to Theseus. It's enough to make you more than a little excited for Cavill's return to the realm of outlandish fantasy movie adventures with his upcoming "Highlander" reboot.

#3494. ‘The Rings of Power’ Season 3 Review: Amazon’s ‘Lord of the Rings’ Series Is Just Going Through the Motions

The charges against Amazon’s epic (and epically priced) “Lord of the Rings” series, “The Rings of Power,” stacked up quickly. The first two seasons were pretty good by blockbuster standards — and I wasn’t alone in saying so — but the record-breaking costs, as well as the franchise’s lofty pedigree, set expectations higher than Great Eagles can soar. When the most expensive TV series ever made struggled to yield the requisite viewership spikes and comparable cultural impact, the claws came out.

Showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay’s series was, among other prominent complaints, a lackluster imitation of Peter Jackson’s films and an all-too-obvious ploy to become TV’s next “Game of Thrones.” Even when the visuals wowed, the characters weren’t memorable enough (save for the dwarves), the stories weren’t fun enough (again, except for the dwarves), and the twists weren’t smart enough. (The dwarves, in their infinite wisdom, did not partake.) Perhaps most damning for a show paid and made for an audience of one, Jeff Bezos’ pet project didn’t get J.R.R. Tolkien’s text — at least, not on at any depth. Related Stories Casey Bloys to Receive the Milestone Award at 2027 PGAs ‘Victorian Psycho’ Review: Maika Monroe Scares Up a Very Different Kind of Final Girl

On the whole, these criticisms weren’t enough to spoil a flawed but ambitious saga. Sure, “The Rings of Power” was made with too much deference to the past and too little innovation for the present — repeating itself (and other “Lord of the Rings” adaptations) while lacking the deft touch and sweeping imagination viewers crave from their greatest fantasy series. But it was still thrilling in its spectacle, from sets to sound design, costumes to vivid colors. (“House of the Dragon” it was not.) Episodes easily conveyed the filmmakers’ giddy excitement for the next big battle scene, the next big twist, and the next big moment in their Tolkien translation. All that money was on the screen, where it belonged, and dreams of spending it elsewhere — like, say, on many shows instead of just one — were set aside when Mount Doom erupted and the Siege of Eregion was underway.

I say all this, dear reader, not just as a handy recap of where things stand for yet another series with lengthy breaks between seasons, but to establish my position on a franchise that’s reached its sudden, somewhat unexpected nadir (for now, at least). While flaws were evident before, “The Rings of Power” Season 3 is undone by them. The listless episodes aren’t just hamstrung by additional exposition and a dearth of deadly combat; there’s a lingering wariness to it all, as if the filmmakers have run out of surprises and settled for treating their adaptation like the supplementary material it’s based on.

The third season begins with a recap of its own: Five years have passed since the Elven city of Eregion fell, and Sauron (Charlie Vickers) controls more of Middle Earth than ever. His army of orcs are tracking down the rest of the titular rings, which are safe(ish) with the elves in the luxe strongholds of Lindon and Rivendell, as well as my beloved dwarves in the sonorous mines of Khazad-dûm. But the Dark Lord himself is right where we left him, trying to forge the one ring to rule them all. Celembrimbor (Charles Edwards) was the only Elf who knew how to forge it, and now that he’s dead, Sauron grows more desperate by the day.

Not that you could tell from Vickers’ affectless portrayal. In “The Rings of Power,” the Australian actor is saddled with an arguably impossible task: Take the very presence of evil — which Tolkien so profoundly established in readers’ limitless imaginations as “an image of malice and hatred,” before Jackson sagely (and cinematically) channeled that energy into a giant, all-seeing eye — and embody that transcendent menace within a guy who looks like the guitarist next door. Vickers was able to hide his Sauron in plain sight during Season 1, when no one knew who Halbrand really was, but the big reveal didn’t lead to a bigger (or more sinister) performance, and attempts to lend human dimensions to evil incarnate similarly suffered.

What Sauron means to the series is more powerful than what he does on a scene-by-scene basis, and Season 3 throws that balance way out of whack. Absent significant conflict elsewhere, the story keeps returning to Sauron and his schemes, but none of his scenes have enough juice to elevate him to adequate levels of intimidation. A lengthy climactic sequence near the end of the season deploys shifting aspect ratios, operatic music cues, and dead-eyes stares aplenty, but they don’t add up to the riveting spectacle its creators intended. Instead, they only remind audiences how little Season 3 has to show off, not to mention how misguided some of those showcases can get.

Númenor, with its warring cousins Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) and Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle), remains a bland, human-centered snooze-fest. (My god, these people are boring.) The desert empire of Rhûn fares slightly better with Ciarán Hinds’ Dark Wizard (those eyebrows!), but the man long known and now confirmed as Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) is still little more than a mysterious symbol. (Just wait ’til you see him… put on his hat?)

And what’s become of Prince Durin (Owain Arthur), Princess Disa (Sophia Nomvete), and my rambunctious, sunless dwarves? You’d think lifelong cave dwellers would thrive in a season that’s lost a considerable amount of its light (times are tough in Middle Earth, and “The Rings of Power” has never been subtle), but my feisty friends are stuck in a plot so predictable it’s all but spelled out in the very first episode by accident! (When the wisest dwarf speaks, we all know to listen.)

New additions feel slotted in, as if emotional attachments are expected to emerge from name recognition alone (sorry to Celeborn, Galadriel’s long-lost hubby), while old favorites are nowhere to be found. (Nori and Poppy are entirely absent through seven episodes.) Others that do show up aren’t developed thoroughly enough to support their dramatic turns, like the Southlands boy turned tree-chopping, Mordor-enslaved man Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin), or get wasted in order to prop up other, less compelling characters, like Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova).

Perhaps “The Rings of Power” Season 3 is just a temporary dip — the midway point of a five-season plan that needs to set the table so we can feast for the two final seasons. Even if that’s the case, it’s no excuse. “The Lord of the Rings” may engender enough goodwill to give “The Rings of Power” a little leeway, but a full season lacking in evident ingenuity and attentive investment is enough to strip away the nostalgic sheen.

The biggest slight against the series has always been its status as a prequel: Based on appendices to “The Lord of the Rings,” this is the story the movies ran through as an epilogue, so it’s going to take a little extra sumthin’ sumthin’ to prove expanding into a five-season series is warranted. Instead, we’re given the same ol’, same ol’. Not everything needs to be realized onscreen just for the sake of seeing it happen, step by step, beat by beat, ring by ring. Yet bearing witness to the inevitable is Season 3’s greatest ambition.

“The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” premieres Wednesday, November 11 on Amazon Prime Video with four episodes. Two episodes will be released November 18 and 25 to complete the season.

#3493. This Handheld Vacuum Fixed My Biggest Problem With Cleaning

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

I may not be “messy,” exactly, but no one would describe me as “neat,” either. One of my biggest issues is that I tend to wait for a mess to get big enough to justify dragging out a full-size vacuum before I deal with it, because a full-size vacuum means finding the cord or the charger, wrestling it out of the closet, going room to room, and then putting it all away again. When the mess in question is still only a few cracker crumbs? Forget it—I'm just too lazy.

The solution to my laziness has been removing all the friction and hassle of my full-size vacuum, and instead keeping a handheld vacuum always within reach.

Though there are many handheld vacuums out there, I use the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, which I got from Target. It's great for quickly sucking up crumbs and everyday messes, and that's exactly the job I need it to handle. The "dual air" part is what makes it more interesting than your average handheld: It's both a vacuum and a blower, so it can pull debris in or push it out, depending on what you're dealing with. I didn’t expect to need the blower at all, but I’m surprised how handy it is for blasting crumbs out of keyboard keys or loosening up stubborn debris before I suck it up.

The result is that my apartment is simply cleaner. Not because I'm spending more time cleaning overall, but because I'm no longer letting small messes pile up into big ones. When my monthly (or quarterly) deep clean does roll around, it's far less painful, because there's so much less to deal with. Perhaps this is the real upgrade: cleaning up messes the moment they happen instead of saving them up.

I love the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, but there are plenty of similar cordless handheld vacuum and air duster combos out there, and they tend to land in a pretty similar price range. If another one catches your eye, or goes on sale, or has a design you prefer, go for it.

When comparing models, here are my handheld vacuum musts:

It should offer both vacuum and blower modes.

It should be both cordless and rechargeable. If it needs an outlet, you'll have another barrier to using it, and that defeats the purpose.

It should be lightweight and slim. You want something you can grab and use one-handed without thinking about it.

The dust cup should be easy to empty. If emptying it is a hassle, you'll use it less.

You should be able to keep it in plain sight. The closer it lives to where messes happen (the kitchen, the entryway), the more you'll use it.

I used to think a clean apartment meant big, scheduled cleaning sessions. Now I think it's mostly about making the small stuff effortless. A handheld vacuum and blower won't replace your regular vacuum, but it will make you far less likely to need it as often. If you've been waiting for the next big mess, or the next big clean, to get things tidy, consider changing the system instead.

#3492. My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic Is Back, And It's Better Than Ever

BOOM! Studios’ November 2026 My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic series opens with a story that understands what makes the Mane Six an entertaining and beloved group. Their personalities are funniest when they collide, but their differences also give them room to help one another. Written by Seanan McGuire, illustrated by Amy Meberson, and colored by Joana Lafuente, issue #1 reunites the familiar cast for a messy, friendship-focused adventure.

Rather than introduce a sweeping threat or a new corner of Equestria, the premiere starts with a party gone wrong. Pinkie Pie’s attempt at a prank leads to an accident involving something Twilight Sparkle treasures, and the friends have to work out how to make things right. The setup is light, but the damaged object gives the issue a question to explore.

The comic establishes its comedic rhythm through Pinkie and Rainbow Dash’s antics in Twilight’s castle. Pinkie’s contraptions and confidence repeatedly create problems, while Rainbow’s impatience adds another layer of chaos. Applejack gets caught in the mess, and the frosting-covered mishaps turn the opening pages into a lively showcase for the cast’s timing. Meberson’s expressive poses and Lafuente’s vivid frosting splashes make the chaos easy to read.

That slapstick is not just background decoration. The accident leaves the castle library in disarray and damages a book Twilight had been studying. The Mane Six clean up together, with Rainbow using her speed, Applejack pitching in, and Rarity bringing her standards to the task. Their teamwork gives the opening a recognizable Friendship Is Magic feel, while keeping the pace moving.

The story becomes more interesting when Twilight explains why the ruined book matters. It is her only known copy, and its author disappeared after completing it. The book is a friendship story, but not a simple celebration of companionship as it examines how a friendship can fracture. That premise gives Twilight a personal reason to recover it, beyond its rarity.

McGuire connects Twilight’s interest in the book to Fluttershy’s news that she has made a new friend. The parallel is gentle rather than heavy-handed. While the Mane Six prepare a surprise party for Fluttershy, the comic shows how good intentions, distraction, and Pinkie’s enthusiasm combine into an unintended disaster. The conflict suits the series’ focus on relationships.

The comic’s history adds a wistful note. Its author, Posey Pan, once lived in Seaward Shoals with her best friend, Merry Weather. The panels show the two fillies sharing books before their futures pull them apart. Twilight wants to understand what happened and preserve the lesson, making the missing volume more than a rare collectible. The flashback gives the adventure an emotional mystery.

#3489. Where are all the rings in The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 3?

As the name of the series implies, The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is focused on how the Dark Lord Sauron (Charlie Vickers) forged the Rings of Power as part of a scheme to control all of Middle-earth. As of season 3, the three Elven Rings, Seven Rings for the Dwarf-lords, and the Nine Rings for Mortal Men have all been made, while Sauron is working endlessly to complete his project by building the One Ring to rule them all.

That's a lot of magic jewelry to keep track of! If you need a refresher, we’ve put together a list of where the rings are and who is currently wearing them.

This story contains spoilers for the first four episodes of The Rings of Power season 3

While in disguise and calling himself Halbrand, Sauron inspired the elven smith Celebrimbor (Charles Edwards) to create three rings that would save the Elves of Middle-earth from losing their immortality. He forged them in the season 1 finale using mithril Elrond (Robert Aramayo) received from his friend Durin IV (Owain Arthur), combined with a knife made of gold and silver from Valinor.

Even though Sauron didn’t have a direct hand in creating these rings, Elrond feared Sauron would use them to manipulate the Elves. So he stole the rings and took them to Círdan the Shipwright (Ben Daniels) in the Elven capital Lindon. Círdan is the oldest and wisest elf in Middle-earth and he offered to throw the rings into the ocean. But after actually seeing them, he changed his mind and donned the ring Narya. He brought the other two back to Lindon, where Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) put on Nenya and the High King of the Elves Gil-galad (Benjamin Walker) donned Vilya. Their power was able to restore the Great Tree of Lindon, which is tied to the vitality of the elves of Middle-earth.

As of season 3, all three of those elves are still wearing those rings, which are the only things that seem capable of stopping Sauron’s advance across Middle-earth. Galadriel is protecting Rivendell, while Gil-galad and Círdan preserve Lindon. Meanwhile, Sauron is scouring Middle-earth for information on how Celebrimbor crafted the Elven rings so he can forge a ring of his own that would bind all the ringbearers to his will.

With just a touch, Sauron was able to corrupt the seven rings that Celebrimbor made for the Dwarves. Durin III (Peter Mullan) wore one in season 2, and it made him paranoid and greedy. He didn’t listen to his son’s pleas to take off the ring even as Khazad-dûm was plunged into darkness. He only realized how much the ring was affecting him when he unleashed the Balrog while digging for mithril. He then took off the ring, gave it to Durin IV, and sacrificed himself to seal the Balrog away again.

As of the beginning of season 3, Durin IV has possession of all the Dwarven rings and has hidden them away, refusing to give them to the other Dwarven lords who paid Durin III for them. Durin’s older brother Thráin (Eddie Marsan) came to Khazad-dûm along with some of these lords, and while he’s acting like he has his brother’s best interests at heart, he’s actually in league with Sauron.

When Durin tells the Dwarf lords that the rings drove his father mad, Thráin points out that the king was wearing a ring when he decided to make Durin his heir. Arguing that their father was not of sound mind, he challenges his brother to a duel for control of Khazad-dûm. He wins and becomes the new king, but he still needs to find those rings.

Sauron was directly involved in the construction of the Nine Rings for Mortal Men and has the most control over their wielders. As of the beginning of season 3, he has already distributed three of them, and these Ring-servants (or Nazgnagôl) are fearsome warriors capable of dark magic.

In the season premiere, the Gaudrim (Men from the desert lands of Rhûn) come to Mordor to accept his proposal of an alliance with the Dark Wizard (Ciarán Hinds). Sauron makes them fight among themselves and gives one ring to the winner, Khamûl the Easterling (Zubin Varla). The ring’s power cures him of the Dark Wizard’s flesh-warping curse and he returns to Rhûn to usurp his former master. While the Dark Wizard demands that Khamûl surrender his ring, the Nazgnagôl refuses and shows off his new power by almost breaking the wizard’s staff.

Sauron also offered a ring to the Men of Númenor, who ignored his missives. Instead, the invite was answered by a group of Men from Pelargir, including Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin) who were looking for an alternative to toiling for their colonial lords. Once again, Sauron made them fight for a ring. This time, he intervened after seeing a scar on Theo’s arm that came from the magical sword hilt used to cause a volcanic eruption in the Southlands and create Mordor.

Sauron uses necromancy to contact Theo’s father, Faldred, son of Hammethreg, explaining that he was a steward of Mordor and that Theo’s mother killed him when she discovered his dark nature. Sauron then offers Theo a ring as a way to claim power for himself as a conqueror, a sorcerer, and a king. Theo dons the ring and accompanies Sauron to Gundabad, but tries to allow Galadriel, Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova), and Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower) to escape. Sauron demonstrates his control of Theo by forcing him to kill his surrogate father, Arondir.

#3488. 10 Years Later, Billy Bob Thornton's Forgotten War Movie Is the Perfect Weekend Watch

Molly DeCastro is a New York-based emerging film and entertainment journalist with a personal passion for poetic prose and impactful storytelling. She graduated from Pace University with a degree in English and a concentration in creative writing. While film analysis is at the heart of her work, she is especially interested in exploring cinema through an anthropological lens and in examining how creative themes reflect cultural identity. She aims to forge a deep connection between audiences and film through thoughtful and evocative writing. She also enjoys keeping up with all things film! That means specializing in industry news, emerging directors, and stand-out projects.

Surprisingly, despite being widely considered a classic must-watch, Billy Bob Thornton's 2016 war-dramedy Whiskey Tango Foxtrot is a rather polarizing film. That said, with comedy legend Tina Fey and, at the time, emerging starlet Margot Robbie at the helm, it's hard to imagine why. It's a classic odd-couple pairing, following Fey's Kim Baker, a mild-mannered, bottom-shelf news outlet reporter, and Robbie's Tanya Venderpoel, a fierce foreign TV war correspondent. The two stumble into one another when, struck by the desire to be a real boots-on-the-ground journalist, Kim takes up a station in Kabul, Afghanistan. The supporting cast, including Billy Bob Thornton as a rough-around-the-edges marine general and Martin Freeman as a hard-drinking Scottish photographer, help round the film, and in some way defines its charm.

Notably, the film is loosely adapted from Kim Baker's memoir, The Taliban Shuffle: Strange Days in Afghanistan and Pakistan, with Fey's character portraying a fictionalized version of the actual journalist. Similar to the film, the novel is a candid, comedic dissection of the post-9/11 "forgotten war", as told through the eyes of a journalist who was present there. Fey's portrayal of the character is quippy yet grounded in her undying pursuit of journalistic greatness.

There's no doubt Tina Fey is a comedy legend. She has a stacked repertoire of both acting and writing props to back it up. From Mean Girls to Baby Mama, watching Fey truly command a scene with such effortlessness is a never-ending pleasure. With that being said, her role as Kim Baker allowed audiences to see a new angle on her capabilities. Her character is in a vulnerable position, both internally and externally. She's essentially a half-failed journalist, putting her career and life on the line, completely dependent on her counterpart, Tanya Venderpoel. Fey's portrayal of this vulnerability, as well as her cohesion with Venderpoel, was wonderfully and warmly executed.

Kim arrives in a chaotic, male-dominated war zone and is quickly thrust into a world of intensive work, high-risk reporting, and heavy partying. Something in particular that this film captures well is the deep bond between women in a male space. Tanya's entrance into the film is disarming in some way, especially when juxtaposed next to Thornton's General Walter Hollanek, who initially intimates Baker but eventually develops a begrudging respect for her. The depth of Baker's experiences doesn't stop there. As she grows comfortable in this space of danger and risk, she eventually finds herself hooked on the high. This forces her to confront not only what she wants out of her career, but also her life. Fey's portrayal of this internal battle is refreshing next to her typically comedic roles.

As stated prior, the supporting cast provided an astounding cushion of extra depth to the foundation of the film. Thornton's character, in particular, added extra motivation not only for Baker but also for the plot itself. His role fills the typical brooding mentor trope, which makes his eventual softening all the more satisfying. In a conversation with Kim, she asks for a quote about the war and the current state of combat. Hollanek replies with a sobering thought: "This war's like f**king a gorilla; you keep on going until the gorilla wants to stop." At that moment, he sees Baker as an inexperienced nuisance. Over time, their dynamic shifts as Kim keeps proving her grit, leading to a pinnacle moment when she uses her skills to lead a large-scale rescue mission.

Martin Freeman's Lain MacKelpie is exactly the opposite. He's a warm, charming, romantic-leaning colleague to Kim. His character provides a lightness to the plot which is otherwise pretty gritty. Together, their scenes break up the chaos and provide a dynamic pace to the story. He's a wisecracking, heavy-drinking guy, and as the two grow closer, he becomes incredibly lovable as a character. Overall, each of the respective supporting characters helps build the story into what it is.

Two horror stars are ready for deployment.

In summary, Whiskey Tango Foxtrot ​​​​​​is a thrilling, bumpy ride. Each moving part of the film breathes so much life into the story. Though it at times relies on cliché tropes, the expert performances from Fey, Freeman, Robbie, and Thornton helped differentiate it from the masses. It's gritty, fun, and a wonderful combination of the best of each genre it pulled from.

In November, Prime members can get two free Kindle e-books from Amazon's First Reads program.

Amazon First Reads is a program aimed at Prime members that offers early access to new e-books across many genres, as curated by First Reads editors (one of many Prime Member benefits). Prime members can choose to download one free e-book every month from a rotating list—though some months that number is bumped up to two, usually with a free short novel—and non-members get them for a discounted price. These e-books can be read on any compatible Kindle device or via the free Kindle app.

Go to the First Reads landing page to see the full list of e-books available this month. Once you find a book that seems interesting, click the "Shop Now" button from the First Reads landing page. Make sure you’re not being redirected to the Kindle or Amazon mobile application, because you won't see the free book option there; instead, use your internet browser on your phone or computer.

Make sure you’re not clicking the ”Pre-order for...” button, as that will direct you to pay. Instead, click the “Read for Free” or the "Buy Now with 1-Click" button under the "First Reads" banner on the book's Amazon page (don't worry, you won't be charged). This will send the e-book directly to the Kindle linked to your Amazon account. You can see what it should look like from the screenshot below.

You’ll know you did it right when you see a “Thanks, [your name]!” order summary indicating the e-book is being auto-delivered to the Kindle Cloud Reader.

This month, you can choose one from nine new Kindle e-books, plus this month's short read. Amazon notes the genre for each of the books above the title, offering a quick way to narrow down your options. (If you hover over the "See Editor Notes" under the "Shop Now" button, you'll be able to read a short description from the First Reads editor who picked the book.)

#3486. How Casting the New ‘Harry Potter’ Helped ‘Club Kid’ Find Its Adorable 10-Year-Old Star

Jordan Firstman knew that the success of “Club Kid” hinged on finding the perfect preteen actor to play his character’s long-lost son, Arlo.

It was a demanding role that had a lot of boxes to check off: A British kid, whose hard-partying mother had just committed suicide, finds himself dumped in New York City, where he struggles to break out of his protective shell to bond with his party promoter dad, Peter (Firstman, who wrote and directed the film, in addition to starring in it ). But the perfect candidate had to project an effortless coolness that allows him to organically blend in with his newfound father’s social circle of hard-living, LGBTQ+ clubgoers, whose lives revolve around their love of music, dance, and drugs. Related Stories ‘Victorian Psycho’ Review: Maika Monroe Scares Up a Very Different Kind of Final Girl ‘Steps’ Review: A Disposable Fairy Tale Reminds Us That Cinderella Is Someone’s Hated Stepsister Too

“[Arlo’s] not just cool, he’s empathetic and wise; there’s a lot of stuff about that kid that was on the page that needed to be there,” said Firstman, who on this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, called the casting search the most “nerve-wracking” part of making “Club Kid.”

“Club Kid” had the right casting director for the job. Carmen Cuba has a legendary track record of finding child stars, including the original “Stranger Things” ensemble. But as Cuba pointed out while participating in IndieWire’s Craft Roundtable of Casting Directors, “Club Kid” was different from those previous assignments.

“I do six-month searches for kids,” said Cuba. “On ’Stranger Things,’ ‘Starfighter,’ you have time and money, and this was a small film.”

The $6 million production could not afford a lengthy search. It didn’t even have the money for Cuba to fly to London with Firstman for auditions. She would be reliant on a UK casting team, working within a limited budget, to help her find a needle in a haystack.

“I was very nervous about just sort of the plan of attack, because I was going to have a UK team, and you need a British kid who looks like he’s half-Jordan,” said Cuba.

Right before jumping into “Club Kid,” Cuba went on her yearly vacation with a group of close casting director friends. As the holiday wound down, Cuba tried to work through her upcoming casting dilemma with some of her closest colleagues.

“I [said], ‘How am I going do this?’ just trying to map it out for myself before I left to go start it,” recalled Cuba of the conversation. “And one of those friends is Lucy Bevan, who had just finished her ‘Harry Potter’ search, so she so generously said, ‘Why don’t I share some of the names.’”

To cast the first season of the $200 million-plus upcoming HBO series — based on the first Harry Potter book, “The Philosopher’s Stone,” in which Harry turns 11 — Bevans had just finished her own six-month search. She had auditioned thousands of young British actors to play the next generation of Harry, Hermione, Ron, and their Hogwarts classmates.

“This is just a testament to our relationship because Lucy would not normally do UK casting on a tiny movie,” said Cuba of the prominent British casting director, whose credits include “Barbie,” “F1,” and “The Batman.”

“She had just seen 40,000 kids,” said Firstman of Beaven, who early on showed him a photo of Reggie Absolom. “I saw his face and I was like, ‘that is the face that I’ve seen in my head.’ Even in the script, he’s supposed to be a quarter Indian – “Innit Babes” [Peter and his friends’ nickname for Reggie’s mom based on her favorite expression] is supposed to be like half Indian — and Lucy [said], ‘Let’s not focus on that. That’s not going happen.’ And Reggie’s a quarter Indian. Every single thing that I had asked God for, this kid came to me in Reggie.”

In total, according to Cuba, Bevan showed Firstman 90 kids, with a wider range of ages — Cuba and Firstman went back and forth about how old Reggie should be, with the character originally skewing younger than 10 — but Firstman never wavered from Absalom, whose résumé included roles in “Silo” and “The Other Bennet Sister.”

“Lucy was so generous. They had no money to fly me to London to do the session in person, so she hosted the callback session there,” said Cuba. “Jordan is incredible with kids, he was like, ‘Let’s not do it in this casting office, let’s take it outside.’ So suddenly Lucy’s assistant is outside with the camera, and they’re walking and talking. I rewatched that audition recently, and it’s just amazing. Jordan’s brain, and how he connects to everyone that he casts. I think that’s what you feel in the movie; it’s so familial.”

On the podcast, Firstman talked about how beyond his decade of drug-fueled clubbing in Europe and New York City, one of the inspirations for “Club Kid” was the bond he formed with one of his close friend’s child, something he felt would be essential to replicate with Absolom.

“The reason kids like me is I don’t treat them as kids,” said Firstman. “They’re surprised at my candor, or the inappropriate things that most adults wouldn’t be willing to say in front of a kid. I know what Reggie sees on the internet. I’m not going to say something too much, but I can push it a little bit.  I think he always appreciated that in me, and once he understood that I liked to be made fun of too, everything shifted. Once he got permission to make fun of me, the whole dynamic shifted, and we just got so much more comfortable around each other.”

Much like his unorthodox, take-it-outside, walk-and-talk callback audition with Absolom, Firstman quickly realized, after casting the young actor, traditional preparation wouldn’t work.

“We tried doing traditional rehearsals, and it was awkward,” said Firstman. “I [said], ‘Let’s just keep hanging out, and keep having pizza together, and keep talking about music, and keep talking about TikTok clips we’ve seen, and send each other TikToks,’ and that’s how we bonded.”

An A24 release, “Club Kid” is now in New York City and Los Angeles theaters, and will expand on Friday, November 13.

#3485. The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel Gets Official Update For Skyrim's Anniversary

After eight extremely long years since its initial announcement, The Elder Scrolls VI finally broke cover the other day to give the waiting masses a title for the game they've been so desperate to see more of. Sentinel, as it is now known, is likely taking us back to Hammerfell, and it will be really interesting to see the important region in a modern game from the series.

Outside of that, though, we still don't really know anything about the game, or what it will look and play like. That's because it is almost certainly still a couple of years away from being in our hands at a minimum, and the announcement of the title was likely just to placate us for as long as they can, for the most part.

Unfortunately, it seems as though we have now had confirmation that nothing is coming for a while, and it comes from the developer themselves.

As first reported by ComicBook.com, a post on Reddit is drawing attention right now as it has attracted Bethesda themselves, who stopped by to put pay to a particular rumor that's circulating. Specifically, several members of the community felt that a full reveal could be on the way to mark the 15th anniversary of the release of Skyrim, which actually dropped today (at the time of writing), November 11, 2011.

Unfortunately, that's absolutely not going to be the case, as Bethesda's official Reddit profile shared the following response to quash that burgeoning speculation:

"Hey everyone, wanted to pop in to say that we aren’t going to have any big announcements tomorrow. We’re excited you’re excited but we will not be sharing anything new on Sentinel for some time," the comment read.

As you might expect, that led to humorous conspiratorial responses from the community, who felt as though this was simply Bethesda obfuscating their plans.

"This sub getting so unhinged the last few days that Bethesda has had to literally step in has made me so proud lmao." one comment read.

While another added, "I'm reading this as 'Wanted to let you know we are launching tomorrow. We are excited to keep you busy in Sentinel for some time'".

The recent teaser for the game gave us a look at a titular Elder Scroll being revealed from underneath sand which, while it doesn't reveal much on the face of it, could provide certain clues. One leading theory is that it symbolizes the Alik'r Desert, which stretches across the northwestern part of the province of Hammerfell, and could easily serve as a hidden location for the scroll.

That said, there is lots of existing lore around the Elder Scrolls that should mean they aren't able to be simply wielded by the player, or anyone else for that matter. It will be interesting to see how Bethesda puts them at the center of the narrative in Sentinel, as it relates to our character, without overriding much of the lore that made them compelling in the first place.

#3484. All the Health and Fitness Products You Didn't Realize You Could Buy With HSA Funds

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), it's that time of year: Use those funds, or you'll lose them. Luckily, there are plenty of clever ways to spend your remaining FSA funds on qualifying healthcare costs—some that you may never have considered as "qualifying."

For instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch (even the latest Fitbit Air). At least, that's what plenty of brands like Whoop, Oura, and even Nike want you to think. Is the process really as straightforward as the marketing suggests? Here's what to know about all the unexpected ways you can spend your FSA funds before the end of the year.

Right off the bat, when it comes to most of these fitness trackers and smartwatches, your HSA/FSA dollars won't be able to cover the entire purchase; instead, you'll save an average of 30% on eligible health purchases.

There is some more fine print, although it’s not as tricky as you might think. For the most part, if a device is necessary for treating or monitoring a specific medical condition—and not just “general wellness”—it could be eligible to purchase with those pre-tax health dollars.

The main “catch” here (as I’ve previously explained) is proving that device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN). Your LMN is basically a doctor's note required to classify certain purchases as qualified medical expenses under IRS guidelines, proving that the device will be used to treat a legitimate medical condition, such as obesity or a heart condition. Let’s take a look at what you can actually expect if you want to get a fitness wearable approved as a medical necessity.

When it comes to securing your LMN, you might not even need to make a doctor's appointment, thanks to third-party players like Truemed. When you browse sites like Coros, Amazfit, and more, you'll see the option to “Pay With Truemed” at checkout. From there, you'll be asked a few questions about your health circumstances, and you’ll be matched with a provider to determine your eligibility. If you qualify, you’ll get an LMN that will allow you to use your HSA or FSA funds to complete your purchase—all without ever having to meet with your primary doctor.

Truemed is one of the most popular payment platforms in this space, with the company claiming on its site that “90% of LMNs are issued within seven hours.” I spoke with Truemed’s co-founder and CEO Justin Mares to find out how it works behind the scenes. After you take that short survey about your health, an independent licensed provider reviews your answers before deciding whether the purchase looks medically necessary. If it doesn't, Truemed won't bother forwarding the request at all. Because Truemed screens your case before it has a chance of getting denied, those approval numbers get to stay mighty high. And the reality is, most Americans will have at least one health marker—like weight or cholesterol levels—that they can self-report to prove that, say, a Fitbit Air is necessary tool for prevention and maintenance.

For the purchases that do go through to a medical professional, approval turns out to be surprisingly straightforward. It comes down to the idea of "standard of care" in general. “If you go into a doctor's office and say your family has a history of high blood pressure,” Mares says, “your doctor probably is not going to ask for lab work before they'll talk to you about it. They simply take you at your word and help you manage the risk.” Proving HSA/FSA eligibility works on that same standard fairly often, according to Mares. You're not submitting a stack of medical records; you're answering a simple intake form about your health history, and a licensed clinician uses that, plus their own judgment, to decide whether a given product is appropriate for you.

Before you get your hopes up too high, FSA/HSA eligibility for wearables is still far from a free-for-all. An LMN only covers you, personally, for a specific product from a specific merchant, and it's usually tied to a specific condition, like cardiovascular risk, pre-diabetes, sleep issues, chronic pain, and so on. Some employers' FSA administrators scrutinize wearable purchases more closely than others, and even a fully compliant LMN doesn't guarantee your plan will approve the claim. Some companies (like Coros, for one) are more transparent about walking customers through the required medical consultation at checkout, while other brands market "HSA/FSA eligible" prominently without explaining that the LMN step is what actually makes that true. Luckily, I’ve saved you some time and rounded up some of the major wearables—and other unexpected items—that you might be able to prove as FSA/HSA eligible.

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. These tend to draw more scrutiny from plan administrators simply because they're marketed as lifestyle products first, so the strength of your intake answers matters more here than it does for something obviously medical, like a blood pressure cuff.

If cardiovascular monitoring, training load tracking, or heart rate accuracy is relevant to a documented health concern, these watches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches. Sadly, no Garmin watches are HSA/FSA-eligible. Still, the following Garmin-brand products are eligible for an HSA/FSA purchase:

You can filter by HSA/FSA eligibility and browse all eligible Garmin items here.

Think adjustable dumbbells, rowing machines, and connected bikes. It's the same logic doctors use when they tell a patient with pre-diabetes or high cholesterol to start exercising regularly; if a clinician is willing to attest that structured exercise is part of your treatment plan, equipment that enables that can qualify. For instance, here are some HSA/FSA eligible products from Nike Strength:

The common thread across all of these is that the product itself doesn't determine eligibility—your health history does. A Whoop band might be an easy approval for someone managing a cardiac condition, but it'll get more pushback for someone with no relevant health history at all. If you're curious whether something on your wish list might qualify, it's worth filling out the intake process just to see how creatively you can spend those pre-tax health dollars. However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste.

#3483. Tom Morello Joins Critical Role for New Bard-Themed Adventure

Critters have been looking forward to this classic team-up for quite some time

The founders of Critical Role have always taken pride in shaking up the way they play tabletop role-playing games. But next week, a new adventure will push the cast and crew further than ever: a "Battle of the Bards," with Matthew Mercer as Game Master.

Joining Mercer in this charity one-shot are fellow founders Ashley Johnson and Sam Riegel, along with an incredible lineup of musicians, including Tom Morello of Rage Against the Machine, K.Flay, Blake Roman, THOT SQUAD, and Wayne Brady, who also appeared in The Legend of Vox Machina as the magnificent Taryon Darrington.

Donations made throughout the night will benefit the following charities: Comic Relief, Outright International, First Nations Development Institute, Shanti Bhavan, National Center for Women & Information Technology, The Pablove Foundation, and 826LA. Additionally, 10% of each donation will be set aside for an emergency fund to be used in the event of unforeseen natural disasters.

Battle of the Bards brings Critters back to Exandria, with Sam Riegel reprising his role as Scanlan Shorthalt, the lovably horny bard of the legendary adventuring party Vox Machina. Riegel will also serve as the game's co–Game Master.

The summary of the adventure is as follows:

Scanlan Shorthalt is hosting the competition of the century, in search for the next greatest entertainer (besides him, of course). Bards from across Exandria will come together to compete in challenges that will showcase their talents and push their limits. It’ll be a night of awe and spectacle where nothing will go wrong…

Below is the full cast for Battle of the Bards.

Critters will be able to donate to Critical Role’s charity organization, the Critical Role Foundation, throughout this week, right up until the game debuts on Nov. 17, when live in-game donations become unlockable. Pre-game donations will be closed an hour before the game starts, at 6 p.m. PT.

Donors will be able to affect how the adventure unfolds through changes in the weather, inspiration for players, and more. Full details on what can be unlocked are available on Critical Role’s official website.

At the time of writing, it’s unclear whether the one-shot will use the Daggerheart or Dungeons & Dragons system, though the official website's reference to both Mercer and Riegel as Game Masters leads us to assume it will use Daggerheart going forward.

Regardless of the system, it’s hard not to enjoy the classic, entertaining idea of an “Oops, All Bards!” setup. Having played that exact combination, I can say a party where every player is a bard is far more diverse and creative than you might expect.

How an all-bards team will fare for the Critical Role crew remains to be seen, but we can’t wait to find out when the one-shot premieres live on Beacon, Twitch, and YouTube on Tuesday, November 17th, at 7 p.m. PT.
