#3482. ‘Ink’ Star Jack O’Connell on His ‘New Era’ as a Leading Man: ‘Thank F**k for Danny Boyle’

Jack O’Connell was feeling a little bashful. Seated outside for coffee, taking in the fresh fall air at the remote Salamander Resort in Middleburg, Virginia, the actor revealed that communication between him and Oscar-winning filmmaker Danny Boyle began long before he was cast as the lead in the director’s latest film, “Ink.”

“I used to write to Danny a lot. I wrote all the directors that I admire,” said the 36-year-old star from Derbyshire, England. “Not cap in hand, trying to get anything out of them, just letters of appreciation, lovely stuff that’s affected me and inspired me. ‘I hope we get to do it someday.’ And, in Danny’s case, we did.” Related Stories How Casting the New ‘Harry Potter’ Helped ‘Club Kid’ Find Its Adorable 10-Year-Old Star Casey Bloys to Receive the Milestone Award at 2027 PGAs

Technically “Ink,” in which O’Connell plays influential newspaper editor Larry Lamb after he’s recruited by outcast media magnate Rupert Murdoch to take over The Sun tabloid in 1969, is the second time the actor has worked with Boyle. The pair first officially met when he was brought in to play antagonist Jimmy Crystal in last year’s “28 Years Later,” directed by Boyle, and more prominently in January’s “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple,” directed by Nia DaCosta.

“It was right before I went and shot ‘Sinners,’” he said, referencing another major turn as a villain that loomed prominently over cinema this year. “The initial meeting wasn’t an audition. I just didn’t have the role. It was a meeting discussing the role with Danny and Nia.” It was the first time Boyle had acknowledged O’Connell, though he had a sneaking suspicion that he had been on the director’s radar for a while, having starred on the same iconic British teen drama “Skins” from which Boyle had found the star of his Best Picture winner “Slumdog Millionaire.”

“Listen, he cast Dev [Patel]. He knew about ‘Skins.’ I think his daughter put him onto ‘Skins’ in the first place. So whether or not he stuck it out for our generation, I don’t know,” said O’Connell.

It’s been almost two decades since he first played fan favorite Cook as part of the second generation of the trailblazing E4 series, which ran from 2007 to 2013. “Skins” still stands out as an experience that helped shape his ethos as an actor. “I certainly felt like we were on the coolest show around. It was so amazingly written. The directors we had were brilliant. The whole model of the way that you audition en masse and then they find their characters. I love that,” said O’Connell. “It’s really quite pure, isn’t it? People are just getting the roles because of ability.”

The “Ink” star first trained as an actor at a free program in Nottingham called the Television Workshop, which eventually helped lead to his first breakout film role in the coming-of-age drama “This Is England.” However, it was “Skins” that felt like a “crash course” continuing education. “You’re doing all the heavy stuff, the tough stuff, the really laborious side of doing a TV show like that. But also the fun and the joy that gets provoked by all the art, the amazing writing and everything else,” said O’Connell. He’s quick to remind that notable “Skins” alumni include not just Patel, but also writers like Emmy winner Jack Thorne and Tony-nominated playwright Lucy Kirkwood.

But free programs like the Television Workshop are increasingly hard to come by, meaning there are less and less egalitarian-type opportunities in the United Kingdom for an actor from a working-class background like O’Connell’s to find their own “Skins.” Asked what he would tell the next generation of artists, the “Ink” star said, “I wouldn’t know what advice I would give nowadays, which is a shocking indictment.”

What attracted O’Connell to playing Lamb in “Ink,” a role that has brought him to the Middleburg Film Festival to receive the Spotlight Actor Award, was the opportunity to address how the UK, and the world in general, reached this place of inequality. “We see this man just excavate his morals, and his soul, and his decisions, and this newspaper. Being the best-selling newspaper, he’s had to part with what makes people more human. To me, it’s a comment on capitalism,” said the star. “The beginning of hyper capitalism, post-war England, and individual opportunity versus looking after everyone else and your responsibility within society. That was all just getting ripped up.”

“Ink” is an adaptation of James Graham’s 2017 play of the same name, with Graham also serving as the screenwriter of Boyle’s film. Another major factor in O’Connell’s decision to play Larry Lamb was working with the playwright and the director, who had come from a similar background. With Boyle, “I came to his work as a fan first, before I knew I was going to try and be an actor,” he said. “I remember watching ‘The Beach,’ and that made me want to go and see the world. And watching ‘Trainspotting’ and that made me want to never take heroin. But also the amazing soundtrack that’s in there and the fucking unforgettable performances.”

With “Ink” they were preparing to tell what O’Connell sees as a quintessentially British story, and “what [Danny’s] films have meant for British cinema and British culture as a result is undeniable. Thank fuck for Danny Boyle. He is an artist by every stretch of the word. I would argue that his films have perhaps meant the most to us as a collective growing up. His work at the Olympics opening ceremony makes you tingle to watch it. It is fucking monumental.”

Boyle is why O’Connell, an outsider to the film and TV industry in the same way Lamb was to the publishing industry, could still envision himself becoming an actor one day. “His style has been able to make you feel part of the film. It takes you along. You feel like you’re in the movie somehow. You don’t feel like an observer, like a spectator. They give you a feeling and mood as well,” he said.

As for Graham, “We’re not too far from each other in a particular pocket of the UK. And although my town and his town famously don’t get on — that’s all to do with football and Brian Clough and whatever else — but he is a dramatist. He’s also interested in analyzing culture and the culture around him and examining it,” said O’Connell. “He’s a great spokesman for under-representation in the industry at home because eight percent of the entire industry are from our background.”

The actor added, “Once he knew that I was somebody that could be trusted with his words, not someone who was going to try and fucking destroy them, we really hit it off.”

Here the three were, as what some would call a band of outsiders, telling a story about these insurgents to the distinguished Fleet Street, where the most esteemed newspapers like The Daily Mirror were published. Playing Lamb was a bit of an exercise in what would happen if O’Connell’s comeuppance led him toward the dark side. “The intoxication of power is something that really interests me. And Larry, he began as a socialist, voted Labour, celebrated socialist politicians. He left Fleet Street having been knighted by Margaret Thatcher. … Talk about excavation, a whole U-turn politics there, colluded with Rupert Murdoch in tearing up the unions and workers’ rights. Sold his soul,” said O’Connell.

“There’s a great contradiction with Larry that he begins as an outsider. Even within the duration of our film, he’s trying to become an insider. He wants to be part of that gang. In fact, that’s where he ended up, Sir Larry. So there’s a great contradiction in the man. So I can’t afford to go all the way ‘outsider with a chip on his shoulder,’” said the actor.

With “Ink” following the successes of “Sinners” and “28 Years Later” so quickly, O’Connell has a newfound feeling of security and sense of becoming that sought-after leading man. “It probably is my most mature role to date,” he said. “I look back on my career and I just feel so fortunate. There’s not a single regret. So if this is a new era, yeah, brilliant, bring it on. A lot of my heroes, a lot of their work that I really celebrate, were around my age, so maybe that is inspiring and gives me cause to kick on.”

Netflix will release “Ink” in select theaters across the United States on Friday, December 11. The film will debut on the streaming service on January 8, 2027.

#3481. We Officially Ranked the 8 Best HBO Shows of All Time

HBO is responsible for creating some of the best television shows of all time. Originals like Sex and the City, The White Lotus, and Euphoria have changed television as we know it, and were responsible for many stars' breakout performances. Actors that fall under this success list include Sarah Jessica Parker, Sydney Sweeney, and Idris Elba.

The network has produced over 200 shows since 1983, many of which became award winners, cult classics, or both. Its pattern of skyrocketing celebrities' careers appears to be never-ending, and it is only a matter of time when new stars will enter the spotlight following the debuts of upcoming shows. In the end, some shows are better than others, and here is our list of the 8 best HBO shows of all time.

The Wire focussed on a specific issue in Baltimore for each of its six seasons, and its connection to law enforcement. While the first season focuses on ceasing the illegal drug trade by the Barksdale family, Season 2 shines light on how deindustrialization affects labor unions, particularly the Baltimore docks. Other issues addressed during the show include city government, public school systems, urban reform, city politics in the media, and the Baltimore Sun newspaper combined with the decline of journalism.

The crime drama's choice of not making anyone a true main character is a rare thing on television, but it was a smart decision for this show, as it doesn't take one or two main characters to initiate change all the time. The characters needed to do the work, and not just have determination and passion to improve Baltimore, and The Wire did a phenomenal job in proving that to viewers who were looking to make a difference. Unlike most shows on this list, The Wire did not receive many awards following its universal praise, but its plot lines and diverse cast were groundbreakers that changed television for the better.

The Gilded Age has become one of HBO's top television shows following its series premiere in 2022. The historical drama is set in the 1880s, and begins with Marian Brook (Louisa Jacobson) moving in with her aunts, Agnes van Rhijn (Christine Baranski), and Ada Forte (Cynthia Nixon), following the death of her father. What she didn't expect to witness was tension between families that came from new and old money, along with the things that aquaintances would do to be one step closer to climbing the Manhattan social ladder.

The show's characters are an accurate representation of the New York elite in the 19th century. Not only do the actors portray their characters with grace, but they also fully embrace the time period, and make each scene feel like a piece of history one won't read in a textbook. The drama is currently airing its fourth season, and like its previous seasons, it received universal acclaim from fans and critics.

Larry David was known for co-creating Seinfeld before starring as a fictionalized version of himself in Curb Your Enthusiasm. In the show, Larry is a semi-retired television writer who finds himself in hundreds of unusual circumstances. Those situations and resolutions helped make the show an instant success, and featured a string of celebrities portraying characters or fictionalized versions of themselves, including John Hamm, Lin-Manuel Miranda, and the late Catherine O'Hara.

Unlike most popular HBO shows, Curb Your Enthusiasm aimed to make viewers smile from beginning to end rather than have them fear something dreadful would happen. It brought out the whacky sides of every actor who appeared on the show, and provided a new level of comedic relief to fans who needed it. Even though Curb Your Enthusiasm concluded its 12-season run in 2024, the award-winning show is still missed by fans looking to laugh before going to sleep.

The must-see fantasy drama of the 2010s was Game of Thrones, which featured a long list of celebrities portraying complex characters in their breakout roles. The show featured several story arcs during all 8 seasons, including political conflicts between noble houses and fights to reclaim power that characters believe they deserve. The impressive plot lines and actors' performances alone were enough to score higher viewership, but its frequent nudity and fight sequences prevented it from ever being something appropriate for young children.

Although the show's final season wasn't a favorite amongst fans, it does not take away from the excitement it provided them throughout the first seven seasons. It reignited the popularity of fantasy, and turned a nerdy genre into a global sensation for adults who believed fantasy was only for kids. The iconic show also inspired HBO to create two spin-offs: House of the Dragon and A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms.

HBO had originally billed Big Little Lies as a miniseries, but the show's overwhelming praise led to the network renewing the show for a second season. Season 1 begins with the arrival of Jane Chapman (Shailene Woodley), a single mom who befriends Madeline Mackenzie (Reese Witherspoon) and Celeste Wright (Nicole Kidman). As the season progresses, the darkness in their lives comes to light, and it leads to deathly consequences they, along with fellow moms Renata Klein (Laura Dern) and Bonnie Carlson (Zoë Kravitz), must face throughout Season 2.

Every actress in Big Little Lies showed audiences that no matter how hard one tries to pretend everything is fine, nothing is ever perfect. Fans could feel the guilt, sadness, and fright each character had, and even though it took time, the women showed viewers the perfect example of an unbreakable bond. The emotions and chemistry portrayed by the actors contributed to the show's Emmy and Golden Globe Award wins, and fans are antsy to learn when full production of the show's upcoming third season will begin.

Succession is a prominent HBO classic that showed viewers what happens when a family is ruined by greed. The show centered around the Roys, and the fight to take over the family-owned company, Waystar RoyCo. The three frontrunners in the takeover were Kendall Roy (Jeremy Strong), Roman Roy (Kieran Culkin), and Siobhan "Shiv" Roy (Sarah Snook), all of whom were children of the company's CEO, Logan Roy (Brian Cox).

The race for the CEO position was terrifying to watch, as viewers watched the children ruin their own lives for the possibility of a fancy job. In the end, Logan's third son, Connor Roy (Alan Ruck), was the sibling with the happiest ending, and the only one who wanted nothing to do with running the company. Although none of Logan's children became the CEO, the actors portraying them did win Golden Globes for their performances, and they taught audiences throughout the show's four-season run that no life of privilege is worth ruining one's life or family over.

Fans immediately fell in love with Dr. Michael "Robby" Robinavitch (Noah Wyle) within the first five minutes of the series premiere of The Pitt for his hardworking demeanor. The show centers around Robby and the events of his shifts at the Pittsburgh Trauma Medical Center's ER, which he and his co-workers call The Pitt. Some of the cases were minor, others were life-threatening, but what they all had in common was the ability to surprise viewers who believed every patient would have a happy ending.

Critics and medical professionals praised the show for its realistic depiction of the lives of ER doctors and nurses. It gives audiences the gift of understanding what an ER is like in real life, and even though some cases are truly heartbreaking, it's the reality of the medical field that fans aren't used to seeing. The show has already won Emmy and Golden Globe Awards, and its third season is set to premiere next year.

The Sopranos is not only the best HBO series, but it's also one of the only mafia shows where audiences have trouble despising members of the mob. The show introduced viewers to Tony Soprano (James Gandolfini), a mob boss who managed to balance work and family life in his own twisted way. Tony committed heinous crimes with friends and relatives, but after six seasons, it was impossible to hate or want him in jail.

The diabolical behavior of some of these mobsters never got boring, and the show always found ways to add twists to pivotal plot points throughout all six seasons. No one can imagine a criminal getting away with everything forever, but this show made fans hope the members of Tony's crime family were immortal. Even though audiences will never know if Tony Soprano lived or died, the character will always be one of the most inspirational and evil protagonists of all time.

#3480. CBS Is Officially Ending NCIS Series' Undisputed Best Run

Ana Dumaraog is a Writer and Editor at Screen Rant, where she expertly covers Network TV offerings, among other things She has spearheaded the effort to make the site an authority on broadcast shows, initially starting with The Big Bang Theory franchise, NCIS, and One Chicago before taking on the specialization in general. Ana has also covered a wide-spread of topics in the past — from franchises like, the MCU and Star Wars, to classic TV favorites, such as Frasier and MASH.

Ana brings clarity and enthusiasm to every story she tackles—whether reporting on new releases or offering deep dives into fan-favorite franchises. Her coverage translates complex entertainment developments into engaging, audience-focused content.

Warning! Spoilers ahead for the NCIS franchise.The NCIS franchise has been a hit on all cylinders this cycle, but one series is ending its best run disappointingly earlier than the rest. Donald Bellisario and Don McGill's famed procedural has been a staple of CBS's programming since 2003. Since then, the flagship has created the franchise, birthing multiple spinoffs along the way. In CBS's fall 2026 slate, the Eye Network strengthens its commitment to the universe with its revamped Super Tuesday lineup, which groups all the Navy-related projects in one night.

Each show in NCIS's active lineup has something fresh and interesting to offer viewers. NCIS season 24 marks the beginning of a new era with the return of Michael Weatherly's Tony Dinozzo; NCIS: New York sees LL Cool J's Sam Hanna leading his own team, and NCIS: Origins gets Mark Harmon's Leroy Jethro Gibbs out of retirement in Alaska. While everyone has their favorites, it's arguably fair to say that the way David J. North's prequel series has been the best in terms of storytelling among the three. Unfortunately, CBS is ending its run earlier than its peers.

Ahead of the ongoing network TV cycle, CBS announced that NCIS: Origins season 3's run will be significantly shortened — slashing its episode count from 18 to just 10 episodes. Thus far, the prequel has already released five episodes, which means that it has officially arrived at the midpoint mark of its run. The decision to slash its output stems from CBS's scheduling, slotting NCIS: Sydney season 4 to the same timeslot once the winter season rolls around — something that is becoming more popular among traditional broadcasters.

That said, the verdict came long before the public found out about what's in store for the period series for its junior year run. Bolstered by Harmon's full-time return as Old Gibbs, not to mention the string of beloved franchise characters coming back, all on top of the procedural aspect of the series from its '90s timeline, and NCIS: Origins season 3 has been such a delight to watch every week. So much so, that there was hope that somehow, CBS might have a surprise twist regarding its run with a last-minute extension in any form. Sadly, that isn't the case, as NCIS: Origins season 3 is re-affirmed to be ending early as originally planned.

With only five episodes left before NCIS: Origins season 3 ends, expect that long-running stories introduced early on will have some sort of resolution. It has already been confirmed that CBS is bringing back three more key people from Gibbs' story — Roma Maffia, Muse Watson, and Joe Spano as Old Vera Strickland, Frank Gibbs, and Tobias Fornell. They join Weatherly and Emily Wickersham as Dinozzo and Ellie Bishop in this modern arc for Old Gibbs.

Six years after their final appearance, the original young Gibbs is officially recast in the NCIS franchise playing a more interesting character.

Considering the major reveal that Lala Dominguez didn't die in that plane crash that Old Gibbs previously revealed, it's safe to say that Vera and Mike's respective comebacks will have something to do with that. As for Fornell, his storyline might be tied to the bigger conspiracy at hand. In any case, seeing them back would be a big treat, not just for fans of NCIS: Origins, but also those who have followed Harmon's character from his days in the NCIS flagship.

#3479. Apple Is About to Release a Touchscreen MacBook Pro (Plus Four More Devices)

Apple has had a busy fall. Head to the company's website, and you'll immediately be greeted by a sea of new products: the foldable iPhone Duo; the iPhone 18 Pro; HomePod mini 2; Apple Watch Series 12; the list goes on. It seems, under new Apple CEO Jon Ternus, the company is ready for a refresh of just about every product it sells. To that point, the company seems far from finished. Just this week, Apple is planning to release five brand new products, each launching on Friday. While four of these are Macs, Apple does have a new iPad in the works, as well. Here's everything new Apple is releasing this week.

Finally. For the first time, the iPad mini is about to ship with an OLED display. Apple's smallest tablet has always come with a standard screen. Despite its price tag, the iPad mini has never come with an OLED display, or even a mini-LED screen, until now. With this new model, there is no backlight. As such, each individual pixel on the iPad's display will be able to shut itself off when displaying dark content. That will benefit the content you watch on this device, as well as the overall contrast of the screen.

Beyond the new OLED panel, the new iPad mini is thinner and lighter than the previous model. It also comes with Apple's newest A20 Pro chip, the same processor the company put in its iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo smartphones. The new device starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, though there are various upgrades, including nano-texture glass (add $100) and cellular (add $150).

Good news: There's a new iMac. Bad news: Not much is different here from the previous model. The biggest change here is the new M6 chip, which Apple says is up to five times faster than the iMac with M4 and up to 12 times faster than the iMac with M1. With that M6 chip, the iMac now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Other than that, this is the same iMac you may already know: It comes with a 24-inch LED display (no OLED, unfortunately), two or four USB-C ports (depending on the configuration), and a built-in 12MP webcam. If you're looking for a new all-in-one computer, or you've been considering upgrading your older iMac, this is likely a great choice. But if you already have an M-series iMac, it's not such an obvious upgrade. (My M1 iMac may be up to 12 times slower, but it's still plenty fast for me.) Apple didn't change the price here: The M6 iMac still starts at $1,499 for two ports, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage.

Similarly, Apple's newest 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't much different from the previous model—save for the new processor. This model also comes with Apple's M6 chip, which Apple says is up to 13 times faster for AI processing than the M1 MacBook Pro. (Apple seems keen on convincing stubborn M1 users to upgrade this cycle.) Now, the company is offering this model of MacBook Pro in three chipsets, depending on use case: M6 for "entry-level" pro work; M5 Pro for mid-tier pro work; and M5 Max for the most demanding situations.

But, like the M6 iMac, this is the same MacBook Pro Apple sold before. It has a 14-inch mini-LED display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz. It comes with three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, an HDMI port, and an SDXC card slot. It, too, has a 12MP webcam for video calls. Apple's newest MacBook Pro starts at $1,999, but you can quickly ramp up that price tag with screen, chip, memory, or storage upgrades.

Apple's most exciting product launch this week is undoubtedly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros. Unlike the M6 MacBook Pro, which only comes in the 14-inch variant, Apple's first touchscreen laptop comes in both 14- and 16-inch options. Apple says this touchscreen lets you scroll, zoom, or draw on the display. That works with basic functions, like web browsing or selecting files, but also with specific workflows, like playing virtual instruments in Logic Pro, or manipulating an object in a 3D modeling app. Like the iPad mini, this laptop comes with an OLED display (Apple calls it PROLED XDR), with up to 1,000 nits of typical brightness and 2,000 nits of HDR brightness. It also brings back the backlit Apple logo, something I've missed on my last two MacBooks.

This MacBook Pro also comes with the iPhone's Dynamic Island for the first time. This replaces the "notch" that other MacBook Pros and MacBook Airs currently ship with. It can function as a basic webcam, but also as a dedicated zone for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI. This machine comes in either M5 Pro or M5 Max variants—no M6 for this model—as Apple seems to be positioning it exclusively for the most taxing situations (particularly AI). The company says the new MacBook Pro has up to 13 more hours of battery life than Intel-based MacBook Pros, and can fast charge up to 50% in 30 minutes. It's essentially a supercharged version of the existing MacBook Pro.

As such, this is Apple's most expensive laptop. The 14-inch M5 Pro version starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. However, you can configure these machines to have outrageous price tags. The maxed-out 16-inch MacBook Pro is $14,549, roughly half of which is the 16TB of RAM.

#3478. All Zelda: Ocarina of Time Dungeons, Ranked From Worst to Best

While every moment of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is memorable, it’s the Nintendo 64 game’s dungeons that really stick in your memory. Each one is a tightly constructed puzzle box built around the tools you collect inside, culminating in an often-excellent boss fight. The game’s terrific Switch 2 remake doesn’t mess with that strength; it only refines some of Zelda’s best dungeons in tasteful ways.

It was a joy to revisit those dungeons during my playthrough, not just to experience some nostalgia, but to appreciate some timeless Nintendo design. Since I left the remake with some strong opinions about which ones are best in class, I’ve decided to definitively rank the eight primary dungeons in Ocarina of Time from worst to best. (I’ve left out side-dungeons like the Gerudo Training Ground and the Bottom of the Well, though those contain some killer bits of puzzle design, too.)

On paper, the Shadow Temple sounds fantastic. It’s a dungeon that fully realizes Ocarina of Time’s underlying horror by forcing Link to face off with Gibdos, Like Likes, and Dead Hands. In reality, it’s a fairly straightforward temple that revolves around a gimmick that sounds cooler than it is: a ghost ship ride. The remake misses an opportunity to make that sequence more exciting, leaving it feeling like an amusement park ride. The one saving grace here is Bongo Bongo, a bizarre boss that comes totally out of left field to make for one of Ocarina of Time’s most delightfully weird combat encounters.

Like the Shadow Temple, Jabu-Jabu’s Belly is an iconic temple that doesn’t quite hold up to its reputation. Don’t get me wrong: It’s perhaps the most creative dungeon in the entire game. Link gets swallowed by a giant fish and has to cut his way out of it by attacking its electrified uvulas. But the reality is that it’s a fairly small dungeon with an underexplored Princess Ruto escort gimmick and the least memorable boss in the entire game. It still deserves all of its flowers for being a funny, gross-out idea, though.

Dodongo Cavern is by no means a weak dungeon. It’s a fun, early-game area that gives you a lot of room to play with bombs. (That ends with you feeding them to King Dodongo, one of Zelda’s most classic boss mechanics.) It’s more that it’s outclassed by the Fire Temple later in Link’s adventure. The only way that Dodongo’s Cavern really stands out is in its central room, which has a massive skeleton looming over it. Dropping bombs in its eyes to unlock the route to King Dodongo remains a great final puzzle, as does setting off a bomb chain reaction to knock down a staircase.

Depending on who you ask, the Water Temple is either an abomination or the best Zelda dungeon. The truth is that it’s neither: It’s just a pretty good dungeon held back by some repeated backtracking. The idea of unlocking new areas in a flooded temple by changing the water level makes for a great gimmick that adds some clever spatial reasoning to the mix. The remake even makes it easier to navigate, thanks to better visual signposting and streamlined controls. Even with those changes, it’s still easy to get mixed up and wind up trekking back through routes to reset the water. The Longshot is a bit of a cop-out key item too, but the area’s pair of standout bosses in Dark Link and Morpha more than make up for that.

Even though it’s little more than an introductory dungeon, The Great Deku Tree is a perfect bit of Zelda design. The opening section, which has you climbing webs and avoiding Skulltulas, is a unique bit of vertical exploration that makes it special. Falling through the big web at the center of the dungeon to get to the bottom floor is a magical moment, too. And then there’s Gohma, a top-notch first foe that’s easier than ever to appreciate with the remake’s control tweaks. It’s a little small and the puzzles are simple, but it’s a delightful first challenge for Link.

As a dungeon that lands right near the midpoint of Ocarina of Time, the Fire Temple does a great job of (ahem) heating things up. It’s one of the more complex dungeons in the game, combining high-stakes platforming with a Goron-searching throughline that really shakes up the linear dungeon design at just the right time. It also features one of the best items in the game, the Megaton Hammer, which is especially satisfying to use in the remake. Volvagia might just be the most spectacular boss fight in the entire game too, aside from the final showdown. Top to bottom, it’s a meat and potatoes dungeon that nails all the essentials.

Key item: Silver Gauntlets, Mirror Shield

As the last dungeon in the game before Ganon’s Castle, the Spirit Temple makes for a great final exam. Its defining feature is the fact that it’s a dungeon in two parts, as Link needs to explore it as both a child and an adult to complete it. It’s the kind of ingenious idea that you would find in a game like Link’s Awakening, and it’s a little surprising that Ocarina of Time doesn’t play with that time-travel dynamic more elsewhere. That unique hook makes it feel like two dungeons in one, as you solve puzzles with both the Silver Gauntlets and the Mirror Shield. The final battle against Twinrova is a high point too — especially in the remake, which does an excellent job turning the witches into lovable foes. It’s a wonderfully creative way to send Link on his way to his journey’s end.

Zelda dungeons don’t get much better than the Forest Temple. Really dialing into Ocarina of Time’s spooky side, it’s a literal ghost house where Link has to track down and defeat four Poes. That quest sends him through twisted hallways and flipped rooms that require just enough spatial reasoning to feel gratifying without being a headache. Using Link’s arrows to shoot Poes out of picture frames, reorient rooms, and light torches makes for a strong puzzle dungeon that gives you multiple uses for your newfound item. The fact that it all ends in the memorable Phantom Ganon fight, a battle that brilliantly teases the ending encounter, makes it that much stronger. It’s a quintessential Zelda dungeon, and Ocarina of Time wouldn’t feel as magical as it does without it.

#3477. Six Fitness 'Rules' That Don't Actually Matter

I’ve learned a lot in my many years in the gym, and beginner-me would be shocked and appalled by the things present-me does during workouts. With the benefit of experience, I now do exercises I used to think one should “never” do, and I’ve broken pretty much every other rule besides.

I've already explained a bunch of things you can stop worrying about as a beginner, but I’d like to expand on that list with a few more rules that even intermediate-level exercisers can ditch without consequence.

If you can theoretically do 13 bicep curls with a certain weight, how many curls should you actually do? One common misconception is that if you don’t do all 13, you’re leaving gains on the table. The rule kind of makes sense if you have truly no clue where to start; if you go until you can’t do a single rep more, then at least you know you’re not slacking off.

But the downside is that going to failure for every set of every lift is just going to make you exhausted. On bicep curls, maybe not so much, but once you’re squatting pretty heavy weights, you’re going to feel spent if you do every single set to failure, and that fatigue will get in the way of getting a good workout in consistently. What’s better is to follow a program that advises you on when to hold back and when it’s a good time to really push your limits. You’ll find that most of the time, you stop a set at least 2-3 reps shy of failure, and sometimes even more.

Rest days are a convenient tool for making sure you’re not overworking yourself, but that’s all. Organizations like the American College of Sports Medicine recommend leaving 48 hours between intense strength-training sessions for a given muscle, but if you look at where they get that number, it’s meant to be a general recommendation for beginners and for people who are exercising just to stay healthy. Once you’re talking about athletes or enthusiasts, the ACSM acknowledges that training most days of the week is fine if your program manages fatigue effectively. That may mean alternating between heavier and lighter days, rather than taking complete rest days.

The “10% rule” is a not-terrible guideline for figuring out how quickly to ramp up your training. But like many of these other myths, it’s a suggestion, not a commandment to be strictly obeyed.

As running coach Jason Fitzgerald told Lifehacker, “While the adage is to only increase weekly mileage by 10%, this may be either too conservative or even too aggressive depending on where you start from.” When you’re coming back from a short layoff, you can probably increase mileage a lot faster. Same goes if you’re a beginner and your mileage is overall very low; if you took the rule literally, you wouldn’t be able to increase from zero to any other number.

Meanwhile, serious running programs—once again, a program is a wonderful thing—may give you a bigger increase for a few weeks in a row, then cut back and decrease your mileage temporarily before ramping up again. Or they may keep you at the same mileage for weeks at a time before venturing a larger increase. If you were to stick to the 10% rule, you would miss out on the advantages of programs that work this way.

There are pros and cons to lifting before cardio, and to doing cardio before lifting. It’s more of an “it depends” than a rule. So here are some of the ways to decide which makes sense.

Your lifts tend to suffer when you’re fatigued, and doing them fresh is important to you

Cardio is your top priority, and you want to have more energy for it

Your lifts are the kind of thing that can get done even when you’re fatigued

Or you only intend to do a small amount of cardio before lifting

So a cyclist may prefer to do a strength workout after hopping off the bike, but a powerlifter would probably rather get their conditioning in after finishing squats for the day. Either is fine if you don’t care, or if you prefer to mix it up.

There are a few supplements that can help you in your fitness journey, but none of them are necessary. Creatine is one of the best-known muscle-building supplements. It’s understood to be effective, but here’s the thing: Just because it does something for most people doesn’t mean it does very much. If you decide it’s too expensive or just that you would rather not have another thing to remember to take every day, you’re not missing out on any substantial amount of gains.

Likewise, protein powder is a helpful way to get more protein in your diet, but you don’t need to use a supplement; you can just eat more protein-containing foods.

And finally, pre-workout drinks can give you more energy in the gym (it’s mostly caffeine), but the idea that you need it is a very recent development. Even ten years ago, it wasn’t really a thing. People showed up to the gym with a coffee or a coke or with no caffeine at all in their stomach, and worked out just fine.

Look, people have been exercising successfully for millennia, but all of our apps and devices weren't even a thing until the 2000s. Tracking every minute, every step, or every mile of your routine is not actually necessary. You’re still a runner even if you don’t have an app that knows how many miles you ran. You don’t even have to track your sets and reps in your lifting journal if you don’t want to. Your body is what knows how much work you put in, even if your phone were to get wiped overnight.

#3476. Spawn Returns Today With New Sequel Ahead Of Movie Reboot

Every Spawn fan is on pins and needles as we await news about Todd McFarlane’s upcoming live-action reboot. Many will remember that McFarlane first announced his partnership with Blumhouse to develop the reboot in 2017, and that Jamie Foxx was officially announced as Spawn in 2018. However, it has been a grueling, near-decade-long wait, with still no end in sight for when we might finally see the movie. Thankfully, today is still a great day for fans, as the first installment of a two-part Spawn sequel has officially arrived.

’Tis the season for Santa Claus, serial killers, and Spawn! Arriving today is the highly anticipated sequel to last year’s acclaimed Christmas horror story, I Saw Santa: A Spawn Universe Story. Titled I Saw Spawn: A Twisted Christmas Tale, this sequel will be a two-part special, just like its predecessor. With issue #1 launching today, fans can expect the second and final issue to arrive on December 16, 2026.

Last year, Chris Killian, Andrew Sanders, and artist Thomas Nachlik brought us a horrifying tale about what happens when one disturbed child takes offense to Santa's gift of coal and makes it his life's mission to torment Jolly Ol' Saint Nick for the rest of his life. The two-part special also answered the question of who you call when naughty kids take their misbehavior to diabolical levels: Spawn, of course!

2027 is already a huge year for Witcher fans, and now Geralt and Jaskier are returning for another release set in the franchise's golden era.

Now, Killian and Sanders return, this time alongside artist Todor Hristov, for the official sequel to this story. For a spoiler-free idea of what happens in the first issue of I Saw Spawn, check out the official synopsis: "The North Pole is shaken by a gruesome massacre that bears the signature of serial killer, Charlie Kohl. As Santa Claus investigates, dark forces begin to corrupt Santa's workshop from within, and it’s clear Spawn is the only one who might be able to put a stop to this terribly twisted Christmas."

While the 48-page I Saw Spawn: A Twisted Christmas Tale #1 is available now for $5.99, we highly recommend checking out I Saw Santa #1-2 first. Not only is this the proper reading order and a way to elevate your reading experience, but the original two-part story is also a PHENOMENAL read. This story gives a whole new meaning to the Christmas song "Santa Claus Is Coming to Town," especially the jingle's famous warning: "You better watch out."

This story is perfect for those who love a smorgasbord of genres. Here, you'll find a collision of Christmas, horror, mystery, and a surprising amount of nonstop fun. However, this is far more than just a brutal Christmas story, as the writing for this two-part special is superb. Don't believe our praise? Then check out I Saw Santa: A Spawn Universe Christmas Story #1 on League of Comic Geeks, where readers gave the story an "exceptional" 4.5-out-of-5-star rating.

With Killian and Sanders returning for the sequel, readers already know the quality they can expect. And while Nachlik's artwork was perfection in last year's special, fans will likely appreciate Hristov's work just as much. So, if you're starting to feel that Christmas fever and want to experience the holiday spirit through the brutal lens of the Spawn universe, then bump this holiday special to the top of your TBR.

I SAW SPAWN A TWISTED CHRISTMAS TALE #1 from Image Comics is available now!

#3475. Taylor Sheridan Star Officially Addresses That Devastating Season 3 Finale Death

Editor's Note: The following contains spoilers for 'Lioness' Season 3If there's one thing Taylor Sheridan has demonstrated throughout his television career, it's that getting attached to his characters can be something of a poisoned chalice because, whether it's Yellowstone, 1923, or Lioness, Sheridan isn't exactly a fan of happy endings, and that's especially true when his characters all find themselves caught up in situations where survival is anything but certain. And one of the main characters in his spy thriller felt the sharp end of his pen.

Elizaveta Neretin, who portrayed Oleksandra in Lioness Season 3, has officially spoken out on her character's death in the season finale, saying that she understood Sheridan's decision even though she obviously hoped it wouldn't happen. Speaking about the storyline, Neretin also discussed the decision to have the character die off-screen, a creative choice that left viewers confronting the aftermath rather than witnessing the moment itself. Speaking with Fox News Digital, Neretin explained:

"I thought it was going to happen. So when he called, and he told me, I was like, 'Yeah, I get it.' I'm sad for Oleksandra and what Oleksandra represents, but I understand the choice. It does serve this. It serves to show how the whole system is. Like American or not American, the whole system and the people that work in the system. It's all sharks, you know, so it just demonstrates how people are."

Surprisingly, we don't even see the murder. Instead, the finale shows two Delta Force operators removing her from a safehouse before a later scene reveals that a jogger has discovered her body near a trail. For a series that has never been particularly shy about depicting violence, it's an odd choice but Neretin believes there may have been a good reason for leaving the character's final moments to the imagination. Speaking with Decider, she added:

"We didn't film her actual murder, but I wonder if that's more of a question for Taylor. He writes some pretty gruesome things... Good writing means you don't write the things that are obvious. The viewers already knew she was going to die. So, what would be the purpose of showing her being murdered? Every scene has to have a purpose. Again, I don't want to speak for Taylor, but perhaps that's why the audience only saw her dead body. That's all they needed to see."

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

#3473. How Harry Potter’s New Snape Will Compare To Alan Rickman Addressed By HBO Star

New Harry Potter star Paapa Essiedu explains how his take on Severus Snape compares to Alan Rickman.

Except for Warwick Davis as Filius Flitwick, the cast of HBO's Harry Potter series is completely different from the eight movies that were released from 2001-2011. This has naturally led to comparisons between the previous and new actors playing the iconic fantasy characters created by J.K. Rowling, from Daniel Radcliffe and now Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter to Rickman and now Essiedu as Snape.

In an interview with Vanity Fair, Essiedu explains that he is not trying to erase the films or imitate the performance of Rickman, who he calls "an icon" and "a legend," but is instead focusing on fully fleshing out Snape amid all the character's contradictions and complexities. Essiedu feels that whether he has done the character justice cannot be fully assessed until the series is complete, and also expresses appreciation for the "goodwill" and those who were close to Rickman reaching out to him. Check out his comments below:

The guy is an icon. He’s a legend. Anyone who’s ever met Alan or spoken to him or been friends with him have all reached out to me and spoken about what Alan would’ve thought about my casting. There’s so much goodwill, and I really feel him with me. There are people who have got such a tight and deeply felt connection to something that they believe is theirs, and it feels like somebody is trying to take their thing and break their thing. I know that’s not what I’m trying to do. I’m not trying to break anybody’s nothing. After this, we’re not going to burn the books. We’re not going to remove the DVDs of the films. It’s not the end of that. That all still exists. I’m very clear-minded in my head about what I want to do and what I’m trying to achieve, and the potential of it. [H]opefully I get the opportunity to pull the contradictions and the unexpected masks of Severus so that eventually we get a human being that is fully fleshed [out] and living and breathing. That was my ambition, and is my ambition. And you can judge me sometime—in 2039 or whatever it is—as to whether it’s been successful or not.

While Essiedu is focused on his interpretation of the character, he also shared that he's read the books, but hasn't watched the movies, so he has not seen Rickman's performance for himself: "To be honest, I never watched the movies when I was younger. I still don’t think I really know what happens in Deathly Hallows because I read it so quickly that it didn’t really seep in."

Essiedu's mention of not being able to judge the success of his performance until 2039 is a reference to the show's ambitious plan, which is to make one season for each of the seven Harry Potter books. Given the scale of the high-budget HBO fantasy show, it will likely take over a decade to fulfill the plan of making seven seasons that adapt the full book series.

While season 1 took several years to make, season 2 is already in production, which is meant to avoid overly long hiatuses in the coming years, but it will still end up being a lengthy process.

With seven seasons, which as of now are eight episodes each, as opposed to eight movies, Essiedu is poised to end up having more scenes as Snape than Rickman ever did, including potential additions to the character's story that go beyond the source material and the films.

At the same time, his response emphasizes that the show is not overwriting the movies, which will continue to exist and be celebrated for their adaptation of the novels, and Alan Rickman's performance is an integral part of that legacy. Rickman passed away at the age of 69 in 2016.

#3471. ‘The Rings of Power’ Just Confirmed Our Biggest Theory About the Dark Wizard

Editor's note: The below contains spoilers for The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 Episode 3.

After years of speculation, The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power has finally granted fans an answer about the true identity of the notorious Dark Wizard (Ciarán Hinds). Ever since we first encountered this desert ruler, who holds sway over the eastern land of Rhûn, there have been many theories about which Istari he might be. Season 3 finally confirms that this Dark Wizard of the East is none other than one of the famed Blue Wizards sent to Middle-earth before Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) himself.

Season 3's reveal probably won't surprise diehard Tolkien fans, even if the particulars are a bit surprising. Previously, Tolkien wrote that only five Istari made their way to Arda in physical form. Given that viewers have already met Gandalf and know the fates of characters like Saruman the White and Radagast the Brown, that left only the two Blue Wizards. Between them, Tolkien wrote very little, with most of the material coming from Unfinished Tales, but The Rings of Power fills out the story in Season 3's third episode as Gandalf communes with the Secret Fire. "He was once called Pallando," Gandalf hears, "one of two wizards sent to protect these lands, but he wanted more. So, he betrayed and murdered his partner, an act so evil that it laid all of Rhûn to waste." Thus, it is due to Pallando's lust for power that the east was cursed, destined to never be made right.

Although the decision to kill off Alatar (the other Blue Wizard) is certainly shocking, this development (as well as their arrival in the Second Age) isn't beyond the realm of possibility when examining Tolkien's legendarium. In The Peoples of Middle-earth, the Blue Wizards are described as having been sent to Middle-earth likely around the same time as Glorfindel during the Second Age. "Their task was to circumvent Sauron," Tolkien explains, "to bring help to the few tribes of Men that had rebelled..." These tribes were meant to be some of those furthest from the Kingdom of Númenor. Interestingly, Tolkien concludes that, while the Blue Wizards most likely failed in their efforts, they had some hand in reducing Sauron's potential allies by the time of the Third Age. Even so, their failures would have major ramifications, giving the Dark Lord a true hold over that part of the map.

The cast and creators break down the show's most personal storyline yet for Tolkien's most iconic wizard.

"I suspect they were the founders or beginners of secret cults and 'magic' traditions that outlasted the fall of Sauron," Tolkien added in a letter collected in The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien. While there has never been anything written about one wizard killing the other, it's certainly not implausible, especially since neither of them appears in any form during the climactic events of The Lord of the Rings. After all, even Tolkien himself continued to shift and change their backstory, including their names, which he altered to Morinehtar and Rómestámo near the end of his life. Since Tolkien appeared to believe that both wizards failed in their task, Pallando's betrayal could absolutely work within the context of The Rings of Power.

However you slice it, the Dark Wizard's biggest reveal has been a long time coming. The Rings of Power spent way too long teasing the Stranger's true identity as Gandalf over the first two seasons (despite it being quite obvious), and it's clear that the show's creators have no intention of leading fans on any further here. Indeed, intersecting the lives of Gandalf — who, unlike the Blue Wizards, really shouldn't be around in the Second Age — and Pallando is certainly an interesting direction. His new divinely-inspired mission to redeem his wizard brother is a compelling idea when seen in light of Saruman's eventual corruption during the Third Age. As the Secret Fire tells the Grey Wizard, "Only together can you prevent the armies of Rhûn from joining Sauron."

Whether Gandalf succeeds or not, The Rings of Power continues to dive deeper into Tolkien lore this season, and it's about time. Some page-to-screen translations may leave a bit to be desired (Tom Bombadil should be much jollier), but the route the show is pursuing with the Istari seems to be the right — or at the very least, fascinating — direction. Would it have perhaps been more lore-accurate for Gandalf to be a Blue Wizard? Sure, but it's great to see the show finally exploring one of these lesser-known sorcerers. With the Harfoots out of the story, this reveal comes at just the right time to offer more hope for the future of Middle-earth.

New episodes of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power are available for streaming Wednesdays on Prime Video.

#3470. Why Ari Aster and Lars Knudsen’s Square Peg Built a Therapy Circle for Hollywood’s Next Generation in Texas

Talent labs and mentorship programs are plentiful for aspiring filmmakers — but where do you turn when your career has already started, after your first movie or on the precipice of one, and especially when filmmaking can be such a lonely enterprise?

Enter Square Peg Social, the Austin, Texas-based filmmaking summit launched by Lars and Amy Knudsen and Ari Aster that offers four days of singular community-building: brutally honest advice, commiseration, and idea exchange shared among 35 participants, with the program now in its second year.

A weekend of panels, discussion, and camaraderie designed for filmmakers at the early stages of their career, this year’s talent-incubating event was even crashed by the likes of Zach Cregger and Richard Linklater — both of whom were down to get frank about their filmmaking highs and lows. (In fall 2025, IndieWire did a deep dive into Square Peg Social’s first year, just to show how much the event has already grown.) Related Stories ‘Ink’ Star Jack O’Connell on His ‘New Era’ as a Leading Man: ‘Thank F**k for Danny Boyle’ How Casting the New ‘Harry Potter’ Helped ‘Club Kid’ Find Its Adorable 10-Year-Old Star

But the program’s stable of 2026 mentors and panelists — i.e., filmmakers keen not only to open up to new filmmakers about their own struggles, but also to scout new talent — also counted “Primetime” and “You Can See Everything” director Lance Oppenheim, “Sing Sing” filmmaker Greg Kwedar, “The First Omen” director Arkasha Stevenson, and “Mother Mary” director David Lowery among them.

The closed-door, off-the-record, noncompetitive summit opened to applicants in May, later unfolding from September 17-21. Partners including the Austin Film Society, Belvedere, and Airbnb offset the cost, besides a modest application fee, for participants to hole up for four days and nights at Soho House that don’t promise job opportunities — but instead, the kind of lasting industry connections that can take years (and many starts and stops) to build. Also, no job opportunities isn’t entirely true. Take last year’s Square Peg Social mentee Yona Strauss, who’s now working for Knudsen and Aster’s Square Peg.

Just a sampling of this year’s participating producers and directors: producer Annie Huang, who worked on franchise IP like “Barbie” and “Wicked” at major studios; Jack Auen, co-founder of the filmmaking collective Cosmic Salon, which this year directed the New York critics’ favorite “Chronovisor”; Emmy-winning director of the Netflix short “The Turnaround,” Kyle Thrash; SXSW 2026 Neon Auteur Award winner Oliver Woolf; and many more who have their foot in the door, but are ready to cross the threshold.

IndieWire spoke to Lars Knudsen and Aster (who also co-founded the production company Square Peg, which this year backed “The Drama” and “Primetime”), plus Stevenson, Oppenheim, and Kwedar, along with three participants, to replay the on-the-ground experience in Austin. Late nights, early mornings, and vulnerabilities abounded across a long (but in some ways too short) weekend of intimate panels, small group sessions, and candid remarks from established filmmakers about the times they were trying to hold their own projects together with Scotch tape and paper clips. Think of it like a mini summer camp devoted to obsessive ambition.

“When you’ve been doing it for this long, sometimes it feels like you’re just a little bit going through the motions. You’re going from movie to movie to movie, and you sometimes forget why we do this thing that we do. We’re in this world working with these artists where they don’t have a plan B. Having now worked with 30, 40 filmmakers, I realized that when my wife brought up the idea of doing something because she has her own aversions to the industry, and that there isn’t really — it sounds cliché — but there just isn’t a lot of kindness or compassion or openness in our industry.

“There’s a lot of fear, there’s a lot of rejection. We wanted to create a space for filmmakers where there’s radical transparency and where it was truly, truly focused on a selfless thing: helping young filmmakers navigate the industry at a time in their career where things can either take off or not, and really demystifying the process of making movies, especially during the stage where they’re often in the back seat, which is financing or casting. Because for all these filmmakers that I work with and all the filmmakers that we’ve invited there, even the producers, it’s the first thing to think about when they wake up and the last thing to think about when they go to bed. Nothing is more important. I wanted to create an event where that is treated with the utmost importance, almost like it’s a life-or-death thing because it is all they want to do.”

“When Lars and Amy first broached the idea with me, I realized that it was something that I wish I had when I got out of school [at AFI], because I really did have to navigate that on my own. I was making a lot of shorts with whatever money I could raise and writing screenplays and trying to get one screenplay going. When that failed, writing something else and really looking for any sort of mentorship or guidance, It’s a very demoralizing process, and it was very, very hard for me to find traction, and it hasn’t gotten easier. It’s as bad as it’s ever been. There’s just so much uncertainty right now in the industry, not just for filmmakers. Even the lives of these studios are suddenly in danger and in question.

“There are a lot of filmmakers that Lars and I have been championing and films that we’ve been trying to get financing for that have proven almost impossible… It felt like a good thing to create a space where filmmakers can come together and commiserate and share experiences and connect. More important than even the connections that are made between the mentors and the mentees here are actually the relationships made among the people who are attending. A lot of them end up working together because we have producers and directors coming in. Last year proved really successful, and I would just say it was refreshing for us, too, that it galvanized us to keep doing this. Because last year it was almost an experiment: Will this work? How will we feel having done this? … Everybody walked away feeling good and feeling like it was a really useful and positive experience.”

“I’ve never really had the opportunity to just hang out with so many great filmmakers, not only just working filmmakers whose work I’ve loved, like David Lowery, who I’ve idolized for so long, but there’s so many filmmakers that were actually in the program as participants whose work I also have really admired. So having a space where we could all just kind of talk and vent and really nerd out on stuff that you never really get the opportunity to do.

“Because this was so filmmaker-driven and filmmaker-led, it encouraged the spirit of vulnerability [where] everyone really went there. I felt like maybe I should go back to therapy or something, but I felt like this was a great opportunity to therapize and also dump all of my feelings into a forum where you could just be open and honest about the process of making films… Most people had made features before, and were in the process of making features. It felt much more like we were at a film festival and everyone was able to connect with each other in a much deeper way, more than anything I’ve been to before.

“The first night I was there, I stayed up till like three in the morning, and I went on one of those electric scooters, the limes with Lars and Christian [Vasquez], my producer, and a producer from the event, too. We went to Whataburger and just kept talking. I think that was sort of the vibe. I don’t know. I guess everyone was encouraged to hang out for as long as they wanted to and to kick back and relax. There was another night we closed down the Soho House lounge bar, and Amy was like, ‘Let’s keep hanging out.’ So we were outside the bar, and everybody pulled together all of the drinks in their mini bar, and we created an ad hoc bar outside of the Soho House, and we kept drinking and hanging.”

“I don’t think you can really do film if you have a plan B because there’s always an escape hatch, and film requires every single atom of your body, mind and soul. It naturally becomes a very therapeutic place. I think because we’re all in this constant state of obsession, that can get really tiring, and it can get really lonely. … [The industry] attracts very sensitive souls. [With Square Peg Social] I didn’t even realize how badly I needed it until the first year. I’d known Amy and Lars before that, and Amy said that she wanted to start a Social. … I thought it would be much smaller, smaller. It ended up being this great big thing where, yeah, it does feel like a therapy circle, really.

“Everyone was really struck by the safety of the event. There was this unspoken agreement that everybody would be checking your egos at the door, and that this would be a very safe place to share your personal vulnerabilities, which is exceptionally rare in film because resources are so limited, and it’s just naturally a very competitive industry. Letting yourself be very, very vulnerable in front of your peers is something you were, in a sense, trained not to do but sometimes desperately need. At Square Peg, also, the line between mentee and mentor blurs quite a bit, which is why I think it’s so beneficial for everybody who goes there.

“It kind of reminds me of summer camp a little bit because you’re up until two or three in the morning talking to people, and then you’re up at eight again.”

“I always think of this term, like, whenever you take an elevator up, if you get to the top floor, send it back down for someone else to get on. [Square Peg] is one of the busiest production companies working today. To dedicate this weekend for emerging artists to have a forum where they can come and feel completely comfortable being very vulnerable with their ambitions, but also the things that they’re afraid of, and to hear that echoed from industry mentors who are being just as vulnerable about their ambitions and the things that they struggle with and the heartbreaks they’ve had, it’s an amazing table that’s set.

“I had ulterior motives in the, in the sense that Clint [Bentley] and I have started this new company, Ethos, and we have a deal at Netflix to finance films from emerging artists, and so I was also there … to look for talent. We’ll be following up with a lot of these artists to just hear more about the films they want to make. One thing that I appreciated about it was that it wasn’t like a pitch fest. You’re not there to pitch your project. You’re there to soak it in and learn.

“It had this healthy blend of these panels, and not the normal kind of panel. One was a panel of filmmakers led off by Ari and Lars, telling a very, very brutally honest story of how hard one of their films was to make. That kind of created a pathway for how the rest of the weekend would unfold.”

“I think the whole reason anyone works in film is that we were once kids making videos in the woods with our friends, making with a shitty camera. And there’s nothing else in this world, and I think I probably speak for everyone, where I can’t imagine film is the only thing that’s our main passion and hobby and something we can also make a career out of. So there was never a plan B at all. Whenever someone asked me, ‘What do you think you’d do if you couldn’t do anything film-adjacent?’ I have literally no idea, maybe a teacher or something. That’s super nice that Lars and the rest of Square Peg was saying that there is no plan B. There’s only: If it takes longer to get to Plan A, then it takes longer to get to Plan A.

“I remember on the very first day before we even properly began, Lars did a little speech with Ari, and Lars was like, ‘We’re going to be 100 percent transparent with you guys.’ And I remember thinking, ‘Oh, that’s cool, but I wonder how transparent.’ And by the end of it, I was like, ‘Fuck me, that was transparent.’ There really was nothing off the table.”

“It was definitely something that I’ve never experienced before in this industry, to experience that level of candor and to hear these traumatic experiences that they have gone through in not a sensationalistic way, but almost in a very personal and almost relatable way, despite me having never experienced that level of millions of dollars of movie budget making — but on a personal level of how the heartbreaks had felt for them individually and the hardships of filmmaking. Coming into this program, there are so many people within our cohort who are incredibly talented, who have accomplished so many things. And coming into it, oftentimes you’ll have a fear of: ‘OK, how do I compare in relation to their accomplishments?’ But in hearing Lars and Ari talk about their own hardships, I think that’s what influenced me to really share some of mine coming up in the industry and producing independently.

“Some of the traumatic experiences that I have also faced are ones that I feel like I have to not talk about or hide from people, for fear of them looking like mistakes or of me looking like I’m not good enough to be doing this. And we were able to share that, like Ollie [Woolf] and I, in our own little producer’s therapy session with the mentors, with Lars. That was really healing for me.”

“[Ari, Lars, and the mentors are] on, not a different level, but they’re all going through similar issues and this and that, whether it’s a low budget or a higher budget type of ordeal. Everyone’s going through the same thing in their own way, in a sense. Just to know the people that I’ve been looking up to for a very long time, the reason in large part why I got into making films, to know that they’re going through similar things and just keep going, and it’s fine. No matter what level we’re going to be at, there’s still something to navigate. So I thought it was very cool to see, over the course of five days, to hear these individual experiences and stuff and how you could relate it back to what we’re going through right now and where we are.

“It was information overload in the best way possible. At a certain point, I hope I’m retaining everything that was said over those five days because it was nonstop, all useful information. I wasn’t even taking notes at a certain point because I’m like, ‘I can’t write all this stuff down. I’m just going to try and soak it all in.'”

#3469. Apple Is Already Getting The Mistborn Movie Casting Right After Brandon Sanderson's Update

The upcoming Mistborn movie has revealed its casting strategy, and it's the perfect choice for what could wind up being one of Apple TV's biggest franchises. With adaptations planned across movies, television, and even board games, Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere could become one of the biggest series ever seen on big and small screens alike.

All of this is set to begin with Mistborn, a huge feature film based on the popular 2006 novel Mistborn: The Final Empire. Crafted with a complex magic system, the novel depicts a deeply atmospheric dystopian world where a group of the oppressed must band together to resist the tyrannical leadership of the Lord Ruler.

The Mistborn franchise has the potential to be enormous. Three novels explore the original setting and characters, while a whole additional series of Mistborn books is set hundreds of years later. Brandon Sanderson continues to write novels in the series, with a new trilogy of Mistborn novels planned for release in the coming years.

While it is already too late for the most popular Mistborn casting to happen, it is still important that great performers take on the iconic roles of Vin and Kelsier in the upcoming film.

And while stars as big as Millie Bobby Brown and Henry Cavill have routinely been fancast for the lead roles, the film's strategy appears to be looking for different kinds of stars.

A new update from Brandon Sanderson recently revealed the casting strategy for the upcoming Mistborn movie, and it looks to be the right choice. In a mailbag video on the author's YouTube channel, Sanderson revealed that the plan for casting Vin and Elend in the upcoming film will be to "look for talented new actors."

This immediately disqualifies many of the most popular fancasting choices for the roles. Virtually every dark-haired young actress has been suggested for the part of Vin, from Dafne Keen to Jenna Ortega, while names like Louis Partridge have been suggested for Elend. However, this revealed strategy is a much stronger proposition.

In the first novel, Vin is a teenager, while Elend is in his early twenties. With that in mind, many of the proposed names are already too old for the roles, and even those who might be the right age now will likely have aged out of it by the time that filming begins.

With that considered, it makes much more sense to look for lesser-known faces.

Like roles such as Katniss in The Hunger Games, or Edward and Bella in Twilight, Mistborn's most important characters, Vin and Elend, have the potential to be career-defining parts. Securing actors who do not have too much baggage or awareness already attached to them makes sense, although the film will still need the anchor of at least one star.

In the same video, Sanderson revealed that "the only big name" cast in the film will be for the role of Kelsier. As the leader of the skaa rebellion, Kelsier works as an excellent entry point into the larger story for Vin, and using him in that same fashion, to draw general audiences to the Mistborn film, also makes sense.

Doing this with a strong and familiar performer is the right move. Fancasts for Kelsier have suggested a plethora of names, many of which could be a good fit for the role, including John David Washington and Charlie Hunnam.

While it is also necessary to recognize that Kelsier is 38 years old in the first novel, his exact age is not as important as Vin's. So long as Kelsier is old enough to serve as a mentor to Vin, it is possible that he could be cast younger or older than he appears in the novel.

Casting a big name as Kelsier also makes sense because the character's role in the sequel novels is significantly reduced. With this in mind, the part is not nearly as much of a franchise commitment as roles like Vin and Elend, who go on to become the faces of the Mistborn trilogy.

Getting the right star for Kelsier is an important move for the Mistborn movie. The film has the potential to be one of the biggest and best fantasy movies ever made, and casting the roles well will go a long way in securing a rich future for the Cosmere on the big screen.
