#3468. The Out of Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Does 'Code Rot' Mean?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's Out-of-Touch guide takes a look at a phenomena that's probably going to define the lives of generations of young people: Code rot—both actual computer-style code rot, and the more elusive cultural kind. I'm also taking a look at the fake controversy over the "cancellation" of Freddy Krueger, and finally, bringing things home with viral videos of boyfriends dancing.

Expect to hear young people talking about code rot for awhile, maybe for the rest of their lives. It's a concept that's going to affect them more than any previous generation. Code rot, or software rot, describes what happens to a computer program when the hardware and operating system it runs on advance. If older programs aren't updated, they become less stable and glitchy until they eventually become unusable.

The idea of code rot has really caught on in the young people's popular imagination, probably because they're going to spend a lot of their lives dealing with it. They've even taken the idea of code rot into life, and use the phrase to describe anything that is worn out or malfunctioning. If the ice cream machine isn't working at McDonald's, it's code rotted. Bad grades on a report card? Code rot.

Kids are making videos where they demonstrate actual code rot:

or point out physical things that are code rotted, like a cat:

Interestingly, a lot of the online discourse around code rotting concerns the massive video game platform Roblox. Because Roblox games there are made by users, there's often not a lot of incentive for the creators to keep the games current with the platform's changes, so a lot of Gen Z's childhood memories of playing games are sinking into code rot. Here's a video about it:

Another interesting wrinkle is the tone these videos take. Code rot is seen as apocalyptic. While it's mostly hyperbole, I think part of it is the realization that the entire world is code rotted. The old programs that used to run within the "Western Culture" operating system no longer apply and everything is starting to glitch out.

The meaning of "PDF file" depends on the context. If you're at work, it refers to a Portable Document Format file, a format created by Adobe that is famously hard for older people to open. In slang, though, PDF file is algo speak for "pedophile." Because that word is flagged by moderation software online, people say "PDF File" to skirt the censorship.

The run-up to Halloween brought a lot of online discourse about Nightmare on Elm Street villain Freddy Krueger. The supernatural serial murder/PDF File was supposedly cancelled online by overly woke, Gen-Z Tiktokers outraged that he is a child predator. The controversy started with a post from Entertainment Industry Reporter that points out how strange it is that in the '80s and '90s, Freddy Krueger, depicted in 1984's A Nightmare on Elm Street as a child murderer so driven by bloodlust he transcended death, was featured on dolls, board games, and lunchboxes aimed at children. It's a good point, but not a call for "cancellation."

Although the article does say that "Freddy Krueger lunchboxes shouldn’t exist," and that parents "shouldn’t have been buying their kids action figures of a child murderer," this is not a call to action. It's not suggesting cancellation of any kind, and it's hard to even conceive of what cancellation of a fictional character in an old horror franchise would even mean. The article is actually an observation about how merchandising (and low-quality sequels) change the meaning of art. But people online missed the point entirely and invented a scenario where "woke" young people are calling for the cancellations of a fictional villain for doing bad things.

I've been scouring TikTok, looking for even one video where someone is calling for "canceling" Freddy Krueger, and I can't find any, but there are hundreds, maybe thousands of videos like this:

In these videos, people point out how enraging it is that the woke people are calling for Krueger's cancellation and vowing that they won't let it happen. Even though it is not happening. There are even levels to the myths about woke mobs canceling Freddy. Supposedly, younger users were unaware that Krueger is depicted as a "PDF file" as well as a murderer in the 2010 reboot of the franchise, so there are online arguments about whether that's the reason he's being canceled. Even though no one is canceling anything. These anti-woke folks are, ironically, defending a fictional villain from cancellation by creating another fictional villain, the shadowy woke mob that's ruining horror movies. Meanwhile, the real villain is a lack of media literacy. Saying "wow, it's crazy that previous generations made a comedy mascot of such a terrible character and marketed him to children" is not the same as cancellation.

This week's viral videos are of boyfriends dancing. The newest thing on the TikTok is young women sharing video of their boyfriends getting down accompanied by a clip from the song "gay alligations fr. my girlfriend" by TikToker OH MICKEY. Like this:

It's a simple, silly template that maybe doesn't mean a whole lot, but this generation of young men are so messed up when it comes to relationships and masculinity, I'm always happy when a meme becomes popular that indicates that young women want goofy dudes, dudes who know how to dance, and dudes who act silly as boyfriends more than they want red-pilled, manosphere, looksmaxxing types. I don't know if these kinds of messages ever really "break through" to the underground of internet incels, but I like to hope they do, because a lot of young men are not OK.

#3465. You Can Get Microsoft Visual Studio Pro 2026 on Sale for Just $30 Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Microsoft’s flagship development tool, Visual Studio Professional 2026, reduces much of the friction that used to come with large projects, and it’s on sale for just $29.97 on StackSocial right now, which is far less than what most developers expect to pay for a professional-grade IDE.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a desktop-only Windows product built as a 64-bit application, designed for people working on real-world codebases. Think multi-project solutions, long build times, and code that’s touched by more than one person. In day-to-day use, the biggest benefit is the context the software provides while you work. Visual Studio 2026 supports C#, C++, .NET, ASP.NET, Blazor, and .NET MAUI, so you can move between desktop, web, and cross-platform projects without switching tools. You also get Hot Reload, which helps reduce rebuild time by letting you edit code in .NET and C++ apps and see changes immediately. And CodeLens adds useful context right inside the editor—who last edited a method, which tests cover it, and whether recent changes broke anything—without forcing you to dig through menus or version history. The software’s AI-powered IntelliCode suggestions also feel more restrained than flashy. They tend to fill in logical patterns based on your existing code. It saves time on repetitive work, but you’ll still want to read what it writes.

Collaboration is another area where this version earns its keep. Live Share allows teammates to jump into a debugging or editing session without cloning the repo or matching environments. That’s useful for code reviews or troubleshooting, but it depends heavily on a stable internet connection. System requirements are also worth noting: While it can technically run on 4GB of RAM, 8GB or more is far more realistic, especially for larger solutions, and storage needs can balloon depending on workloads, reaching well over 100GB in some setups. Also, it doesn’t support 32-bit systems and won’t run on mobile devices or Chromebooks. For developers already working in the Windows ecosystem, this is a solid long-term license. For everyone else, those limitations can be deal breakers.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a full-featured, 64-bit IDE for Windows designed for developers working on complex, multi-project codebases, and it's on sale right now for a one-time price of $29.97 on StackSocial.

#3464. CleanMyMac now helps you clean up Gmail and manage Chrome tabs

MacPaw today announced an expansion of CleanMyMac’s capabilities beyond the app’s traditional Mac maintenance and optimization tools. Here are the details.

CleanMyMac got two new features today, Email Cleanup and Browser Care, which are “designed to help users tackle digital clutter throughout their workday,” MacPaw explains.

Interestingly, both features focus on Google services, with Email Cleanup targeting Gmail and Browser Care designed specifically for Chrome.

Email Cleanup also helps users identify emails taking up storage space shared across Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Photos, allowing them to reclaim it once those messages are permanently deleted.

As for Browser Care, it “helps users reclaim Mac memory and stay focused by identifying Google Chrome tabs that consume valuable resources or create unnecessary clutter,” according to the company’s press release.

It works via a Chrome browser extension that connects directly to CleanMyMac, and lets users access “near real-time,” as MacPaw put it, “memory usage, pause resource-intensive tabs, find duplicates across browser windows and identify pages that have been left open for hours or days.”

In practice, MacPaw says, Browser Care makes it easier to identify which background tabs are affecting the Mac’s performance, helping users address slowdowns and reduce distractions.

MacPaw also emphasizes that Email Cleanup requires confirmation before making changes, while Browser Care only closes or suspends tabs when users choose to do so. The company adds that page content, titles, and browsing history remain stored locally on the Mac.

Both features are rolling out today to users with an active CleanMyMac subscription. To learn more about today’s announcement, follow this link.

#3463. Netflix Officially Revives One of the Worst Fantasy Remakes Ever Made

Tom Cruise has spent most of his career making the impossible look ridiculously easy, whether that's hanging off airplanes, jumping motorcycles off cliffs, or somehow finding increasingly dangerous ways to save the world as Ethan Hunt. But even Hollywood's most committed action star has the occasional misfire. Nearly a decade later, however, it's getting another opportunity to find its audience.

The Mummy has returned to Netflix's Top 10 movie rankings, bringing Cruise's much-maligned fantasy adventure back into the streaming spotlight. The 2017 release earned approximately $410 million worldwide, a respectable-sounding figure that wasn't enough to make the movie the franchise-launching success Universal had envisioned. Intended to launch an entire cinematic universe of classic monsters, the movie instead became a rather expensive reminder that audiences aren't always interested in another big-budget IP.

Thought safely entombed in a tomb deep beneath the unforgiving desert, an ancient princess whose destiny was unjustly taken from her is awakened in our current day, bringing with her malevolence grown over millennia and terrors that defy human comprehension. The movie takes us on a globe-trotting adventure from the sweeping sands of the Middle East through hidden labyrinths under modern-day London, in a new world of gods and monsters.

The movie stars Tom Cruise (Mission: Impossible) as Nick Morton, Sofia Boutella (Kingsman: The Secret Service) as Princess Ahmanet, Annabelle Wallis (Peaky Blinders) as Jenny Halsey, Russell Crowe (Gladiator) as Dr. Henry Jekyll, Jake Johnson (New Girl) as Chris Vail, Courtney B. Vance (The People v. O. J. Simpson) as Colonel Greenway, and Marwan Kenzari (Aladdin) as Malik.

Crowe's Dr. Jekyll was intended to help connect the movie to a wider world of supernatural creatures, with Universal announcing plans for future installments involving characters such as Frankenstein's Monster and the Invisible Man. Yes, they also planned to bring in the likes of Javier Bardem and Johnny Depp for a new Dark Universe.

Despite Cruise’s star power and a big marketing push (remember that awkward cast promo image with him, Bardem, Depp, and Crowe?), the film bombed critically and commercially, earning dreadful reviews and losing an estimated $100 million for Universal. The entire Dark Universe crumbled before a second movie could even shoot.

#3462. The Gilded Age Beats Downton Abbey To The Modern World By 28 Years

Warning: SPOILERS for The Gilded Age Season 4, Episode 2 - "You Won't Hear Me Beg"

If Ada Forte (Cynthia Nixon) makes good on her idea, The Gilded Age will beat Downton Abbey to the modern world by 28 years. Academy Award winner Julian Fellowes created both Downton Abbey and The Gilded Age, the latter of which is now growing into the kind of ratings and cultural phenomenon on HBO that Downton was for six seasons on PBS Masterpiece before spawning three feature films.

The Gilded Age season 4, episode 2 ended with George Russell (Morgan Spector) confronting the man who shot him, Will Morris (Will Pullen). Russell spared Morris' life after a dramatic confrontation. Will blamed Mr. Russell for the suicide of his father, Patrick Morris (Michel Gill), in The Gilded Age season 1 after George ruined Patrick financially when Morris reneged on their business deal.

Across East 61st Street, Agnes Van Rhijn (Christine Baranski) is jumping through hoops from The Heritage Society as she prepares to host a dinner for President Grover Cleveland (Jim Gaffigan). Meanwhile, Aunt Agnes bristles as Ada pulls her financial support for the President's dinner. Instead, Ada is redecorating their home and hiring a new footman.

Aunt Ada also has another plan to inject a symbol of modernity into the Van Rhijn and Forte house.

Ada suggests that she will have a telephone installed in her home with Agnes. Naturally, Agnes is appalled by the idea and questions who would even call Ada. Her sister responds that someone eventually will. The matter was left there, but Ada is likely to follow through on her desire for a telephone. When she has it installed, The Gilded Age will beat Downton Abbey to owning a telephone by 28 years.

The Gilded Age returns for its fourth season with supreme confidence and a renewed focus on family drama and testing its huge cast of characters.

The Gilded Age season 4 is set in 1886, four years after the series began with Ada and Agnes' niece, Marian Brook (Louisa Jacobson), arriving in New York as George and Bertha Russell (Carrie Coon) move into their newly completed East 61st Street palace. Downton Abbey began with the sinking of the Titanic in April 1912, and season 1 ended in August 1914, when England entered World War I.

Downton Abbey's season 1 finale saw two telephones installed in 1914, one upstairs in the main house, and one downstairs in Mr. Carson's (Jim Carter) office. The telephone in Downton Abbey changed the life of Gwen (Rose Leslie), one of the maids. Thanks to Lady Sybil (Jessica Brown Findlay), Gwen was hired by Mr. Bromidge (Sean McKenzie) to work for the telephone company. This lifted Gwen out of service, and she eventually married and became Mrs. Harding.

A telephone in The Gilded Age's Van Rhijn home would truly one-up Downton Abbey, which takes place in the early 20th century. One of Downton's themes is how slowly and begrudgingly the Crawleys let go of Edwardian tradition and embrace the modern world. Meanwhile, Ada is remarkably progressive for a woman in 19th-century New York society, and it fits her character to embrace something as modern as a telephone.

The Gilded Age season 3 garnered record ratings on HBO, and it became the most-watched streaming show in the world with The Gilded Age season 4's premiere on November 1st. The Gilded Age has captured the hearts of audiences, many of whom originally sampled Julian Fellowes' HBO series because they were already Downton Abbey fanatics.

After four seasons, many servants in The Gilded Age remain underdeveloped.

While The Gilded Age has come into its own narratively and is as addictive as Downton Abbey was at its peak, the predecessor series is still superior at balancing its lords and ladies with the servants who toil for them. After four seasons, many servants in The Gilded Age remain underdeveloped, like butlers Church (Jack Gilpin) and Bannister (Simon Jones),

In Downton Abbey, the servants were equally important as the Crawley family, and their stories carried the same weight. Indeed, the Crawleys and their servants' lives were inextricable. This is much harder to achieve in The Gilded Age, with two households, the Van Rhijns and the Russells, having two sets of servants. There isn't enough screen time in an hour-long episode to service everyone.

As a tale set in America, The Gilded Age also feels more immediately relevant than Downton Abbey, despite its posh 19th century trappings. The haves and have-nots in The Gilded Age, with its greedy millionaire tycoons, feels like a mirror to today.

Aunt Ada installing a telephone is just one step closer to The Gilded Age embracing the 20th century, which Downton Abbey tried to avoid for as long as possible.

#3461. Report: Apple captured half of global smartphone revenue in Q3

According to a new report from Counterpoint Research, Apple just recorded its highest-ever global smartphone revenue for a third calendar quarter. Here are the details.

In a report released earlier this week, Counterpoint Research mapped out the global smartphone market’s performance during the third quarter, which saw Apple capture its highest-ever share of industry revenue for the period.

Samsung, which came in second, accounted for 19% of global smartphone revenue, followed by Xiaomi at 6%, OPPO at 5%, and vivo at 4%.

In another record, Counterpoint says Apple saw the iPhone average selling price (ASP) hit an all-time-high of $1,031, up 19% year-over-year.

Counterpoint’s Research Director Tarun Pathak explained that the iPhone 18 Pro series contributed to Apple’s ASP growth, despite launching toward the end of the third calendar quarter:

“Apple remained the most resilient major brand in Q3 2026, with shipments nearly flat YoY. Apple has the pricing power to absorb rising memory costs and pass them on to consumers with minimal impact on demand. At the same time, ASP growth was supported by higher launch prices for the iPhone 18 Pro series, the absence of the base iPhone 18 from the launch and price increases across older models in September. Together, these factors helped Apple deliver strong revenue growth in an otherwise challenging market.”

Finally, the report noted that while Samsung still led the market in shipment share, its lead over Apple narrowed slightly, with the companies accounting for 22% and 21% of global smartphone shipments, respectively.

Stacy Keach, the highly prolific screen and stage actor known to audiences for his television role as the private detective Mike Hammer and other tough guy characters, died of heart failure on Tuesday at his family residence in Magdalenka, Poland. He was 85.

Keach’s death was confirmed by his wife, Malgosia, in a statement sent by representation at Guttman Associates.

“It is with profound sadness and a broken heart that I announce the passing of my darling husband, Stacy Keach, who passed away on November 10, 2026, at our family home in Magdalenka, Poland,” reads the release. “After a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure, Stacy peacefully departed this world. He fought for so long, with extraordinary courage, determination and strength. She continues: “Stacy was not only a legendary actor, admired and loved by audiences the world over, but also my beloved husband, my companion and the heart of our family. His passing leaves an immeasurable emptiness in our lives. But his extraordinary spirit, his unforgettable voice and the love he gave so generously will remain with us forever.”

Keach rose to the stature of one of the preeminent classical stage actors in the United States through the ’60s and 70s, venturing into avant garde productions and playing roles like Falstaff and Hamlet in his early career. He first appeared on Broadway in 1969, playing Buffalo Bill in Arthur Kopit’s “Indians,” for which he received a Tony nomination. He was also a four-time Drama Desk award winner.

It was after establishing his onstage bona fides that Keach was tapped to play the detective Mike Hammer for CBS’ television film “Murder Me, Murder You,” adapting the character of Mickey Spillane novels that had previously been brought to the screen in noirs like “Kiss Me Deadly.” The film spawned a three-season run of “Mickey Spillane’s Mike Hammer,” with nearly 50 episodes and two more TV movies featuring Keach as the tough PI. A revival, “Mike Hammer, Private Eye,” was produced in the late ’90s.

In film, Keach established his star in 1972 with early featured roles in John Huston’s classic boxing drama “Fat City” and Richard Fleischer’s intense cop thriller “The New Centurions,” along with a starring role of Doc Holliday in Frank Perry’s 1971 Western “Doc.” Though he never quite rose to marquee stardom, Keach’s character actor skills were called upon regularly by Hollywood, oftentimes playing military authorities in titles ranging from “Up in Smoke” to “Escape from L.A.” to “Truth.” In 1980, he starred in, co-wrote and executive produced the Walter Hill Western “The Long Riders,” alongside his brother James Keach.

Other notable credits for Keach include the lead of “Exorcist” creator William Peter Blatty’s horror oddity “The Ninth Configuration” (1980), the voice of the mysterious villain Phantasm in the classic superhero animated feature “Batman: Mask of the Phantasm” (1993), and the Bakersfield-loving father to George Clooney’s movie star in “Jay Kelly” (2025).

Born June 2, 1941 in Savannah, Ga., Walter Stacy Keach Jr.’s family moved to Pasadena after his drama teacher father signed a day-player contract with Universal. Keach attended University of Calfornia, Berkeley and later studied theater at Yale School of Drama and the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art.

Along with Malogisa, Keach is also survived by his their children, Karolina and Shannon; their grandchildren; their spouses; and his brother, James.

#3457. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

#3456. 8 DC Characters Who Should Make Their DCU Debut on TV

While the DCU has seen some success in cinemas with the likes of Superman and Clayface, they've actually been doing just as well on television—some even arguing they've been doing better. With Creature Commandos and Lanterns both being critical smash hits, it's clear that the DCU will not be having the Marvel Cinematic Universe's television problem moving forward.

This is good because the DCU actually has a lot of plans for television in their upcoming slate, and that means even more great stories to come. Through the previous two series, audiences got introduced to Clayface (before his cinema debut), the Creature Commandos, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler), and so many more iconic characters. With this and these upcoming announced projects in mind, there are some legendary DC Comics characters that should most definitely be making their DCU debut on television.

While not well-known to the general public, anyone who's seen the ever-beloved animated series, Young Justice—and the more niche-but-critically-acclaimed Mister Miracle (2017) comic—knows exactly who Granny Goodness is (played in that series by Deborah Strang). With how important of a character Granny Goodness is to the story of Mister Miracle, it'd be an incredible disservice to the DCU iteration of the hero (to be played by Josh Hutcherson) not to have her be included.

She is a master brainwasher, but most importantly, she is the top recruiter of the planet Apokolips' militaristic forces. This, of course, makes her very close to the Thanos of the DC Comics world . . . Darkseid. Audiences already know the terrifying villain will be making his first appearance in Mister Miracle, but with how important Granny Goodness is, it would feel odd not having her around at his right hand.

Fans of the Scarlet Speedster—both in comics and the television show, The Flash—are well aware that the classic Flash villain, Gorilla Grodd, will be making his DCU entrance in The People v. Gorilla Grodd. The show will follow reporter Jimmy Olsen (Skyler Gisondo) as he investigates the murder of Grodd's father, of which Grodd himself is wrongfully convicted of. If Olsen is going to truly investigate something like this, he needs to look into other potential suspects and those who have similar enemies that Grodd does—aka, other Flash villains.

Audiences have already come across a major rumor that Flash villain, Weather Wizard, is going to appear, so why not have one of the greatest Flash villains up there, with Grodd, also make an appearance—the one and only Captain Cold? Aside from the Reverse Flash, this Cold Gun-wielding baddie is one of the most recognizable Flash foes of all time. It would be a dang shame if audiences didn't get to see him find a place in The People v. Gorilla Grodd.

If anyone has ever heard of Booster Gold, they know of his close relationship with Blue Beetle—Ted Kord, not Jaime Reyes. With the latter finally being added to the DCU and getting his own animated series, Xolo Maridueña's Jaime Reyes still acts as the perfect hallway for Booster Gold to enter the cinematic universe. Despite the gold-clad hero being a good friend to Ted Kord, he's still teamed up with Jaime from time to time.

Not to mention, with the Blue Beetle film itself not being confirmed to be DCU canon, and only Xolo's iteration, there's a very good chance Kord could have a place in this new animated story regardless. If they choose to include Jaime's predecessor in some way, then Booster Gold is the perfect addition to this series—especially for comedic relief. Now, all that DC Studios needs to do is listen to the fans and get Shayne Topp on the cast for the iconic character.

As stated, with Xolo's Blue Beetle only being canon as a character and the movie itself not being canon (at least not yet, anyway), the disappearance of Ted Kord in that film may not end up being canon. So, this means audiences could finally see the old Blue Beetle in the DCU. This iteration of the hero differs vastly from Jaime's.

While the younger hero has the Scarab to power him up, Ted Kord is more of a gadget-based hero—almost in a Batman sense, just not dark and gritty. He's a funny, relatable, and a bit of an outsider in the DC Comics universe. He would be a perfect addition to the animated series and, as previously said, would be a great way to bring in Booster Gold, too.

Another character extremely important to the Mister Miracle mythology is his adoptive brother, Orion. Fans of the classic animated series, Justice League Unlimited, might recognize him. He is a living contrast—being born into a world of war and violence, but chooses to embrace light and heroism regardless. He's very compelling for this very reason.

Everyone loves a hero who has some darkness within them and Orion is a great example of this. There's no question he'll be appearing in Mister Miracle, and hopefully this means he'll be sticking around in the DCU moving onward post-Mister Miracle. These two brothers have a great dynamic, so adding Orion to the cast of characters currently in the cinematic universe is perfect.

The major question regarding the Flash in the DCU at the moment is whether the main mantle-holder will be Barry Allen or, the once Kid Flash, Wally West—who became the Flash in the comics after Barry's death in Crisis on Infinite Earths (1985). Regardless of if he's the main Flash, Kid Flash, or still powerless, though, Wally could be a perfect addition to The People v. Gorilla Grodd, thanks to one of the main locations within said series.

If the young hero is still, well, young, he could be perfect to have at the college that Grodd attends at one point in the show. If he isn't younger, and is the main Flash at the moment, it would only make sense for the hero to make an appearance to help Grodd—or believe that he's still evil and try to prove Jimmy wrong. Wally (as Flash) was one of the most popular characters in the Justice League and Justice League Unlimited animated shows, so it'd be a shame not to see him in the DCU soon.

With Lanterns being successful enough to warrant a greenlight for Season 2, one can only hope that the DCU continues to expand the Green Lantern corner of the universe. Unlike the cinematic universe, though, the comics have multiple Green Lanterns from Earth, and a fan favorite just so happens to be the likes of Kyle Rayner. Where John Stewart is more tactical and precise with his constructs and heroism, Kyle has always been one of, if not the most creative, Green Lanterns.

While John still needs a lot more time to be Earth's Green Lantern on his own for a bit, Lanterns Season 2 is still a great opportunity to introduce this fan favorite green-suited hero. It wouldn't be the best choice to make him a Green Lantern right away, but bringing him into the fold in some way, to being building him up to eventually be a hero, would be an excellent move on DC Studios' part.

If it isn't already clear—based on what was already stated about Wally West—it would be a gigantic missed opportunity to not have the Flash help out or be an antagonist in some way, shape, or form in The People v. Gorilla Grodd. While Wally would be cool to see, it actually makes far more sense to include Barry, as he has a direct connection to matters like this, being a CSI, and someone who has faced Grodd multiple times in the past—the gorilla has always been more of a Barry villain.

It's genuinely so difficult to believe that Barry wouldn't use his CSI work as a way to insert himself in the investigation and learn more. Flash is a hero that typically believes in redemption for his villains, meaning he would definitely want to get behind what actually happened between Grodd and his father—if anything even did. Honestly, if Barry—any Flash, really—doesn't show up in The People v. Gorilla Grodd, it'd be a bit absurd.

#3455. Report: iPad shipments drop 27.5% as global tablet market plunges in Q3

Despite global iPad shipments dropping 27.5% year-over-year in the third calendar quarter, Apple maintained its lead in the tablet market, according to a new report released today. Here are the details.

According to a new report published by Omdia (via MacMagazine), Apple shipped 11,5 million iPads during Q3 2026, accounting for 36% of all shipments.

Compared to Q3 2025, that was a 27.5% drop in shipments, and a 2.2 percentage-point decline in market share.

For context, the global tablet market saw a 23% year-over-year drop, with total shipments going from 41.8 million to 32.2 million units. Omdia noted this was the lowest level in nearly three years.

As for Apple’s competitors, Samsung remained in second place with 16.9% market share, followed by Lenovo with 12.7%, Xiaomi with 7.3%, and Huawei with 5.7%.

I don’t think Apple increasing the price of the 12.9"/13" iPad Pro by 36% in four years has helped iPad sales. I get that every company is feeling a pinch because of Memory and Storage prices and is needing to raise prices. But Apple’s prices for these components were already ridiculously overpriced to begin with. They could’ve not raised prices at all and still been making a killing in comparison with everyone else. I really do not like what Tim Cook turned Apple into, greedier than they already were and I’m not hopeful that John Ternus is going to be any better. Maybe he’ll surprise us though. 🙂

When it comes to shipment growth, Lenovo was the only company among the top five to post a positive result, up 11.9% year over year. Huawei saw the steepest decline at 43%, followed by Apple at 27.5%, Samsung at 21.7%, and Xiaomi at 10.6%.

Commenting on the results, Omdia Research Manager Himani Mukka said supply constraints are “limiting vendors’ ability to deliver meaningful specification upgrades, leaving fewer compelling differences between new models and their predecessors.”

“As a result,” she added, “consumers are increasingly expected to delay purchases until more substantial improvements become available.”

#3454. PlayStation Unveils New Hardware You Can Officially Pre-Order Now

Sony has found itself in hot water this year after announcing some major changes for PlayStation users. Not only has there been even more price increases for its PlayStation Plus service, but it was revealed that, by 2028, all physical disks for upcoming first-party PlayStation games would be phased out.

Whilst there is no doubt that we are a lot more digitally-minded than we were a few decades ago, fans have been left reeling over no longer being able to amass a physical collection of games, leaving some to boycott Sony until it reverses the decision. However, with Sony standing firm, the future remains uncertain, especially during the inevitable launch of the PlayStation 6.

Nevertheless, the ongoing conflict has not stopped Sony from doing what it does best: making money, and now, a brand-new piece of hardware is on the way, and pre-orders are live.

If we cast our minds back a few years, we will remember the transparent gaming controllers that we all owned and now, history does indeed repeat itself as Sony is set to bring them back courtesy of the Prism Collection.

Now, players will have the opportunity to customize both their PlayStation 5 and accompanying DualSense controllers with pre-orders now officially open in the USA as of 7 AM PT/10 AM ET on November 10.

The collection comes alongside three transparent DualSense Wireless Controllers, and matching PS5 covers, each available in Flare Orange, Emerald Green, and Graphite Gray. However, as you can imagine, this brand-new set comes alongside a hefty price tag. Whilst the DualSense controllers come in at $84.99, the accompanying console covers are slightly less at $74.99.

As you can already guess from the transparent design, each color will give you a glimpse into the internal technology that goes into the production of the controller and console. Whilst the Flare Orange design is the boldest of the bunch, the Emerald Green would probably be my pick. However, the Graphite Gray is definitely the most understated, featuring a darker appearance set off by a glossy finish.

According to PlayStation designer, Satoshi Aoyagi, each color was picked carefully, revealing, "To complement the futuristic aesthetic, we carefully selected three distinct colors: a vibrant orange that subtly takes on a rosy hue where the transparent material overlaps, a deep hunter green that gains depth through its transparency, and a cool-toned storm gray.”

Sony has confirmed that the collection was inspired by the transparent controllers of the late 90s/early 00s, with fellow PlayStation designer Leo Cardoso claiming that fans had been campaigning for their return for many years in a PlayStation blog post. He wrote:

“We know how much our fans have been looking forward to the return of transparent controllers. We wanted to bring back the iconic see-through trend of the late ’90s in a fresh, modern way that complements the PS5’s industrial design.”

The entire Prism Collection is now available for pre-order via the official PlayStation Direct website, but you will be in for quite a wait until you finally get your hands on these nostalgic accessories, as they do not begin shipping until 4 February 2027.

#3451. Why I'd Choose the Oura Ring 5 Over the Cheaper Ultrahuman Pro

Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro is now officially on sale in the U.S., which makes this the perfect time to consider how this new device compares to the reigning champ in the smart ring market, the Oura Ring 5. Here's the short answer: While there’s a lot to like in the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, ultimately I think the Oura Ring 5 is just better at doing its job.

I’ve spent plenty of time with both rings, and admittedly, many of the differences between the two will come down to personal preference—for example, do you like the biohacking concept and the “next best actions” suggestions in the Ultrahuman app, or do you favor the soothing vibes of the Oura app? But when it comes to the devices themselves, there are big differences between them in terms of size, cost, and overall ease of use. Here’s my take on each, and why Oura is still my top choice.

The Oura Ring 5 is impressively small, and when you have to wear something on your finger, size matters a lot—and generally, smaller is better. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I’ve ever worn. I have a ton of photos here comparing it in size to other smart rings (including RingConn, older Oura rings, and an older Ultrahuman); suffice it to say, the Oura Ring 5 wins this category easily.

When it comes to the interior fit, both rings are similar: mostly smooth on the inside, without any intrusive bumps. But considering the overall shape and feel, the Oura Ring 5 is just more comfortable to wear throughout an entire day.

The Oura Ring 5 comes with a plug-in charger, which isn’t very convenient, but will get the job done. You can buy a slim, rounded charging case that easily fits in your pocket for $99. You need to match the size of the case to the size of your ring, and the charging case is not compatible with earlier versions of the device. It’s good for 30 days of charge, according to Oura.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro comes with a charging case that is heavy and bulky with prominent corners, but good for an extra 45 days of battery life. The case fits any size of Ultrahuman Ring Pro, but is not compatible with previous versions. You can have the case play sounds if you’ve misplaced it.

The Ultrahuman ring lasts slightly longer on a charge: up to 15 days, according to the company, versus six to nine for the Oura Ring 5. The Ultrahuman ring also has several different battery modes, with “chill mode” lasting me about two weeks when I tested it. The company says some users are finding the latest software update extends battery a bit further.

To sum up: the Ultrahuman ring lasts longer on a charge and has more capacity in its charging case. You also get the charging case for free. But the Oura Ring 5’s charging case is smaller and much easier to carry around. Once again, we’re looking at two decent options: The Oura case is more expensive for what you get, but it’s also nicer to use.

Oura is the most expensive smart ring out there, and it requires a subscription. That makes it the priciest option, giving Ultrahuman an opening to beat it simply by virtue of being cheaper. But this one is closer to a wash, depending on the choices you make. If you’re looking for the cheapest possible smart ring, well, you’d probably end up with something else entirely, like a RingConn Air. But between the Oura Ring 5 and the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, the latter is cheaper than the Oura Ring 5...but only if you’re saying no to all the extras. Let me break it down.

The Oura Ring 5 costs $399 for the shiny black and silver models, and $499 for gold, rose, and the matte versions of the black and silver. The subscription costs $5.99/month (or $69.99/year, which is only a $2 savings), and the Oura is basically useless without the subscription.

Here's how the cost works out on an annual basis:

Oura Ring 5 in black or silver: $399 + $5.99/month subscription = $470.88 for one year, $542.76 for two years

Oura Ring 5 in other colors: $499 + $5.99/month subscription = $570.88 for one year, $642.76 for two years.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is $479 for all colors, and there is no subscription for basic use of the ring. But you can't necessarily stop there, because the Ultrahuman app includes “PowerPlugs” that will give you extra features or analysis screens. Some are totally free, including the caffeine window,  smart alarms, a new parent mode, and a limited version of the cycle and ovulation tracker, but others carry a monthly fee. And if you consider all the optional subscription fees for different PowerPlugs, they can quickly add up:

HealthEx, to connect medical records: $4.99/month

Most people probably wouldn't choose all of them, but even if you just wanted, say, respiratory health and cycle & ovulation pro, you’d quickly outstrip the price of an Oura Ring’s subscription. On the other hand, Ultrahuman also offers an Ultrahuman Max plan for $9.99/month or $99.99/year that includes all the PowerPlugs mentioned above, plus the Les Mills workouts that normally run $11.99/month. That's cheaper than subscribing to all of the options individually, but it will also make the Ultrahuman Ring Pro more expensive than the Oura Ring 5: $578.99 total for one year, or $678.98 for two years. In short, if you want everything that each ring has to offer, the Ultrahuman will cost you more.

Here's the big caveat: I wouldn't recommend bothering with most of the PowerPlugs. For example, "UltraSync for Tesla" recommends settings for your car based on how rested you are, which will be useless if you don't have a Tesla, and probably even if you do. "Cardio adaptability" measures a metric that Ultrahuman says is subtly different from HRV; Oura doesn't measure this adaptability metric, but it's not clear to me whether it's even worth measuring at all (I'd argue probably not).

Ultrahuman's respiratory health PowerPlug ($3.99/month) records sounds while you sleep, which Oura doesn't do; but Oura reports breathing disturbances based on the ring's data, which Ultrahuman doesn't do. Ultrahuman's feature is more expensive.

Ultrahuman offers a premium version of its cycle tracker for $3.99/month, while Oura has a partnership with Natural Cycles that cost $149.99/year. Either will provide more detailed (and, each company says, more accurate) cycle tracking than the basic tracking each app provides without the extras. Oura's option is more expensive.

Ultrahuman's HealthEx Powerplug ($4.99/month) displays information from your medical records throughout the app; Oura lets you import your medical records for free, but uses them mainly in the Advisor (chatbot) and dedicated areas of the app. Ultrahuman's option is more expensive.

Oura's app gives you scores for your readiness, sleep, and recent activity, and it tracks how stressed you seem to be throughout the day. A message at the top of the main screen gives you advice for what to do that day—for example, scaling back your workouts if you seem to be tired or stressed. Ultrahuman does pretty much the same thing, giving you a "next best action" that changes throughout the day, but tends to stick to predictable themes: get more activity if you've been sitting, and that sort of thing.

Both give detailed breakdowns of the factors that contribute to your scores, and both likely overstate how useful their scores are (you don't actually need to change your workout plans just because you had a less-than-perfect night of sleep). But the apps handle the basics pretty similarly: Both have partners and integrations, and you can book blood tests through either app, if you want to do that for some reason.

Ultrahuman gives you a bit more guidance on circadian rhythms, urging you to get in extra steps during certain times of day, and offering to micromanage your caffeine intake. It has a "longevity" tab that puts your long-term habits in terms of how many years they are supposedly subtracting from (or adding to) your lifespan, including measurable metrics like VO2max and a few things that are more inscrutable, like arterial stiffness.

Oura has a whole tab of "vitals" that it calculates from your day-to-day data, which I find more useful than Ultrahuman's data views. The items here include "resilience," which compares your stress to your recovery; a "symptom radar" that can sometimes flag when you're sick; and metrics of sleep regularity and how you're breathing. And, of course, you can check your "cardiovascular age" to see how much younger (or older) you should feel.

Overall, I prefer Oura's approach because the metrics make more sense, are easier to find, and are less likely to feel like they're going way out on a limb relative to the underlying science. Ultrahuman wants you to feel like a cutting-edge biohacker; Oura does a bit more to keep things down to earth. It is a bit funny to remember that both apps, and their wealth of data, are basically just pulling from heart rate readings throughout the day and night. Neither app gives you any truly important information the other doesn't, but Oura's makes more sense to me.

Updated 11/10/2026 to note that the Ultrahuman Ring Pro's stated battery life is up to 15 days, not 8-10 days.

#3450. Apple explains how to turn off the new MacBook Pro’s glowing logo

While the illuminated Apple logo on the new MacBook Pro drew one of the biggest cheers during last week’s announcement, Apple knows that not everyone will want to keep it on. Here’s the company’s official guide to turning it off.

The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display marks the return of the illuminated Apple logo on its lid after a decade.

As Chance Miller explained in his review of the new MacBook Pro, “unlike older MacBooks, which used light from the display’s backlight to illuminate the logo, the new OLED MacBook Pro has no backlight to draw from, requiring a different approach.”

He added that, as with the old Macs, the logo’s brightness is tied to the screen brightness, though it also accounts for overall ambient brightness. He also noted that “when the MacBook Pro is closed, the logo looks like polished metal, just like it has since the 2016 redesign.”

The review echoed some of the findings developer Gui Rambo shared on X a few days ago:

The glowing Apple logo on the new MacBook Pro is controllable by software. It has 25kHz PWM and per-device calibration. CoreBrightness controls the relationship between screen and logo brightness. The brightness of the logo is adjusted differently depending on the enclosure color pic.twitter.com/baqBEkzJUo

Now, Apple has published an official support document that also explains how the illuminated logo works and how to turn it off completely.

The Apple logo behind the built-in display is illuminated whenever the Mac is awake. It automatically dims or brightens based on the brightness level of the built-in screen and the lighting conditions detected by the computer’s ambient light sensor. For all screen-brightness levels, the Apple logo will be dimmer in a dim room and brighter in a bright room.

For users who’d rather keep the logo turned off at all times, Apple explains that they can run the following command in Terminal, provided they have the administrator password:

sudo defaults write com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode -int 0

Since it's actually two, opposite, single line command states;

Why can't it simply be an on/off button, in Settings?

To revert the command and have the logo be illuminated again, users will need to run the following command:

sudo defaults delete com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode

Apple notes that reinstalling macOS will also turn the logo illumination back on.

To read Apple’s full support article, follow this link. And make sure to also catch 9to5Mac’s review of the new MacBook Pro.

Warning: This article includes MAJOR SPOILERS for Netflix's The Body!

Quinn Shephard's campy, sapphic horror show, The Body, builds toward a dramatic ending that explains the cause of the visions while also opening up questions for season 2. The Netflix original show centers on a dance team at a Catholic church that starts experiencing strange visions and convulsions after a ritual initiation sacrifice goes wrong. As a result, the whole community devolves into hysteria.

Netflix had the perfect formula going into its new religious horror teen psychodrama. A dance team? Check. A stellar 2000s soundtrack? Checkity check. A ritual sacrifice gone wrong? Add a third check. Sapphic raunchiness? Quadruple check. Luckily, these great components push the admittedly messy story along. Lisbeth becomes unbearably creepy with her manipulative, charismatic preacher behavior, leaving us to wonder about her background. Elise and Anya try to figure out how to be together without outing themselves. The audience learns more about what’s really happening with the supernatural visions.

Rather than wrapping things up in a reasonable way and leaving only a few threads open, The Body offers very few conclusions and opens up about a dozen questions. Ultimately, as I said in my review of The Body for ScreenRant, the show’s wonderful vulgarity and unbelievable camp more than make up for its weaknesses. It’s so unbelievably fun to watch. However, Netflix will need to give The Body a second season if they want any of it to make sense.

A supernatural force seems to be at play in The Body after the dance team jokingly sacrifices Grace to the devil to win regionals. By the midpoint, everyone on the team except Maddie Delaney, who feels distraught that Grace hasn’t revealed herself to her. However, the visions and supernatural phenomena are rooted more in mass hysteria and the power of suggestion. Only three people know from the start that the visions are fake: Elise, Anya, and Lisbeth. The others fell into three possible categories.

Firstly, they believed that Anya and Elise saw Grace and wanted to be a part of the in-group. As such, they faked the visions, only admitting the truth when they realized it didn’t bring them social value. Some of the dance team members didn’t admit to lying. They could’ve been lying but were too embarrassed to admit it. It’s also possible that they could be experiencing mass hysteria. This typically occurs in insular groups with pre-existing fears that match the visions or delusions which fit with the Grace visions. Lastly, they could actually be seeing something supernatural.

While most of the visions seem completely fake, a few moments stand out as different. I’m not sure what on Earth was causing Leo Anderson to see visions of Grace as Jesus Christ and the Lamb of God, but that started before the fake visions. He saw he in multiple places, and those visions continued even after he faced negative social ramifications. On top of that, we see Anya looking at a phantom of Grace on at least two occasions. Unless The Body is showing the audience Anya’s hallucination, there’s reason to believe something supernatural is happening. Plus, Grace showing up in Anya's nightmares is real.

Elise and Anya have a hot and steamy relationship throughout The Body season 1. It’s clear that Elise wants something more, instead of having to share Anya with a fake boyfriend. She wants the sex to mean something more. However, Anya denies that she’s gay, finding excuses for her sexual attraction to Elise. Sadly, the two don’t get together by the end of The Body season 1 because Anya is heavily entrenched in the attitudes and culture of the Catholic Church when it comes to being LGBTQ+.

“It’s satirizing some of the trauma of growing up queer and repressed and the confusion around that.” —Quinn Shephard to Autostraddle about The Body.

Elise’s frustration at being a “dirty little secret,” for all intents and purposes, is completely understandable. She’s allowed to want something more. Unfortunately, I can understand Anya’s perspective too, having been a Sapphic Catholic struggling to reconcile faith, expectations, and religious principles. In the finale, Anya seems to realize she’ll completely lose Elise if she doesn’t tell the truth. Her confession to Father Franklin doesn’t necessarily mean that she will come out. However, it does mean that there could be a chance for Elise and Anya.

Father Franklin is the most grounded character in The Body, and he symbolizes people who apply critical thinking to their faith. He and Elise are the most logical characters in the show. Father Franklin may fall into the trap of belief after a while, but the minute he has evidence that contradicts the “miracle” sainthood narrative, he takes steps to fix the damage he has done.

Unfortunately, the Bishop and other members of the diocese don’t have the same kind of integrity. They don’t care that Father Franklin has evidence to explain the coma and testimony from all the dance team members confirms that they lied. They don’t care that they’re overtly lying to the people they’re supposed to guide and protect. For the record, Proverbs 6:16-17 and other passages in the Bible describe a “lying tongue” as an offense to God. They are knowingly committing sin, and they’re perfectly happy to do so.

The reason they give is that people need the faith that Grace’s “miracles” bring. They act like they are doing their parishioners some kind of favor by deceiving them. In actuality, the way they talk at the end of The Body season 1’s finale makes it seem more likely they’re trying to achieve two goals.

The folks in charge want to stop a scandal that would give the Catholic Church a bad reputation, which was particularly important in 2004, at the height of the Catholic Church sex abuse scandal. More importantly, they want to maintain institutional control, which seems to be the goal of every religious institution ever.

Throughout The Body, Lisbeth acts like the leader of a charismatic church. She engages in practices like laying hands on the sick and speaking in tongues. Rather than allowing people to follow her naturally, she finds their weaknesses and uses them as weapons. Lisbeth engages in emotional manipulation tactics, like creating isolation and a sense of shame, leading to the disturbing scene where all the dance girls are shouting out their extremely mundane sins that aren’t actually sins. Last I checked, being Canadian is not a sin, and a parent committing adultery isn’t the sin of a child.

All of these tactics are finally explained towards the end of The Body season 1, when Lisbeth reveals her family history. Her father was the pastor at Signs Following, an extremely fundamentalist charismatic church. In home videos, her father supposedly drinks poison, and Lisbeth holds snakes. They are supposed to represent the true believers, as they have such faith that they can defeat deadly situations.

Her dad was bitten by a rattlesnake during worship, but he didn’t get any medical care. The fact that Lisbeth lost her father, her moral and emotional anchor, makes her actions in The Body so much more understandable, even if they aren’t excusable. She’s searching for a new connection in the same vein.

I wish there was a satisfying answer to, “What’s causing the nosebleeds?” However, this is one of the big mysteries they leave open-ended. Other symptoms, like visions and nightmares, fit with the mass hysteria. That doesn’t really work with the nosebleeds, though, especially since they started before Grace, Lizeth, and the dance girls went to the Halloween party. If Netflix picks the show up for season 2, The Body will need to provide a clear answer.

My educated guess is that some supernatural shenanigans are really going on, even though the dance team thinks they made everything up. The nosebleeds only seem to occur when Lisbeth is nearby. Lisbeth’s pale skin and shaved eyebrows make her seem snake-like. She actually owns pet snakes, which are frequently associated with the devil in the Garden of Eden. She constantly manipulates the folks around her to an almost unnatural degree. This could be building towards a "Lisbeth is the reincarnation of the Devil, and Grace is the reincarnation of Jesus" thing. That’s just my inference, though.

The end of The Body Season 1 leaves too many questions and too few answers. The Church has decided to keep the facade of Grace’s sainthood, and her waking in the final moments declaring, “I am God,” is certainly not going to help anything. The second season will need to show the fallout of the Church’s decision.

Meanwhile, Grace’s declaration raises the question, “Why?” “What is going through her head?” “Does she really believe she’s god?” “Is something supernatural going on?” Considering they billed The Body as a supernatural Catholic horror and there are very few genuine supernatural elements, it could be the center of a second season.

On top of that, the second season of the streaming teen drama will need to follow the dance team now that Lisbeth has convinced them that she’s a miracle worker on behalf of God. Anya finally admitted that she experiences same gender attraction, though it was to her priest. As such, she could still stay closeted after confessing. Ultimately, The Body season 2 has so much ground to cover that it will ruin the show if the streamer doesn’t pick up the horror for another season.

#3447. Prime Video’s Star Wars Replacement Is Hailed as the Best Space Show of All Time

Julio is a Senior Author for Collider. He studied History and International Relations at university, but found his calling in cultural journalism. When he isn't writing, Julio also teaches English at a nearby school. He has lived in São Paulo most of his life, where he covers CCXP and other big events. Having loved movies, music, and TV from an early age, he prides himself in knowing every minute detail about the things he loves. When he is older, he dreams of owning a movie theater in a small countryside town.

Space may be the final frontier, but you don't need to go to galaxies far, far away to find some good space adventures. In fact, the best one is set right here, in our very own Solar System. Over its six seasons, Prime Video's The Expanse has quietly built its reputation as the best space series on television, surpassing even mighty sci-fi franchises like Star Wars and Star Trek, and amassing quite a following among fans of the genre. Having debuted in 2015, it was even brought back from cancellation, proving how beloved it really is — fans just wouldn't let go. All that wouldn't have happened with just any series, of course, so what is it that makes The Expanse so special, even among titans?

Although it is set right here on our cosmic doorstep, The Expanse also takes place roughly some 200 years into the future. It's a time of war, with three main factions fracturing the Solar System: the United Nations of Earth and Luna, the Martian Congressional Republic, and the Outer Planets Alliance. The latter comprises all the planets and stations working in the asteroid belt, which have been part of Earth, but are now fighting for independence. Tensions are at an all-time high, and the tiniest mistake can lead to all-out war.

At the center of all that is an unlikely group of heroes and their aptly named gunship, the Rocinante. Led by James Holden (Steven Strait), they start out working hauling ice to the dwarf planet Ceres, but a distress call from a derelict ship in the middle of nowhere suddenly puts them in the middle of a conspiracy that threatens the whole system. With a sort of "found family" dynamics, the Rocinante crew is at first only looking to stay out of trouble, but, as it often happens in these stories, they quickly grow into heroes.

Meanwhile, on Ceres, the disappearance of a young woman has police investigator Joe Miller (Thomas Jane) rattling some cages that are dangerously close to making the planet the place where the war actually starts. With resources like air and water being rationed because of all the tension, everyone is on edge, and, unbeknownst to everyone, the thread Miller finds himself pulling ties all that together. As this soon-to-be-very-hot war gears up, there are still some people on all sides trying to work a way through it.

Star Wars and Star Trek have a much wider scope than The Expanse, granted, as they deal with a galactic scale, while the latter stretches as far as the asteroid belt, at first. Still, after a while, distances don't seem to matter as much when you have technologies like hyperdrives or warp drives. In The Expanse, however, there is no faster-than-light travel, so distances actually matter. This is one of the ways in which the Prime Video series uses space to its advantage, making it feel much more real than any other sci-fi galaxy.

Considering this, it's only natural that there would eventually be a divide between Earth and Mars, as well as a secessionist movement in the belt. It's precisely there that the most interesting effects of space life are felt. So far away from the two other planets, life in space turned Belters almost into an ethnicity of their own, with physical differences and their own language, Belter Creole. Because of that, they are usually seen as a lower caste by both Earth and Mars, hence the OPA's struggle for independence.

Who doesn't want to hear a Deep Purple cover in a sci-fi dialect?

To go with this rich worldbuilding (or spacebuilding?), The Expanse also pays a lot of attention to production design, particularly ships and space stations. Instead of flat rooms and hallways, ships are built more like skyscrapers, with decks serving different purposes. This allows for acceleration to create a gravitational pull that's small enough for the human body to feel comfortable with, and maneuvers like "flip and burn" turning, and the effect of G-forces on the crew also make The Expanse the most scientifically accurate space series around.

All that makes The Expanse one of the best sci-fi adaptations on TV. Its six seasons adapt only two-thirds of James S.A. Corey's book series, though, so, despite Prime Video having concluded the series with Season 6, we still can't say we've gotten the whole thing. But it could have been even shorter, because, in 2018, The Expanse was cancelled by Syfy after only three seasons for its poor ratings on TV and its complicated business and distribution model.

However, the audience wasn't ready to say goodbye, and they made their feelings known. The resulting #SaveTheExpanse campaign quickly became one of the most memorable fan movements in recent TV history, including crowdfunding efforts, targeting Amazon executives and even Jeff Bezos directly, and even getting an airplane to fly a banner over Amazon Studios. It also helped to have notorious celebrity sci-fi buffs like Wil Wheaton, George R.R. Martin, and Patton Oswalt join in.

This kind of loyalty and dedication isn't seen often, proving just how good The Expanse really is. Amazon picked it up for three more seasons in 2018, raising the bar with production value and consolidating the series as a sci-fi phenomenon. Few series have managed to pull off what The Expanse did in terms of worldbuilding and storytelling in this genre, and, right now, it doesn't look like any other will any time soon, either. Not even Star Wars or Star Trek.

The Expanse is available to stream on Prime Video.

#3446. Five Creative Ways to Spend Your FSA Funds Before the End of the Year

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), you know the drill: Use the funds before the end of the year, or lose them. Unfortunately, chances are slim you can pack the rest of the year with doctor's appointments. Does that mean your hard-earned funds go to waste? Definitely not. You can spend your remaining FSA funds on other qualifying healthcare costs. And what counts as "qualifying" might surprise you—for instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch.

As the end of the year approaches, here are all the ways you can spend any leftover money in your FSA balance.

Many over-the-counter medications and health items are FSA-eligible, including pain relievers, cold medicine, bandages, dental care products, menstrual products, and more. Scan your medicine cabinet and make a list of anything you need to stock up on.

FSA/HSA eligibility for smartwatches and other fitness wearables is real, but the main “catch" (as I’ve previously explained) is proving the device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN).

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. Similarly, smartwatches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does, as long as you can link a relevant documented health concern. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches.

If you want to get creative with it, the official FSA store lets you filter by "surprisingly eligible." Similar to the section above, for some of these items, you'll want to brush up on how exactly to get an LMN to justify certain tech as FSA-eligible for you personally. In the meantime, go crazy and snag yourself Epsom salt for $8.99, Supergoop! sunscreen for $38.00, or perhaps a snazzy massage gun for $349.99.

Knee braces, wrist splints, compression socks, and other orthopedic items can help relieve chronic pain issues. Rather than wait for these issues to rear their heads down the line, use FSA money to offset the costs of these fixes now. If you use eyeglasses or contacts, consider using your FSA dollars to update or refresh your prescriptions. Don't forget to stock up on eye drops and lens solution, too.

If you have medical procedures scheduled for early next year, many healthcare providers will allow you to pre-pay the estimated costs this calendar year using FSA funds. This includes dental work, physical therapy, chiropractic visits, Lasik eye surgery, and more.

However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste. After all, it came out of your paycheck. Check in with your employer’s rules for any balance remaining on Dec. 31 this year, so you aren’t left forfeiting your hard-earned funds. You can find a complete list at the FSA store here.

#3443. These 10 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple dropped the first developer beta for iOS 27.3 on Tuesday. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

Following yesterday’s report that Apple was preparing to raise approximately $7 billion through a bond offering, the company has now finalized terms with the SEC, confirming a slightly larger amount. Here are the details.

Yesterday morning, Apple filed a preliminary prospectus with the SEC, outlining plans to issue a series of bonds maturing between 2028 and 2036.

Soon after, Bloomberg reported that the bond sale was targeting roughly $7 billion, with investor interest already surpassing $30 billion.

Now, Apple has filed the final pricing term sheet for the bond sale with the SEC, confirming a $7.5 billion offering across the seven previously announced series, with the following breakdown:

Floating-rate bonds, as the name implies, have interest rates that fluctuate over time based on certain market conditions, rather than remaining fixed.

Of that $7.5 billion, Apple expects to receive approximately $7.47 billion after deducting underwriting discounts and other offering expenses.

In essence, Apple will pay investors interest over the life of the bonds, then repay the full amount borrowed when each series reaches maturity. Apple may also choose to repay some or all of its fixed-rate bonds early.

As described in yesterday’s prospectus, the company intends to use the proceeds for “general corporate purposes,” which may include stock buybacks, dividends, acquisitions, and debt repayment.
