#3440. The 5 Strongest Opening Chapters in Stephen King Books

Few writers are as prolific, well-regarded, or popular as Stephen King. The iconic author is a certified legend of the horror, thriller, and supernatural genres, producing banger after banger with such consistency that fellow authors like George R. R. Martin have openly expressed their admiration for his speed. Indeed, King has written many of the most beloved and enduring classics of the last 50 years, covering a wide range of genres and introducing some of modern literature's most iconic characters. Not every King book is the same, though, and some stand out because of their strong opening chapters.

In the author's words, "there are books, and there are books," and most of the latter benefit from instantly impactful openers that not only capture the reader's attention but also set the stage for what's to come. Here, we list the five King books with the strongest opening chapters, the ones that immediately compel you to pay attention and keep the pages turning. They benefit from strong prose, confident worldbuilding, and a distinct sense of atmosphere that cements King as a master of his craft.

It might be King's best-known novel, and for good reason. The book follows the Losers' Club, a group of eleven-year-olds living in the town of Derry, Maine, where children mysteriously disappear. The Losers eventually discover the existence of the creature responsible, a mysterious being who commonly assumes the guise of Pennywise, the Dancing Clown, and uses fear as a weapon against them. 27 years later, the adult Losers reunite in Derry again to finish the job they couldn't as children.

The opening chapter is well-known by now. In it, Six-year-old Georgie Denbrough chases after his paper boat on a rainy afternoon, eventually reaching a sewer where Pennywise awaits him. Their seemingly sweet conversation quickly takes a turn, and Pennywise rips Georgie's arm before killing him. It's a brutal and profoundly creepy opening even before the gore. The opening line lets you know that the main evil won't be defeated for another 27 years, if ever, making the chapter feel all the more ominous. King is a master at crafting atmosphere, and here, he makes Georgie's last minutes feel like an entire odyssey.

Now on to something a lot grander. The Dark Tower is probably King's magnum opus, a sprawling saga that began in 1982 with The Gunslinger. The story focuses on Roland Deschain, the last gunslinger, and the years-long pursuit of his nemesis, the Man in Black. Here, King balances multiple genres, most notably Western, fantasy, thriller, and science fiction.

The opening line of this book is probably King's most celebrated: "The man in black fled across the desert, and the gunslinger followed." There's such a haunting quality to this line; it may seem simple at first glance, but it packs so much in just a few words, hinting at the backstory behind these two characters and painting a vague but instantly compelling picture of what's to follow. From there, King makes the desert feel alive in its scarcity, depicting a vague and endless land that threatens to overwhelm with its nothingness. Few chapters are as immersive or atmospheric as this one, and it's quite surprising how little of the larger plot it concerns itself with.

Desperation is among King's scariest yet most underappreciated efforts. The plot centers on a couple traveling the Nevada desert, who are kidnapped by Collie Entragian, the deputy of the remote mining town Desperation. Along with other victims, they realize that Collie has been possessed by a dark entity that controls the desert and wildlife. The entity must also change hosts, meaning they are all trapped in Desperation and subjected to becoming the being's next target.

Desperation's opening chapter is among the tensest, most discomforting things King has ever written. A masterclass in buildup and escalation, the chapter sees Entragian slowly take command of the situation, as the helpless couple slowly realizes, along with the reader, that the situation before them will be far darker than they could imagine. From there, Desperation tells a truly bleak and brutal story full of violence, gore, and supernatural danger. It's probably King's last truly horrific work, and it all begins with a remarkable opening chapter. An upcoming movie adaptation is in the works, which hopefully will live up to the source material's eeriness (the 2006 ABC version is pretty solid).

Now we move on to the book with possibly the best opening line in any King work: “The world had teeth, and it could bite you if you bothered it. Trisha McFarland discovered this when she was nine years old.” The Girl Who Loved Tom Gordon is a survival story centered on Trisha McFarland, a 9-year-old who gets lost in the wilderness during a hiking trip with her mother and older brother. With only a Walkman to keep her company, Trisha hallucinates a version of baseball player Tom Gordon and becomes convinced a being she names The God of the Lost is after her.

The book wastes no time going into the thick of it. In the first chapter, Trisha escapes a complicated family dynamic by trailing off for a bathroom break. Strong character work sets the background for Trisha's story, but the main attraction is how King writes this girl's inner thoughts: it's intimate, childlike, but never dumbed-down. King has enough respect not only for his audience but, most importantly, for his creation. The most important relationship — that of Trisha and Tom Gordon — is also established here. Then, she's lost in the woods, and King's prose gets us as confused and disoriented as the girl herself.

Lastly, we finish with one of King's strongest late-career works. The book chronicles the aftermath of an attack in which the mysterious driver of a Mercedes S-Class drives into the crowd at a job fair in the Midwest, killing eight people and injuring fifteen. Months later, retired, suicidal cop Bill Hodges receives a taunting letter from the perpetrator, dubbing himself Mr. Mercedes, and decides to investigate the crime.

A classic hard-boiled detective novel, Mr. Mercedes is among King's best thriller efforts. As expected, the book opens with the attack, with King putting us in the eyes of Augie Odenkirk, a hopeful who rides the last bus to camp outside a job fair that opens in the morning. Augie is kind and sympathetic, quickly striking up a conversation with desperate single mother Janice Cray, who is there with her young daughter. In just a couple of paragraphs, King makes us care about these two characters before Mr. Mercedes arrives and runs over the crowd twice, killing Augie, Janice, and her daughter. It's a harrowing, unforgiving opening that sets the tone for the rest of the book.

A slow-draining or completely blocked kitchen drain is a major frustration you don’t need. Besides smelling unpleasant and potentially damaging your pipes, it slows you down as you wait for your sink to empty.

Over time, warm fats, cooking oils and butter innocently slip down the drain, but instead of fully descending, they cool and solidify. Before long, that solid grease is catching hold of other small morsels of food, stopping them from making a clear escape.

But before you try to clear your blocked kitchen drain with a harsh chemical cleaner or call in a plumber, there’s an alternative method you can try.

Cleaning expert Lynsey Crombie, known as the Queen of Clean, recommends using a cooking staple to remove grease from kitchen drains. While this common ingredient is used to season food, it also dissolves grease.

And she adds, “Salt absorbs grease and liquid, lifts stubborn stains (even red wine), and is mildly antibacterial — making it perfect for soaking kitchen sponges or scrubbing chopping boards.”

In the social post, she shows herself pouring table salt down her kitchen drain, then boiling water.

A post shared by Lynsey Queen Of Clean (@lynsey_queenofclean)

This cleaning method is also recommended by Ato Energy, which shares on its blog how much salt to use. After removing the standing water from your sink, it says, “Pour about half a cup of table salt down the drain before pouring in the hot water. Let it sit for a few minutes, and then flush with hot water to clear the mixture.”

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

This flexible tool is designed to unclog drains by reaching 18 inches inside your drain. Once inserted, it can spin 360° to wrap around hair and other gunk before being removed. The set includes 5 disposable wand sticks for easy use, which can be attached to the removable handle.

For general maintenance and to keep your kitchen drain smelling fresh and free-flowing, Ato Energy suggests using vinegar and baking soda.

It suggests removing any standing water before pouring about a cup of baking soda into the drain. Then, follow with an equal amount of white or apple cider vinegar.

“The solution will bubble. That’s good! It means the chemical reaction is working,” it says.

Then, once the bubbles subside, it says to place a stopper on the drain and wait 15 minutes. You can then finish by running hot water down the drain to see if the clog has cleared. If there’s still a blockage, it advises repeating the above steps.

To avoid future blockages, ATCO Energy advises, “You can avoid tough clogs by watching what you pour down your sink. Never put bacon grease, coffee grounds or oils down your kitchen drain.”

#3432. James Cameron’s $1.5 Billion Sci-Fi Thriller Officially Returns With New Release

The first film, which became the highest-grossing film of all time (twice) follows ex-Marine who finds himself thrust into hostilities on an alien planet filled with exotic life forms. As an Avatar, a human mind in an alien body, he finds himself torn between two worlds for himself and for the planet’s indigenous people. 13 years later, The Way of Water follows Jake Sully and Neytiri, and their children, as they're driven from their jungle homes to the coasts of Pandora while battling to stay alive and discovering new sea creatures and Na'vi cultures.

Fire and Ash brings us back to the Sully family, still dealing with the death of Neteyam, while a new threat emerges from the Mangkwan Clan, also known as the Ash People, led by Varang. Their arrival creates further conflict as Jake and Neytiri struggle to protect their family from the threat of Quaritch.

#3427. Eight 'Winter Arc' Rules That Will Actually Deliver Results

There are a lot of terrible social media trends out there aimed at self-improvement, yet even though everybody has been making fun of the "Winter Arc" craze, I actually think it’s a good one. During your Winter Arc, you promise yourself you’ll stick to your fitness and self-care routines during (and despite) the end-of-year chaos. It's a good goal, with one caveat: Make sure you choose rules that will actually improve your life and deliver results.

Think of the “arc” in the sense of a “story arc.” The Winter Arc is a self-improvement journey that unfolds over the last few months of the calendar year. The most hardcore #gymtok-ers will tell you the Winter Arc officially begins on Oct. 1, but others start in early November, or whenever they get around to it. The "when" isn't critical, though—whenever you read this is a fine time to start. The close of the Winter Arc is fixed, however: It ends Jan. 1, just as everybody who is less dedicated than you is waking from their holiday food comas and resolving to get in shape.

You get to choose your own terms for your Winter Arc. The general vibe is one of locking in, committing to your goals, and actually doing the things you’re always saying you’ll do. TikToker @carlyupgraded has said that her own mental image of someone nailing their Winter Arc is “hood up, headphones on, getting ready to go for a run in the rain at 5 a.m.”

It turns out I’ve accidentally been Winter-Arc-ing for years; I just didn’t know it had a catchy name. Why save your gym routine for New Year’s when you’ll have the place to yourself all December? We’re even gifted with an extra hour in the mornings to fill with something productive.

I really love the mindset shift involved. Commonly, people are active in the summer (great time for outdoor fun), may or may not stick with their routines in the fall, and let everything fall apart as the holidays approach. Who has time to go to the gym when you’re planning Thanksgiving, attending holiday parties, studying for final exams, or whatever else the end of the year throws in front of you?

But that’s the exact reason why this time of year is the best to start (or restart) a fitness routine, or really any kind of routine. When you start a routine during a busy time of year, you’ll be forced to make it sustainable. The gym routine you can stick with amid the chaos isn’t going to be one you drop after a few months. You’re already training yourself to work around obstacles as they come up, which is a key component of self-efficacy. And when the chaos clears on Jan. 1, your routine will be even easier to stick to.

Of course, there are ways to lean in too hard: Choosing unsustainable habits, falling for bad diet advice, mistaking not masturbating for some kind of health hack, the usual suspects. There’s also the pitfall of focusing too much on the vibes and too little on what you’re actually going to do or how you’ll benefit.

And then there’s the framing: You were working on yourself all year, but you’re in danger of letting up on the gas, but you’re committed to locking in so that you’re a step ahead of everybody who takes this time to slack off. I really don’t love this tack. Self-improvement is not a competition. There’s a difference between being consistent in your training and healthy eating (good) and seeing the pursuit of health and fitness as something where you always have to work harder because you’re at risk of getting left behind.

I also don’t love how gendered the Winter Arc TikToks tend to be. When you search for Winter Arc content, the first few suggestions include “winter arc for women” and “winter arc for men.” When I first started looking at the Winter Arc trend a few years ago, the women’s versions were more likely to include restrictive dieting or to focus on how the Winter Arc will finally (sigh) snatch your waist. These days, the focus is more on personal goal setting: Lots of the girlies filming their Winter Arc rules are doing so in a notebook and talking about journaling exercises that will help you identify what you need to work on to get to your "best self." Sometimes this is all monetized; training plans and journaling prompts can, of course, be purchased at the link in bio.

I do like that many of the women’s versions emphasize sustainability and setting your own goals rather than copying somebody else's. I don't love the enormity of the mental burden you're supposed to shoulder before even beginning. Should I really have to file an in-depth written report with myself before revamping every area of my life with a 100% commitment to multiple goals?

The men’s versions tend to go off the rails in another direction, with rules like “no girls” or “go ghost.” No distractions! Here, I've seen a shift over the years as well: at first there was overly serious content, followed quickly by satire (yelling at the viewer to get divorced and go work out in the dark). Now the men's videos tend to be more vibes-based, featuring images of pre-dawn workouts and plates full of salad with motivational quotes playing in the background. When the men give their rules, they tend to be simpler than the women's—no journaling exercises—but they often boil down to the same overly strict routines. (And then, of course, they'll offer to sell you a 90-day or 60-day plan.)

If you’re going to do a Winter Arc (or if you’re already doing one), make sure to structure it in a way that benefits you. Choosing 10 overly ambitious goals and setting yourself up for failure is not a healthy way to approach self-improvement, OK? Pick goals that are meaningful, achievable without divine intervention, and trackable with tools you already have at hand (for example, tracking your steps with a Fitbit or your running mileage with a Garmin watch).

It’s also helpful to think of developing yourself over this arc, rather than taking it as a three-month (or two-month) challenge where you have to do everything right all the time. If you currently wake up at 8 a.m. and want to wake up at 5 a.m., you don’t have to set your alarm for 5 a.m. tomorrow. It’s OK to aim for 7:30 a.m., make that a habit, then try for 7:00 a.m., and so on.

With that in mind, here are some "rules" I've seen from creators that I'm actually on board with (so long as you don't overwhelm yourself with them):

Wake up earlier. A great goal, especially if you take advantage of the time change to make things easier on your body.

Get to bed on time. Never a bad idea. Cultivating good sleep habits in general is always worthwhile.

Get your steps in. Be thoughtful about what your target is: 10,000 is not for everybody. Better to choose a number that would be a modest improvement on what you already do.

Exercise X times per week. Pick a number that works for you, and get into it. Be realistic about your goal, and for the best results, be consistent even if you’re sore at first.

Eat healthy. This is a great goal, with the major caveat that there are a lot of ways to eat healthy. You don’t need to cut out sugar or pretend that there’s something evil about seed oils. Do get more protein and veggies.

Be more thoughtful about using social media. I’m not going to tell you to delete all your apps (“except TikTok,” as the TikTokers say). But it’s fair to consider whether you might want to delete a few apps, turn off some notifications, or put your phone on Do Not Disturb for more hours of the day.

Journal or read more. Journaling can be great for working through your feelings or cultivating a creative habit. Reading can be entertainment or a great way to learn. Choose whichever you need most.

Learn a new skill. I’ve mostly seen this one in the men’s TikToks, and I love it. They’re often thinking of “skills” that will help in some kind of entrepreneurship grift they’re about to sell you, but there are tons of skills that will come in handy in life, or that are at least fun to learn. Practice a language, get better at cooking, make some art. Skills are, as I’ve noted, a multi-layered exercise for your brain. And they may come in handy someday.

This year I've slacked off on my fitness routine as I've gotten more involved in other hobbies, but I'm actually looking forward to being more consistent. My winter goals include exercising early in the day when possible and reading 20 minutes each day. (I'm even tracking the second one with a sticker chart.)

#3424. It's Officially the End of an Era for Looney Tunes

There aren't many cartoon characters who have survived almost a century of pop culture without losing their ability to make audiences laugh, but Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck are two lads that have managed that big achievement, having been causing chaos since the 1930s alongside the rest of the Looney Tunes gang. But behind those familiar voices are generations of extraordinarily talented performers, many of whom have helped keep the characters alive long after their original creators were gone. This week, one of the most important voices in Looney Tunes history is saying a final farewell.

Warner Bros. Picture Animation has released their first Looney Tunes short in over a decade in the form of Daffy Season, which has been attached to The Cat in the Hat, the Bill Hader-starrer that opened in theaters on November 6, 2026. The short is also particularly noteworthy, and bittersweet, because it marks the final Looney Tunes movie performance of the late Emmy-winning voice actor and icon Eric Bauza, who tragically passed away on October 25. According to a Warner Bros. representative, the short represents Bauza's final movie performance within the Looney Tunes franchise, although it should not be confused with his final screen credit across all productions.

Bauza became one of the most recognizable voices in modern animation, taking on several iconic characters throughout his career, including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Tweety, and Marvin the Martian.

His work helped introduce the characters to younger audiences through projects including Looney Tunes Cartoons, Space Jam: A New Legacy, and The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie.

Bauza died last month at his home in Los Angeles County, with the local medical examiner listing the cause of death as hypertensive cardiovascular disease. His family announced the news in a statement via his official Instagram account, confirming that his passing was sudden:

"Eric Bauza, Emmy Award-winning voice actor and the modern voice of iconic Looney Tunes characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, along with dozens of other beloved cartoon characters, has passed away suddenly. More details to come."

Daffy Season is screening exclusively in theaters ahead of The Cat in the Hat, which opened November 6, 2026. A separate streaming release date has not been announced. #3422. iOS 27.2 adds Apple Photos invisible watermark feature, here’s how it works

iOS 27.2 arrived last week, and among its changes for Apple Photos, the update adds an invisible watermarking feature when you use certain editing tools. Here’s how it works.

In the age of AI, what looks like a genuine photo might actually be a fake—or partly fake. That’s why tools like SynthID have been used to apply invisible watermarks to AI-generated content.

Starting with iOS 27.2, Apple now uses SynthID watermarks when you make AI-generated edits to photos in Apple Photos, or create all-new images with Image Playground.

Starting with iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, macOS 27.2, and visionOS 27.2, some Apple Intelligence tools will add an invisible SynthID watermark to images that you create or edit:

Image Playground generates entirely new images, so it’s more what the average person would consider an “AI image.”

However, as Apple notes, the SynthID invisible watermark is also applied to genuine photos in your Apple Photos library if you use the AI-powered Clean Up, Extend, or Spatial Reframing tools to edit them.

It’s worth emphasizing the word “invisible” here. You won’t see evidence of a watermark anywhere on your photos, nor will others unless they explicitly check the image with a SynthID detector.

If you do want to check for the watermark, Apple recommends going to synthid.com, where you can upload an image and see its result.

#3418. Your Android Can Get Hacked Without You Doing Anything at All

You probably know that clicking suspicious links online or opening attachments from strangers in an email or text is a recipe for hacking. It's a dangerous world out there online, so it's always important to be vigilant. However, the danger doesn't always involve something you do. There are ways to hack your devices without requiring any intervention on your part whatsoever—and one such example is likely plaguing your Android device right now.

As reported by The Hacker News, there is a critical Android security flaw that could enable remote code execution on your device. In other words, bad actors could use the flaw to run their own code on your phone, effectively taking over the device for their own gain. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-58868, isn't universal, but it is widespread: It currently affects Android 14 through Android 17, the latest version of Google's OS. If your phone runs Android 12 or Android 13, it may be unaffected, as Google doesn't identify these versions in its security bulletin, but it doesn't explicitly rule them out, either.

There are two silver linings here, however. One, Google hasn't confirmed any active exploits for this security flaw. While that isn't a guarantee that bad actors have missed this exploit so far, it at least opens that possibility. As such, there may be time for users to patch their devices before hackers truly take advantage of the flaw. Second, Google does have a patch for the flaw. The patch may not be available to you right away, however, as it's up to both the manufacturer of your phone and your carrier to issue these updates. Still, a patch is, at the very least, on its way.

This flaw is perhaps the most important to fix, but it's not the only serious issue. In all, Google's latest bulletin highlights 216 vulnerabilities, and, of those, 23 are "critical." As The Hacker News explains, two other of those critical flaws could also allow remote code execution when exploited.

To see whether the patch is installed on your end, open the Settings app on your phone, tap "About phone" or "About tablet," then choose the Android version on-screen. Look for a date of "2026-11-01" or later. All security patches from Nov. 1 and on will fix this issue. If not, you'll ned to wait for the patch.

#3416. Texas Man Who Beheaded 3 Kids Over 'Demonic Possession' Set to Be Executed

John Allen Rubio is set to be executed for the murders of his 3 children, whose decapitated bodies were discovered inside the family's Texas apartmen

According to reports, John killed his 3-year-old Julissa Quesada, 14-month-old John E. Rubio, and 2-month-old Mary Jane Rubio

In an on-camera interview with KRGV, Rubio claimed he had been witnessing bizarre things in the days leading up to the murders, which convinced him someone was practicing witchcraft against his family.

But things took an even darker turn on March 11, 2003, when Rubio claimed his 3-year-old daughter Julissa began acting strangely.

According to Rubio, Julissa started claiming she was his grandmother ... something he said was particularly disturbing because he'd previously dreamed his daughter was possessed by his grandmother.

The children were killed and decapitated inside the family's apartment.

The following day, Rubio said his brother found the children's bodies inside plastic bags placed beside the beds ... and called cops.

Angela Camacho, Rubio's wife, gave three different accounts of why the children were killed. In one, she claimed the couple believed the children were possessed. In another, she said they couldn't afford to raise them. A third account suggested both financial struggles and their beliefs about possession played a role.

Cameron County District Attorney Luis V. Saenz described the murders as the worst case he'd ever encountered in his career.

The case has now gone through two trials ... and Rubio has been convicted twice.

Rubio was originally convicted and sentenced to death in 2003, but an appeals court overturned that conviction in 2007. He was retried and convicted again on August 2, 2010, receiving another death sentence.

Camacho pleaded guilty to three counts of capital murder in 2005 and is currently serving a life sentence. She will be eligible for parole in 2043.

Now, more than two decades after the murders, Rubio is facing execution ... and he says he's ready to die.

"Now that I have an execution date, I'm ready to be with my children, I'm ready to be with God. I know they know the truth; I adored my children," Rubio said.

Rubio is scheduled for execution by lethal injection on Thursday.

#3415. 'Ocarina of Time' for Switch 2 Might Already Have a Weird Glitch

Thursday is a big day for Zelda fans. That's when the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time officially launches on Switch 2, marking the first major linear (i.e., non-open-world) 3D Zelda game since the 2016 Twilight Princess remake on Wii U. I, for one, have been waiting for this day for years. I loved the N64 original and the 3DS remake, so to have the chance to play a modern take on the definitive Zelda is so exciting—that is, if it actually runs as it should.

I stumbled upon this interesting post on X from Austin John Plays, a YouTuber with a host of Zelda coverage. According to Austin John Plays, Ocarina of Time already ships with a weird glitch that won't necessarily break your experience, but which may slow it down for a while, and perhaps even confuse players into thinking something is wrong with their game or their console.

As his post explains, if you're playing the physical copy of Ocarina of Time, and it's the first game you've ever played on your Switch 2—maybe you got one of those fancy new Zelda anniversary consoles and want to break it in properly?—you may run into glaring performance issues: The game may freeze, your controller may stop working, and the FPS may drop to single digits.

Luckily, Austin John Plays says the fix is easy: just wait. Eventually, your game will boot back to the title screen. When it does, don't try to play right away. Instead, close the game, restart your Switch 2, then try relaunching Ocarina of Time. Austin John Plays advises you may need to repeat this process two or three times, but after that, you shouldn't continue to run into issues. I wouldn't be surprised if Nintendo releases a patch right away for this glitch if it turns out to be as widespread as this post implies.

However, seeing as the game doesn't come out until tomorrow, there's something you can do to prevent it. Austin John Plays thinks the bug only impacts Switch 2 consoles that haven't run other games before. If you've had your console a while, you're likely set. But if you just bought the 40th anniversary Zelda edition of the Switch 2, you might not have had a chance to run a game on it yet. As such, download a game from the e-shop—even a free demo—just to get the system running. Hopefully, that will be enough to circumvent the glitch, and prevent issues when Ocarina of Time launches tomorrow.

The thriller movie options on Prime Video are on the weaker side of the scale in November 2026. The streaming service might have added more than 100 movies to kick off the month, but seasonal holiday flicks dominate the slate.

Still, I've combed through all the latest arrivals and have been able to find three thrillers worthy of your time. Well, cards on the table, one of them is more of a comedy than a thriller, but it does revolve around a heist at least. Meanwhile, the other two, both released in the 1960s, are true classics.

So, if you want to give your Prime Video watchlist an injection of excitement this week, here are the latest thriller movies on the service to watch now.

It might be an overstatement to call “The Manchurian Candidate” a foundational thriller, but this 1960s classic is undeniably influential. Its impact can be seen in 21st-century projects such as “Homeland,” and like all the best classics, its brilliance hasn’t waned with age. Starring Frank Sinatra, Laurence Harvey, Angela Lansbury and Janet Leigh, it’s a twisting watch that was even selected for preservation in the Library of Congress’s National Film Registry, which neatly displays the importance of this John Frankenheimer thriller.

In this psychological, politically charged thriller, Sergeant Raymon Shaw (Harvey) returns from the Korean War after being held as a POW. On the surface, it’s a feel-good homecoming, but in reality, Shaw’s return is part of a sinister plot. He’s been programmed as a sleeper agent by his communist captors. Shaw doesn’t know it, but at any moment his programming could be triggered with devastating consequences for the United States. Rated 96% on Rotten Tomatoes, “The Manchurian Candidate” is a masterpiece.

Watch "The Manchurian Candidate" on Prime Video now

If one classic 1960s masterpiece wasn’t enough for you this week, how about a second? “In the Heat of the Night” is a five-time Oscar winner, including taking home Best Picture at the 40th Academy Awards, and if you’re talking about timeless watches, this neo-noir mystery makes the cut every time. It finds the perfect balance between spinning an engaging murder mystery and exploring the societal prejudices of the American South in the 1960s.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Virgil Tibbs (Sidney Poitier in one of his best-ever roles) is an African-American police detective who is wrongly arrested under suspicion of murder by a Mississippi police chief, Bill Gillespie (Rod Steiger). After proving his innocence, Tibbs’ superior officer asks him to stick around in the small town of Sparta and assist Gillespie in tracking down the real killer. As their investigation brings them closer to the true culprit, they make new enemies but also develop a strong bond, which forces Bill to reconsider his attitudes.

Watch "In the Heat Of The Night" on Prime Video now

An early-2010s heist comedy starring Ben Stiller and Eddie Murphy helmed by Brett Ratner (director of “X-Men: The Last Stand”)? On paper, “Tower Heist” should be absolutely awful. And look, it’s no masterpiece like my two picks above, but when graded on a slightly generous curve, this one does have its charms, mostly found in Murphy's rib-tickling performance as a petty crook. Granted, it’s not a full-blown thriller, but with limited options on Prime Video this week, it makes the cut because it centers on a daring heist, which gives it just enough exciting moments to qualify (but only just).

“Tower Heist” is an ensemble comedy that sees workers at an upscale New York apartment building left devastated after it's revealed they’ve been scammed out of their pensions by a Wall Street billionaire living in the complex. Eager for revenge and to get their money back, they come together to pull off a risky heist that involves breaking into the billionaire’s secure apartment. The high-concept comedy also stars Casey Affleck, Matthew Broderick and Michael Peña.

But lawyers for ITN and The Guardian pushed back ... arguing the allegations were too important to keep hidden and that his mental health concerns should be addressed by medical professionals, not by silencing the press.

Tuesday morning, Judge Matthew Nicklin rejected the celebrity's attempt to block publication ... though his identity remained protected temporarily while a possible appeal was considered.

The legal battle also sparked a wave of online speculation ... prompting Nicklin to warn the public against trying to identify the mystery man, with anyone violating the court order potentially facing jail time.

Now, after weeks of secrecy and courtroom drama ... the mystery surrounding his identity is finally over.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What if you knew your mom wasn't really your mom, but no one believed you? That's the improbable but entertaining premise of Hulu's Phony, which stars Sam Nivola as a teenager who wakes up from a car accident and quickly comes to believe that his mother (Friday Night Lights' Connie Britton) is an imposter. Of course, no one believes him. I'm not sure I believe him, but it'll be pretty boring if it turns out that he just had a really bad concussion the whole time.

It's a coming-of-age drama and a surreal mystery with hints of comedy, and though it borrows elements from other shows, it stands apart for the skill with which it blends everything together. While you wait to see how the story plays out, here are 10 more twisted mysteries to stream now.

A twisty-turny (and well-reviewed) bit of fake identity folderol, Apple Cider Vinegar stars Kaitlyn Dever as Belle Gibson, a real-life Australian cancer survivor (except not really!) With a cheeky sense of humor and a willingness to distort reality, the show follows the wellness influencer as she fakes multiple cancer diagnoses in order to better market her alternative, MAHA-esque app and remedies to the unwitting. As her livelihood comes under threat, her lies grow more elaborate. Stream Apple Cider Vinegar on Netflix.

Alia Shawkat stars here as Dory Sief, an aimless millennial who decides, after seeing a missing-person poster for a college acquaintance, that she's going to make it her purpose to track her down—with the extremely begrudging support of her friends. But neither Chantal nor her disappearance are anything like what Dory expects. The show shifts focus from season to season. Initially a darkly comic take on a Nancy Drew-style mystery, it later finds the gang desperate to cover up a mostly unintentional murder, and getting in deeper each season. It's a funny, smart, and weird and shares talent with Phony in the form of writer/producer Anthony King, who serves as co-showrunner on the new series. Stream Search Party on Netflix.

This one's largely about adults, so it skips the coming-of-age angle central to Phony, but it has a quirky mystery, gaslighting, and a protagonist whose sanity is questioned by just about everyone all the same. This fun and very loose adaptation of the 1989 Tom Hanks film finds Keke Palmer's Samira and Jack Whitehall's Rob moving back to his impossibly safe and tidy hometown. Their house happens to be across the street from a dilapidated Victorian eyesore that may or may not have been the location of a murder a couple of decades before—a murder of a girl who made the mistake of trying to get away. As Samira adjusts to new motherhood and life on the cul-de-sac, she learns that even the nicest of her neighbors have secrets, and comes to suspect that her husband knows more about the missing girl than he's letting on. Stream The 'Burbs on Peacock.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate, working her way into the missing girl's social circle, and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Based on a Harlan Coben novel, Fool Me Once is a bit more of a political thriller than a coming-of-age thing, but we're still in "what the hell is up with my family?" territory: Michelle Keegan plays Maya Stern, a former special ops pilot dealing with the murder of her husband, whom she then impossibly catches playing with their daughter on a nanny cam. The resulting mystery ties into the earlier death of her sister and leads to a web of conspiracy involving her husband's family and a shady pharmaceutical company. Stream Fool Me Once on Netflix.

A vibe match more than anything else, this dark and twisty mystery with a slightly surreal sense of humor also features a single mom who is definitely not what she appears to be. Kim Mo-mi (Lee Han-byeol, initially), the Mask Girl of the title, is a uniquely complicated woman; she always wanted to be a K-Pop idol, but it was always made clear to her that she's not nearly pretty enough for that kind of stardom. So, in order to fill that void, she's got a side hustle. On top of her boring office job, she puts on a blonde wig and a mask to perform as a camgirl for anonymous men. It's a means to express herself creatively and sexually with a level of control—until a mistake causes her to lose that control, a co-worker discovers her secret life, and desperation leads to murder. The show shifts perspectives continually, feeling most like Phony when it focuses on Mo-mi's daughter. Stream Mask Girl on Netflix.

Flipping things around a bit, albeit in a similar "am I just being paranoid?" vein, The Girlfriend deals with a mom who may or may not be freaking out for no reason. Starring Robin Wright as Laura Sanderson, a wealthy art gallery owner in London whose son (Laurie Davidson) brings home a new, working-class girlfriend, Cherry Laine (Olivia Cooke)—immediately strikes Laura as not-our-kind. But is there more to it? Can someone with the name "Cherry Laine" truly be trusted? There's definitely something off, and we're kept guessing as to whether or not this is the story of a dangerous con artist or an overbearing mom—or maybe a little of each. Stream The Girlfriend on Prime Video.

Coming from Irish playwright and Derry Girls creator Lisa McGee, this show eschews the relatively subtle dark comedy of Phony for something much more gloriously surreal. Three high school friends from Belfast reunite after learning that an estranged bestie has died unexpectedly—except that maybe she didn't; a mixed blessing given that they all have secrets that they were hoping would be buried with the maybe departed. Now they're off to investigate the mystery of the murder(?), which turns into a hunt for the friend that they only thought they knew, while inadvertently revealing plenty of secrets of their own. The tone is all over the place in a way that somehow works, with flashes of sincerity balancing out the comedy. Stream How to Get to Heaven From Belfast on Netflix.

Shin Hye-sun offers up a phenomenal performance as Sarah Kim (well: sort of), a wealthy businesswoman who is discovered, at the series' opening, under a sewer grate. The police detective charged to investigate quickly finds inconsistencies in the woman's identity, and after interviewing Sarah's friend and business associate, comes to feel that neither woman is exactly (or anything, like she seems. Though it takes itself more seriously than Phony, it's still an addictively twisty mystery built around a constructed identity. Stream The Art of Sarah on Netflix.

There's a lot going on in this steamy, telenovela-esque drama. Camila Román (Carolina Miranda) finally meets Fernando Castell (Rodolfo Salas), a Tinder match, in Las Vegas, and things get very hot very quickly—he's everything he seemed to be and then some. If anything, she's the sketchy one: a dancer, not a nurse as she said, and with a possessive ex following her around. Still, it's all going great until she decides to surprise Fernando after he flies back to Colombia (which: never do that), and gets a totally different dude when she asks for him at his work. And that's just the beginning! Stream Fake Profile on Netflix.

iOS 27.2 launched last week with a lot of new features, and also several ways you can customize your iPhone. Here’s what’s new for iPhone personalization.

Apps added to the list below will be excluded from Siri, Search, and suggestions.

iOS 27.2 adds a new Messages feature called Suggestions that I’m a big fan of. When relevant content is detected in a conversation, you might see a Suggestion appear underneath a message. For example, if a friend asks you to do them a favor, you might see “Add to Reminders” below the message.

By default there are five supported categories of Suggestions:

You can fully customize these to your own preferences and needs. Just go to Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Messages ⇾ Suggested Actions to disable whichever Suggestions you don’t want to see.

Historically, Apple TV has only ever supported user profiles on tvOS. It’s an odd limitation considering every other streaming service offers profiles across platforms.

Choosing a profile not only gives you personalized recommendations from Apple TV, it also lets you keep the ‘Continue Watching’ queue separate for each person. And if you’re setting up a profile for a child, you can set content restrictions too.

#3408. Stacy Keach, Mike Hammer and Blue Bloods Star, Dead at 85

Mike Hammer's Stacy Keach died at age 85 after a battle with a serious heart condition, his wife Malgosia Tomassi shared on Nov. 10.

The Mike Hammer alum died after a "long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure" at his family home in Magdalenka, Poland, his wife Malgosia Tomassi confirmed. He was 85.

"Stacy peacefully departed this world," she wrote in a Nov. 10 statement obtained by People. "He fought for so long, with extraordinary courage, determination and strength. He was a true warrior, facing his illness with the same remarkable spirit and resilience that defined his life."

Tomassi—with whom Keach shared son Shannon and daughter Karolina—reflected on her husband'sgolden life and his most award-winning roles: dad and husband of 40 years.

"Stacy was not only a legendary actor, admired and loved by audiences the world over, but also my beloved husband, my companion and the heart of our family," she continued. "His passing leaves an immeasurable emptiness in our lives. But his extraordinary spirit, his unforgettable voice and the love he gave so generously will remain with us forever."

Keach, born in 1941 to Mary Caine and theater director and actor Stacy Keach Sr., simply followed in his parents' acting footsteps.

"It started with my family really," he recalled on the Let's Dive In podcast in October 2020. "My dad, God love him, was an actor. My mom studied acting even though she never went into it professionally. I grew up in a theatrical family."

But that's not to say Caine and Keach Sr. were too keen on their son catching the acting bug.

"My parents did not want me to become an actor," he admitted. "Having been in the business, they thought it was an insecure profession. It's fraught with heartache."

Nevertheless, though they hoped Keach would pursue law or medicine, he knew he was meant to be on the stage and in front of a camera. So, after acting in school plays at age 12, he began his professional acting career at age 20 with roles on the stage at the 1962 Oregon Shakespeare Festival in The Comedy of Errors, Henry IV Part 2 and Coriolanus.

Appearing in several Broadway, Off-Broadway and local shows, he earned a Best Actor Tony nomination and Drama Desk Award for 1970's Indian. Keach—often lauded for his roles in William Shakespeare plays, including Hamlet and Macbeth—was also inducted into the Theater Hall of Fame in 2015.

While he continued in theater until 2018's Pamplona, he also earned several television roles, beginning with 1964's Channing before stepping into film with the 1967 TV movie The Winter's Tale. His first main character role came in 1997 as private investigator Mike Hammer in the titular series. He also appeared as a recurring character on Blue Bloods as Archbishop Kevin Kearns from 2016 to 2024.

Keach proved he was a jack of all trades, making his silver screen debut in 1968's The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter as Jake Blount. He even narrated The Duellists, Ridley Scott's directorial debut, in 1977. He would go on to star in other projects like Fat City, Up in Smoke and American History X. His final role was in 2025's Jay Kelly as the father of George Clooney's titular character.

Looking back at his career, the actor opted to focus on the positives, rather than any potential missed opportunities.

"I try not to dwell on mistakes and wallow in regret," he reflected in his 2013 memoir All in All: An Actor's Life On and Off the Stage. "If a script interests me, or a character intrigues me, or the cast features someone I've always wanted to work with, or the location is somewhere exotic, then sign me up."

#3405. HomeKit Weekly: Airversa’s Humelle is the Thread humidifier my house needs this winter

I love natural gas heat for a few reasons, but one is avoiding AUX heat from a heat pump and watching the bill rise. The downside is when the gas heat kicks on, the air in mt house is bone dry. My nose ends up being super dry for months. A humidifier like the Airversa Humelle works with Apple Home over Thread, so it can run itself based on what the air actually needs, and with the temps in my area getting into the 40s in the next week, I am glad I have one.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

The Airversa Humelle humidifier uses Thread, so it does join your existing Thread network via a HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K and communicates with Apple Home locally. In my experience, Thread accessories always respond faster and drop connections less than Wi-Fi-only ones, and they don’t add to the pile of devices fighting for airtime on your router either. Especially since most smart home devices are 2.4 GHz only.

Once the Airversa Humelle is paired with Apple Home, it appears in the Home app as a humidifier with a built-in temperature and humidity sensor. The latter sensor is the key for automations as well. You can set a target humidity level, and in Auto Mode, it ramps the mist up or down on its own to hold that number. For most people, that’s all the automation they’ll ever need. Set it to 45%, and it’ll run forever. By including that sensor in the device, you don’t need to pair it with a separate Apple Home-compatible humidity sensor for the automations. In fact, that is probably the only automation to run with this device.

The Humelle has a 3.2L tank that Airversa rates at up to 60 hours of runtime, and the mist reaches about 40 inches high, so it covers a bedroom or an average-sized living room pretty easily. It’s a top-fill design, which honestly is the only way these should be made at this point. Flipping them over always ends with some water on the floor.

Sleep Mode runs at 28dB, which is good for a baby’s room, etc. There’s a multicolor LED on the base that you can set to whatever color you want from the Home app or the Sleekpoint app, or turn off completely. There’s also a tray for essential oils if you want it to double as a diffuser to improve a room’s smell.

One thing to know about the Airversa Humelle going in: you’ll still want the Sleekpoint app for a few things, like setting a cleaning reminder that pings you when it’s time to rinse the tank. Day-to-day control lives in Apple Home, but the setup and maintenance features live in the manufacturer’s app. That’s just where Matter is as a protocol right now.

Natural gas heat dries out your inside air, and the Airversa Humelle fixes it. It allows me to avoid regretting my heating choice when I built my house. A humidifier that knows when the air is dry and turns on is the secret sauce. The Humelle does that in Apple Home with Thread, giving you a humidity sensor you can build the rest of your winter automations around. If you need a Thread Border Router, one of the new HomePod mini 2 units is the best to get started.

The Airversa Humelle is available on Amazon and directly from Airversa.

#3403. Firefox's New 'Mini Window' Feature Is a Game Changer for Productivity

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

For many of us, web browsing involves juggling dozens of tabs at once, and it's easy for important pages to get lost in the chaos. Now, Firefox has introduced something I think could help us multi-taskers: a "Mini Window." As highlighted by ZDNET's Jack Wallen, this new Firefox feature works like picture-in-picture overlays for videos—only here, that PiP displays a website.

"[Mini Window] lets you move a tab, or a selected section of a page, into a compact window that stays on top of your other windows while you browse," runs Mozilla's official blurb. "It's useful when you're multitasking and need to keep a few sources of information in view at once: Reference docs, a chat, a video call, a form you're filling out." As such, Mini Window doesn't necessarily replace running tabs side-by-side; rather, you can prioritize one tab in a full-size window, while keeping another page in view at all times.

This is a feature that's still in its early stages, and right now you can only get it in the "Nightly" version of Firefox, a very early beta version of the browser. Mozilla says it will push the feature to the full version of the browser later this month.

If you want to try this out as soon as possible, first install Firefox Nightly on your Mac or PC. Once up and running, you can launch Mini Window by right-clicking on a tab header and choosing Move Tab > Move to Mini Window. The tab shrinks and drops down to the lower right corner by default, staying on top of all other windows (not just Firefox). You can then scroll through the page and follow links as normal in the Mini Window—any links set to open in a new tab (manually or automatically) will launch in the main Firefox view, not the window overlay.

By dragging the title bar around, you can put your Mini Window anywhere you want on screen, and you can change its size by dragging the edges of the window too—so it doesn't necessarily have to be all that "mini." Firefox hides all buttons by default—including forward, backward, and refresh buttons, together with the address bar and buttons for closing the window or putting it back as a normal tab—though they appear when you hover over the Mini Window.

I'm finding the feature most useful when writing up articles where I need to refer to something else already on the web (so almost all of them), but there are a host of ways this can be used. It's particularly handy on a small laptop, where you don't necessarily have the screen space to put two tabs side by side, or when running a lower-priority window (like checking a social media site while reading an important document). No doubt, Firefox will continue to refine and improve the feature as it makes its way to the stable version of the browser, and it feels like something other browsers (looking at you, Google Chrome) might adopt as well in the near future. Eventually, using Mini Windows might become as common as opening up a long row of tabs.

#3402. Apple’s DOJ antitrust battle sparks disputes with Epic, Samsung, Oura, Roblox, more

Several tech companies are pushing back against subpoenas issued by Apple and the DOJ in their ongoing antitrust battle. Here are the details.

In March 2024, the Department of Justice and 15 states, plus the District of Columbia, filed a lawsuit accusing Apple of restricting competition, limiting interoperability with rival products, and making it harder for consumers to switch to competing devices. Apple denies these allegations.

Since then, despite recent reports of settlement talks happening behind the scenes, the two sides have clashed repeatedly over discovery, which is the pretrial process through which both sides exchange evidence relevant to the case.

As part of its effort to refute the DOJ’s arguments, Apple has subpoenaed several third-party companies and organizations, seeking documents and information relevant to its defense. That includes Epic Games, Samsung Electronics America, Meta, Oura, Garmin, Playco, Ultrahuman, PayPal, Match Group, and the Connectivity Standards Alliance, among others.

The DOJ and plaintiff states, in turn, have issued their own subpoenas, including to Roblox, Epic Games, Snap, and the Connectivity Standards Alliance, seeking evidence to support their allegations against Apple.

Google, Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, and Capital One are also named in legal documents.

In essence, both sides are trying to use data from Apple’s competitors and companies with which it has commercial relationships to establish how its policies affect competition, and whether those policies are justified or constitute anticompetitive behavior.

Over the past couple of days, multiple letters submitted to the court reveal disagreements over the scope of the subpoenas, the information being requested, and whether the companies should be required to produce certain documents.

Epic Games, for instance, argues that Apple’s requests for documents from three previous lawsuits (Epic v. Apple in the US, Epic v. Apple in Australia, and Epic v. Google in the US), along with extensive searches of internal files belonging to three senior executives, including its CEO, would be disproportionately burdensome.

Still, the company has offered to produce several categories of information, including Fortnite user and revenue data, contracts with Google and Samsung, and records relating to Apple’s Core Technology Fee.

Samsung, in turn, has agreed to search documents belonging to two executives, which the company says have yielded nearly 900,000 documents matching the agreed-upon search terms.

However, Apple wants to expand the searches to six additional executives, including Samsung Electronics America’s current and former CEOs, and obtain deposition transcripts from Samsung executives who testified in the DOJ’s antitrust lawsuit against Google.

The companies also disagree over whether Samsung Electronics America should be required to produce documents held by its South Korean parent company, which is a dispute we covered here before.

As for Oura, the company is pushing back on several fronts, including whether Apple should reimburse it for reviewing more than 32,000 additional documents, and whether it may withhold or redact certain information it considers trade secrets.

Garmin has raised similar objections to Apple’s requests for confidential financial and strategic information.

Roblox, which is the only company among these recent filings subpoenaed by the DOJ and plaintiff states rather than Apple or other plaintiffs, is disputing requests for information about its relationship with Apple and how Apple’s App Store policies are applied. The government, meanwhile, argues that the documents could help establish whether Apple consistently applies its App Store Guidelines to developers.

Another interesting dispute involves Japan-based instant gaming company Playco, which is resisting Apple’s requests for documents concerning its efforts to influence App Store policies, including lobbying activities.

Playco argues that producing these materials would violate its First Amendment rights, citing a 2021 court decision involving similar requests Apple made to Match Group.

Several of the companies have also requested until November 11 to continue negotiations before their disputes are formally declared at an impasse, potentially avoiding further court intervention.

All of this is happening against the backdrop of another dispute between Apple and the DOJ involving the company’s efforts to obtain documents from 14 federal agencies.

Although a special master has twice sided with Apple, the order remains on hold while the court considers the government’s appeal.

Find out when you might be able to watch the latest entry in the 'Godzilla' movie franchise at home

The King of the Monsters is back, and bigger than ever. “Godzilla Minus Zero,” the sequel to 2023’s Oscar-winning “Godzilla Minus One,” stomped into U.S. theaters on November 6, and it's been attracting kaiju-hungry viewers ever since.

Picking up in 1949, two years after the events of the first film, the sequel continues the story of the Shikishima family in a shattered post-war Japan as they face a new threat from the towering kaiju.

The film was shot specifically for IMAX, the first Japanese production ever to do so. It’s playing in theaters right now, but how long before you can watch it from the comfort of your own couch?

Since it just hit theaters, “Godzilla Minus Zero” isn’t available on any of the best streaming services just yet. Here’s the good news, though: based on how its predecessor rolled out, we can make a solid guess about when you’ll be able to rent, buy, and stream it at home.

If you’re curious about when to start planning for a giant lizard-stomping movie night, we’ve got the answers right here. Keep reading to find out.

North American distributor GKIDS hasn’t announced a digital release date yet, but if “Godzilla Minus Zero” follows the typical pattern for a theatrical release, it should hit premium video-on-demand (PVOD) about a month after it opens, at which point you can rent or buy it on platforms like Amazon and Apple TV.

Counting forward from its November 6 release, that points to a digital debut sometime in December 2026.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Physical media is a different story. It typically follows a few weeks after the digital release. “Godzilla Minus One” got a well-regarded 4K UHD and Blu-ray release, so its sequel is likely to get the same treatment.

That means a physical release for “Godzilla Minus Zero” around January 2027 seems like a reasonable bet, though nothing has been confirmed just yet. Since it was shot for IMAX, a 4K disc will be the closest most people get to that presentation at home.

As for streaming the movie with a subscription service, our strongest clue for a release date is how the first film was handled. “Godzilla Minus One” landed on Netflix in the U.S. about six months after its theatrical release, and with Netflix having become the streaming home for that movie, its sequel seems likely to follow suit.

If it sticks to the same roughly six-month timeline, “Godzilla Minus Zero” could reach Netflix sometime around May 2027. A ways off, yes, but good things are worth waiting for.

That said, nothing about the streaming date has been officially confirmed, so the exact platform and timing could still change. For now, the only way to see Godzilla’s latest rampage is on the biggest screen you can find. And you can still enjoy the other 30+ movies in the "Godzilla" franchise while waiting.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is a direct sequel to 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One,” so you'll want to make sure you're caught up before watching this movie. It was set in the ashes of World War II and followed Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), a former kamikaze pilot consumed by guilt after failing to act during an earlier Godzilla attack.

Back in Tokyo, he builds a family with Noriko (Minami Hamabe) and an orphaned child, only for a mutated Godzilla to rise from the sea and lay waste to the city. A group of civilian veterans ultimately got together to take the monster down and succeeded, so you'll want to watch that play out before diving into this movie.

“Minus Zero” picks the story back up in 1949, two years after those events. The Shikishima family has started to rebuild amid a Japan still struggling to recover, but the peace doesn’t last, and Godzilla returns to threaten the country once again.

With the memory of the last devastation still fresh, a disaster-response team scrambles to prepare for the renewed menace, and the Shikishimas are pulled right back into the fight for survival. And yes, it's just as epic in scale as the last movie, so you'll want to catch this one whether you see it at home or on the big screen.

#3397. These Signature Sony Headphones Are Under $200 Ahead of Black Friday

The Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones are the most recent entry in Sony's 1000X series, which has been around since 2016. They're the best over-ear headphones in terms of audio quality currently on the market—but not everyone can (or needs to) drop nearly half a grand on headphones.

The WH-1000XM5 are a generation older and were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (down from the original $399.99) during Amazon's early Black Friday sale. That 50% off brings it down to the lowest price they've ever reached, according to price-tracking tools, a good deal for premium headphones that still sound incredible, even in 2026.

I have been a loyal customer of the 1000X line for many years; they're my go-to headphones for most activities. The WH-1000XM5 received an "outstanding" review from PCMag for their top-notch audio quality and exceptional audio when using the best-in-class active noise cancellation. The headphones are also well-designed to be comfortable for long listening sessions. The ear controls use tapping and swiping, which isn't my favorite, but it's what all modern headphones are moving toward. There's a companion app that lets you adjust your EQ settings to your liking, including what the swiping and tapping functions do.

These headphones also have a stereo 3.5mm connection, which is perfect for those who want to use a cable and not worry about battery life. And speaking of battery life, Sony says you can expect about 30 hours, but it will vary depending on your use of ANC. They are compatible with AAC, LDAC, and SBC codecs and have multipoint connection, meaning you can pair them with more than one device at the same time.

Personally, I think the value for the money you get with the XM5 for $198 is better than paying full price for the XM6. If you're looking to get ahead of the Black Friday chaos and secure an amazing deal on great headphones, this is it.

#3395. watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love

watchOS 27.3 arrived this week in beta alongside iOS 27.3, with a major new feature for the latest Apple Watch models: Siri Recap, which I’m already really loving.

If you bought an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4 this fall, there are two exclusive new features coming in watchOS 27.3: Siri Recap and Live Rewind.

Both ‘Audio Intelligence’ features were announced at Apple’s September keynote, but just debuted in beta this week.

Siri Recap in particular has stirred some controversy. Here’s what the feature does, per Apple:

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Siri Recaps can be set to automatically delete after a period of up to 7 days unless you choose to explicitly save them.

It’s understandable why users would be concerned. Once enabled, Siri Recap can turn your Apple Watch into a device that’s always listening and often takes notes on what it hears.

Speaking strictly of the functionality of Siri Recap itself, however, I’ve been very impressed.

I enabled Siri Recap after installing the iOS and watchOS 27.3 betas on Tuesday. When I checked the first recaps on Wednesday inside the Siri app, I was blown away.

Siri had created a record of the things I’d done Tuesday afternoon and evening with remarkable accuracy and detail, as seen above.

One example that especially shocked me: after shopping for Christmas decorations with my family, Siri documented the size of a table runner we looked at. The thing is, I had no memory of anyone even mentioning its size. My wife must have, but despite me missing it, Siri wrote it down.

Another fun one: Thursday morning during breakfast, my son wanted to listen some music on our HomePod. Later that day, I found that the songs we’d listened to were saved at the bottom of my latest recap.

It’s still very early days with Siri Recap, which is only in beta right now, but what I’ve seen this week has been really exciting. And so far at least, I’ve seen zero information in a recap that I’d consider too sensitive to be included.

What’s your take on Siri Recap? Have you given it a try? Let us know in the comments.

#3394. Five Hacks Every Una Watch User Should Know

The Una watch is pretty much made to be hackable, with its interchangeable parts and open development environment. But it’s also pretty barebones at launch, without many features available yet. However, here are five things I’ve discovered I can do with it—and I hope to expand this list quite a bit as the device and its community mature.

Because the Una watch has a regular USB-C port, you don’t need to remember any specific cable, dongle, or adapter to charge it. I knew that, but it didn’t occur to me until recently that I didn’t need a computer or a wall outlet to plug into the other end. I was able to take a USB-C to USB-C cable—the same kind I might carry around to charge my phone—and plug one end into my watch and the other into my phone. It charged!

(You can also charge some other devices from a phone, including an Apple Watch, but you’d need to carry around that specific adapter, which is why nobody bothers.)

The Una watch doesn’t have any built-in sleep tracking, but a few community-built apps aim to provide it. The Slumber app, for example, will let you know how long you slept and compare your most recent bedtime with when you usually get to bed. There are no sleep stages (honestly: refreshing, since watches are rarely good at this anyway), and the analysis is done on the watch itself.

But if what you’re really hoping for is a recovery score or an overnight HRV reading, the HabitLab app combines that with habit tracking. Every evening, the watch will buzz and ask you to check off which habits or factors played into your day: Alcohol and late meals are among the options, and the watch will automatically detect morning or evening workouts to add them to the list. In the morning, the watch asks you how you slept, and then it gives you a score based on your resting heart rate, HRV, and your subjective rating.

The app is supposed to be able to put together trends and insights from this data, but I haven’t managed to get it to do this. Maybe it’s waiting for more data (I’ve been using it a little over a week), or maybe it’s just buggy.

By contrast, the barcode app worked even better than I expected it to. It’s meant for a parkrun barcode; each participant in the free weekly 5K has a number that you can use to check your results online. But it works just as well for other barcodes.

I installed the Barcode app and entered the number for my library card. Perhaps because of the watch’s MIP screen, I found this barcode scanned more reliably than any barcodes I’ve previously tried to use on a watch. The library scanner picked it up just fine on the first try, and a phone-based scanner also had no problem with it. You can store up to six barcodes, so I’ve also entered a few others, like my grocery discount card.

The app supports QR codes as well as regular barcodes, and to enter a QR code, you just type in a shortened URL. (It needs to be 22 characters or less.) This means that the Barcode app is also a QR code creator, a nifty feature indeed.

Seeing how soon the sun sets is a bit of a downer as we leave daylight saving time and get into the dark winter months, but it’s also helpful in planning. The Sun & Moon Face puts a graphic on your wrist that shows how far along the sun is in its trajectory across the sky for the day. When evening is approaching, you’ll see just how little time you have left.

The app grabs your GPS location once a day, which means that for the first few hours I wore it, the sunrise and sunset times were incorrectly listed as 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. But as long as you aren’t flying to a drastically new location every day, the app does the job just fine. As a bonus, it changes the color of the screen’s sky to show daylight, nighttime, or sunrise/sunset colors.

If you want to hack this hackable watch, you might as well take the plunge and try to build something yourself. Instructions are here to download the development tools for Windows, Mac, or Linux, and there are tutorials for different features you might want to use and implement. There are also about a dozen example apps you can build on, including activity trackers, watch faces, and glances. I'm not much of a coder myself, but this is the friendliest setup I've seen for someone to get into building their own apps for a watch.

#3393. 'American Idol' Alum Caleb Flynn Barred From Collecting Murdered Wife's Life Insurance

Caleb Flynn may be spending the rest of his life behind bars for murdering his wife ... but now there's a new fight over her $100,000 life insurance policy, which named him as the sole beneficiary ... TMZ has learned.

According to court documents, obtained by TMZ, Banner Life Insurance Company filed a lawsuit Tuesday in Ohio federal court ... asking a judge to decide who gets the money from Ashley Flynn's policy.

Here's the kicker ... the insurance company says Caleb was listed as the policy's owner and sole beneficiary when it was issued in March 2016, nearly 10 years before he murdered Ashley ... and no backup beneficiary was named.

But, according to the docs, there's a major problem for Caleb ... the insurance company notes that Ohio's so-called "slayer statute" prevents someone convicted of murder from profiting off their victim's death, meaning he's legally barred from collecting the cash.

Banner says the payout now totals more than $100K with interest and premium refunds ... and is looking to hand the money over to the court so a judge can sort out who gets it.

The lawsuit also names Caleb's parents, his brother, Ashley's parents, her sister and brother-in-law, and the couple's two daughters as defendants ... though the company isn't accusing them of wrongdoing. It simply wants the court to determine who is entitled to the money.

As TMZ previously reported ... Caleb was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole in October after being convicted of shooting Ashley twice in the back of the head and staging the scene to look like a break-in.

His two daughters later ripped into him in emotional statements read at sentencing ... with one declaring she'd never visit him in prison.

Now a judge will have to decide where Ashley's life insurance money goes ... and presumably enforce the slayer statute to prevent Caleb from collecting the proceeds.

A post shared by Tom's Guide (@tomsguide)

Unlike the Always Home Cam, which had a large protuberance on its underside, the Ring Drone Cam looks somewhat like the DJI Neo; it has a small rectangular body with four encaged rotors. Weighing 265 grams (5.8 ounces), it's lighter than most phones. While the demo unit I saw was white, the actual product will be a light gray. The Drone Cam docks and recharges in a square base station.

The drone has a 2K camera with two LEDs on either side, which it uses to light up your home as it's patrolling at night.

When activated, the Drone Cam lifts up out of its base, rises to about 4-5 feet in the air, and then proceeds at a stately pace as it moves throughout your home. Even though it's small, you'll definitely notice its presence, as its rotors make a very loud, high-pitched whine.

Knowing how my dog reacts to a vacuum cleaner, I can only imagine his response to this thing flying around the house. Don't even ask what my cats might think.

The Drone Cam navigates your home using a combination of an Alexa Home map (similar to what you'll see on one of Amazon's smart displays) and the setup process, whereby you hold the drone and carry it through your house, taking it on a trip of where you'd like to go. Ring says the Drone Cam can cover multiple stories of your home.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Unlike previous, unreleased versions, the Drone Cam relies on the cloud for navigation, using Amazon's AI Pilot to get around and interpret what the drone is seeing. If the drone loses its connection, it's designed to immediately land — which is why it's important that you make sure its flight path doesn't go over any delicate objects.

The Ring Drone Cam can be programmed to make regular patrols of your house, or to respond to a particular event — such as a window or a door sensor tripping, or a water leak detector going off. Using the Amazon Alexa Home map, it can fly to the location of the event, and give you a live view of what's happening.

Remember the Amazon Astro? Ring took its parent company's home robot and redesigned the internals to make it a security robot for small businesses and enterprise customers.

Now called the Ring Rover Cam, it's meant to patrol warehouses and stores, and alert you if it detects an intruder. Like the Astro, it has a telescoping camera, but Ring also added a light on the back, which lets you see where the robot is at a glance, and flashes red and screams out a siren when there's an unwanted guest.

The Ring Rover Cam will cost $999, and will ship on December 16.

I am more than a bit skeptical about having a camera drone flying through my house. For starters, my pets get nervous enough around vacuum cleaners; I can only imagine how they'd react to a high-pitched drone flying about. And, the idea of a drone autonomously roaming around, potentially recording everything, feels a bit dystopian.

And, if you want the Ring Drone Camera to be able to access every corner of your house, you'll also have to make sure you leave every door wide open before you leave. And, the drone moves so slowly that if it's set up on one side of your house, by the time it responds to, say, a window breaking on the other side, the potential intruder could be long gone.

I can see some utility in it — I don't have, nor do I want, security cameras in every corner of my house, so I can see it being handy if a sensor is tripped in my basement. But, I'm still not sold on the concept; maybe trying it out will change my mind.

What do you think? Would you want a drone security camera for the inside of your house? Take our poll, and let me know in the comments.
